title: Lightweight Path-Aware Frontier Re-ranking for LiDAR-Based UAV Exploration
authors: Duc Manh Do,Thanh Nguyen Canh,Ngoc Minh Do,Mai Thanh Thai,Xiem HoangVan
comment: Accepted for presentation at RIVF 2026 (20th International Conference on Computing and Communication Technologies)
abstract: Autonomous 3D exploration with UAVs requires efficient target selection under limited flight time and onboard computation. In conventional Euclidean-distance-based frontier pipelines, geometric distance may poorly represent the actual collision-free travel cost in cluttered environments, leading to inefficient frontier choices. This paper presents a lightweight path-aware frontier re-ranking method for LiDAR-based UAV exploration. The method first retains a small top-NN set of promising frontier candidates using a lightweight utility function and then applies time-bounded RRT* planning to estimate their feasible path costs for re-ranking. The path generated for the selected frontier is further reused for navigation to reduce redundant global planning. Experiments in three warehouse-like environments show that the proposed method consistently produces shorter exploration trajectories than conventional frontier baselines, with traveled-distance reductions of up to 14.1%, while reducing exploration time by up to 9.5% in two environments and remaining competitive in the third. The method maintains map detail comparable to the conventional OctoMap-based baseline, demonstrating an effective trade-off between exploration efficiency and mapping quality.
introduction:
Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) have attracted increasing attention for autonomous exploration due to their high mobility in three-dimensional environments and their ability to access complex or hazardous areas [1, 2]. These properties make UAVs suitable for applications such as search and rescue, infrastructure inspection, environmental monitoring, warehousing, and large-scale 3D mapping [3]. In these scenarios, autonomous 3D exploration enables a UAV to incrementally acquire information about an unknown environment and construct a spatial map for subsequent navigation and decision-making tasks [1].

In a typical autonomous exploration process, the robot repeatedly determines where to move next based on the currently available map. During flight, onboard sensors such as LiDAR and cameras provide measurements that are integrated into a 3D representation for mapping, planning, and navigation [4, 5]. The planner then identifies informative unexplored regions, selects the next target, and generates a safe trajectory toward it. For UAVs, this process is particularly challenging because exploration must be performed in large three-dimensional spaces under limited flight time and onboard computational resources [4, 6].

Existing autonomous exploration approaches can be broadly categorized into sampling-based next-best-view (NBV) methods and frontier-based methods [7, 8]. NBV methods sample candidate viewpoints or motion sequences and evaluate their expected information gain, enabling explicit reasoning about visibility and map uncertainty. Several approaches further integrate RRT or RRT∗ to search for informative viewpoints or feasible trajectories in partially known environments [9, 8]. While effective, evaluating a large number of sampled candidates and trajectories can introduce considerable online computational cost, particularly in large 3D environments [8, 1].

Frontier-based exploration offers an alternative paradigm by directing the robot toward frontiers, i.e., boundaries between known free space and unknown regions [10, 7]. Existing methods improve different components of this paradigm. Batinovi’c et al. [11] proposed a multi-resolution frontier-based planner that exploits the octree structure of OctoMap for efficient frontier detection and clustering, while Caiza et al. [2] introduced a frontier collector strategy that stores, validates, and reuses detected frontiers to improve exploration completeness and safety. Several depth-camera-based UAV exploration frameworks further incorporate more sophisticated planning mechanisms. FUEL [12] combines incremental frontier structures with hierarchical planning, Dai et al. [13] incorporate travel-time-aware evaluation of candidate viewpoints, and SCOPE [6] employs a skeleton graph with hierarchical on-demand planning. In contrast, EPIC [4] is a LiDAR-based framework that directly exploits point-cloud observations and maintains an incremental topological representation for large-scale exploration. These approaches demonstrate the effectiveness of path-, time-, and topology-aware reasoning for autonomous UAV exploration.

Nevertheless, conventional frontier-based pipelines that select targets using Euclidean distance and information gain can still underestimate the travel cost of navigating around obstacles. As illustrated in Fig. 1, a geometrically close frontier may require a long collision-free detour, while a more distant frontier may be reachable via a shorter path. Although path-aware and time-aware exploration have been investigated in previous work, incorporating feasible path estimates into a conventional frontier-selection pipeline raises a practical trade-off: planning for more candidates can improve the travel-cost estimate but increases computational effort. Evaluating every detected frontier with a sampling-based planner is therefore not always desirable.

To address this trade-off, we propose a two-stage path-aware frontier re-ranking strategy that augments an existing LiDAR-based frontier exploration pipeline without redesigning its mapping and frontier-generation components. First, candidates are ranked using a low-cost utility based on information gain and Euclidean distance, and only the top-NN candidates are retained. Second, time-bounded RRT∗ planning estimates feasible path costs for the retained candidates, which are then re-ranked accordingly. The feasible path associated with the selected frontier is also reused for navigation when valid, avoiding an otherwise redundant planning request. The contribution is a bounded, selective use of established planning tools within frontier selection, rather than a new frontier detector or motion planner.

The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

A two-stage path-aware frontier re-ranking strategy that combines low-cost top-NN candidate filtering with time-bounded RRT∗ path-cost estimation, restricting expensive path evaluation to a small shortlist.

A reusable-path mechanism that forwards the validated path obtained during frontier evaluation to navigation, avoiding a repeated global planning request when possible.

An evaluation in three simulated warehouse-like environments, including comparisons with existing exploration systems, a path-reuse ablation, and sensitivity analyses of exploration time, travel distance, and map detail.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II presents the proposed method. Section III reports the experimental results. Finally, Section IV concludes the paper and discusses future work.

1. A two-stage path-aware frontier re-ranking strategy that combines low-cost top-NN candidate filtering with time-bounded RRT∗ path-cost estimation, restricting expensive path evaluation to a small shortlist.

2. A reusable-path mechanism that forwards the validated path obtained during frontier evaluation to navigation, avoiding a repeated global planning request when possible.

3. An evaluation in three simulated warehouse-like environments, including comparisons with existing exploration systems, a path-reuse ablation, and sensitivity analyses of exploration time, travel distance, and map detail.

title: CucumberVision at the Edge: Accuracy, Throughput, and Energy of RGB-D Cucumber Sizing on Jetson Orin Nano and Raspberry Pi 4
authors: Manveen Kaur,Rajmeet Singh,Saeed Mozaffari,Majid Ahmadi,Shahpour Alirezaee
abstract: Non-contact fruit sizing from RGB-D imagery reaches sub-centimetre accuracy on workstation hardware, but in-field grading requires the same pipeline to run on a low-power single-board computer, and the cost of that transition is rarely reported. We deploy a curvature-aware cucumber length-measurement pipeline YOLO26n detection, prompt-based segmentation and a medial arc spline estimator on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and a Raspberry Pi 4, and characterise both against an RTX 3050 Ti workstation by replaying 50 identical greenhouse captures of 7 specimens, with specimen-level cluster-bootstrap statistics. Accuracy is preserved: mean absolute error (MAE) is 0.58 cm (95% CI 0.46–0.69) on both the workstation and the Jetson at matched precision, with a paired difference of zero. TensorRT FP16 compilation cuts Jetson detection latency 2.57×2.57\times, giving two operating points on one board: 72 ms per fruit at 0.84 cm, or 2.74 s at 0.64 cm. Four ablations map the design space. For prompted segmentation backends, measurement accuracy is fixed by the backend and reproduces across platforms to within 0.01 cm, while its cost is fixed by the platform and varies 214×214\times, so the two choices are separable. Whole-graph INT8 quantization of the NMS-free detection head fails structurally, returning no detections, because one output tensor carries both pixel coordinates and confidences; we show that no calibration strategy can avoid this. Excluding the head restores function at 1.37×1.37\times. Energy per fruit is 42.2 J on the Jetson, and its 7 W mode consumes 73% more than its 15 W mode. The Raspberry Pi with MobileSAM costs 2.5×2.5\times more per fruit than the Jetson with SAM despite drawing 47% less power, and it runs without thermal throttling under sustained load. The results define an accuracy–throughput–energy envelope with three non-dominated configurations and give rules for selecting among them.
introduction:
Fruit length is the primary grading criterion in commercial greenhouse cucumber production, and non-contact measurement from RGB-D imagery offers a route to automating it. Depth-camera sizing has been demonstrated for several crops [Géné-Mola et al., 2021, Géné-Mola and others, 2023], and our previous originating study established that a curvature-aware estimator fitting a cubic spline through the three-dimensional cross-section centroid spine of a segmented fruit and integrating arc length attains sub-centimetre accuracy under canopy conditions [Kaur et al., 2026]. That result was obtained on workstation hardware with a discrete GPU.

Practical grading does not take place at a workstation. A scouting platform moving between rows carries a single-board computer with a few watts of power budget, no discrete GPU and, in the cheapest case, no active cooling. Whether a method that works on a laptop also works there is not a foregone conclusion: prompt-based segmentation may be one to two orders of magnitude more expensive on embedded silicon [Kirillov and others, 2023, Zhang and others, 2023], reduced-precision arithmetic may or may not preserve the geometry the estimator depends on [Wu et al., 2020], and sustained inference on a passively cooled board may throttle. Existing edge benchmarks in agriculture report detection accuracy and frame rate on a single platform [Alqahtani et al., 2024, Sapkota et al., 2025], but not the joint accuracy–throughput–energy behaviour of a complete measurement pipeline, and not the interaction between segmentation backend and platform.

This paper reports the deployment of that pipeline on two representative embedded platforms an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B and characterises the resulting design space through four controlled ablations. All three platforms replay the same greenhouse captures against the same ground truth, so every reported difference is attributable to the deployment configuration rather than to sensing. The contributions are:

Working deployments of the complete measurement pipeline on a Jetson Orin Nano and a Raspberry Pi 4, with accuracy shown to be statistically indistinguishable from the workstation baseline, together with the TensorRT and ONNX Runtime inference paths that make them practical.

A segmentation-backend ablation establishing that, for prompted backends, measurement accuracy is determined by the mask source and transfers between platforms, while segmentation cost is determined by the platform and does not making backend selection and hardware selection separable design decisions.

Identification of a structural, rather than numerical, failure mode in post-training INT8 quantization of NMS-free detection heads, with a proof that no calibration strategy can avoid it, a fix, and its measured cost.

A characterisation of the deployment design space spline smoothing, power mode, energy per measurement and sustained thermal behaviour yielding an explicit accuracy–throughput–energy envelope and rules for selecting an operating point within it.

title: Mechanical Interaction Sensing for Robotic Kiwifruit Handling with an Optoelectronic Soft Suction Cup
authors: Romina Adhami,Ebrahim Shahabi,Alessio Mondini,Samuel M. Youssef,Cosimo Della Santina,Gualtiero Volpe,Barbara Mazzolai
abstract:

This study investigates an optoelectronic soft suction cup with a kiwifruit-specific bicomponent design for estimating interaction forces during contact with real fruit.

A simple monotonic mapping from the mean optical response alone achieves R2=0.925±0.005R^{2}=0.925\pm 0.005, showing that substantial force-related information is already present in the optical response.
Leave-one-collection-day-out validation remains strong (R2=0.955±0.031R^{2}=0.955\pm 0.031), supporting robustness across acquisition sessions.
As an exploratory secondary analysis, binary Soft/Firm classification from compression-test reference labels achieves moderate balanced accuracy (≈0.705\approx 0.705) under grouped held-out-fruit validation, while finer three-class grading shows limited performance.
introduction:
Post-harvest handling of delicate fruit must combine gentle mechanical contact with awareness of the interaction forces that develop at the interface.
Overloading damages tissue; underloading yields unstable grasps.
Kiwifruit is a demanding test case: the surface is curved, compliant, often irregular, and varies strongly among individual fruits.

Soft robotic end-effectors address part of this challenge by conforming to produce and distributing contact pressure [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6].
Compliance alone, however, does not provide quantitative feedback on interactions.
Embedding sensors in soft structures is therefore attractive, but the sensor must remain informative when the contacted object is a real fruit rather than a laboratory plate or elastomer sample.

Optical and optoelectronic sensing enables deformation measurement in compliant structures without rigid contact-face transducers [7], while sensorized suction cups combine grasping and sensing [8].

The optoelectronic suction-cup sensing principle adopted here was previously demonstrated for estimating contact force and direction on controlled surfaces and was integrated into an underwater soft robotic arm [9].
However, that work did not evaluate the quantitative estimation of the interaction force across biologically variable fruit.
Other studies have investigated tactile force sensing and fruit handling using vision-based [10] and triboelectric [11] approaches, while piezoresistive sensing has been applied to kiwifruit stiffness estimation [12].
What remains insufficiently characterized is the performance of this optoelectronic suction-cup architecture when adapted for contact with real kiwifruit, particularly its force-estimation accuracy and variability across unseen fruits and acquisition conditions.
This study addresses that gap by evaluating contact-mode force estimation under fruit-grouped and leave-one-collection-day-out validation.

Building on the previously established optoelectronic sensing principle, the contributions of this study are:

Adaptation and attachment-force characterization of a soft suction cup for kiwifruit contact, including geometry and material screening and evaluation of a bicomponent Dragon Skin 10 body with an Ecoflex 00-10 fruit-contacting rim (Figs. 2 and 3).

Quantitative interaction-force estimation from optical signals collected during contact without active suction on 70 real kiwifruits, comparing simple and nonlinear models under grouped held-out-fruit validation and examining error variability across fruits, force ranges, loading/unloading phases, and acquisition days (Table II and Figs. 8 and 9).

Exploratory evaluation of fruit firmness classification from the same optical signals using compression-test reference labels and grouped held-out-fruit validation.

1. Adaptation and attachment-force characterization of a soft suction cup for kiwifruit contact, including geometry and material screening and evaluation of a bicomponent Dragon Skin 10 body with an Ecoflex 00-10 fruit-contacting rim (Figs. 2 and 3).

2. Quantitative interaction-force estimation from optical signals collected during contact without active suction on 70 real kiwifruits, comparing simple and nonlinear models under grouped held-out-fruit validation and examining error variability across fruits, force ranges, loading/unloading phases, and acquisition days (Table II and Figs. 8 and 9).

3. Exploratory evaluation of fruit firmness classification from the same optical signals using compression-test reference labels and grouped held-out-fruit validation.

title: Can LLMs Debug Robots by Editing Their Weights?
authors: Jusheng Zhang,Keze Wang,Liang Lin
abstract: A language model can repair a robot policy’s lexical instruction grounding by editing just 65 token-embedding rows. We bring weight-space programming to robot foundation policies: GPT-6 Astra reads weights and uses a CPU workspace and budgeted simulator feedback, without gradient updates or new demonstrations. Three independent sessions on π0.5\pi_{0.5} all improve success on 765 held-out paraphrases; the best raises success from 86.3% to 92.0% (48 repairs, four regressions; exact paired p=1.31×10−10p=1.31\times 10^{-10}). Among the 335 instructions containing edited tokens, success rises from 74.3% to 87.5%; the other 430 episodes have zero outcome changes. Matched random-direction edits do not help. Full replacement using the editor’s own lexicon explains much of the gain but produces more regressions; its direct difference from the editor is not significant at 0.05. Across 13 further robot sessions, the editor declines 12 candidates; the sole retained edit does not show a significant held-out gain. Separately, benchmark metadata lowers FastWAM success from 70.0% to 48.6%, while the evaluated VLA’s aggregate rate is unchanged. The evidence supports precise lexical repair, not general acquisition of missing robot capabilities.
introduction:
A language model can repair some robot-policy failures by changing a few rows of the policy’s weights. Our strongest result changes 65 token-embedding rows: success rises from 74.3% to 87.5% on 335 held-out instructions containing an edited token, with no outcome changes on the other 430 instructions. The manipulation skill is already available; the edit changes which language reaches it.

Consider a policy that turns on the stove under its canonical instruction, but picks up a plate when asked to “activate the cooking appliances heat source” (Figure 1). Both actions are familiar tasks in the same scene. The failure is a mismatch between wording and the task represented by the policy, rather than the absence of a stove-turning behavior. A camera perturbation or a dropped object presents a different debugging problem: changing the interpretation of a word may not supply the required visual or recovery behavior.

Takehi et al. [21] introduced weight-space programming: a general-purpose LLM inspects and changes another network’s parameters directly, without gradient optimization. Their demonstrations span games and language models, and motivate a distinction between removing an obstacle to an existing ability and creating a new ability. We bring this experimental setup to robot foundation policies. We test both whether an editor can find a useful intervention and whether it declines interventions that fail its own checks.

GPT-6 Astra receives policy weights, a persistent CPU Python workspace, and a budgeted forward tool. It can inspect tensors and write replacements, but cannot train the policy or change the deployment program. Practice rollouts and probes guide editing; held-out variants are unavailable to the editor. Across three independent sessions on π0.5\pi_{0.5} [20], Astra converges on sparse lexical remapping. All three submitted edits improve held-out paraphrase success. The best changes less than 0.004% of exported parameters and raises overall success from 86.3% to 92.0% on all 765 held-out language variants.

The boundary matters as much as the gain. In 13 additional sessions over FastWAM [24], LIBERO-Plus [6], LIBERO-PRO [27], and LIBERO-RECOVER [12], the editor declines 12 final candidates. The sole retained candidate has no significant held-out gain. Two archived, declined candidates do have positive aggregate estimates; we report them rather than treating final-directory contents as accepted repairs. These observations support a limited, practical form of debugging, not a general impossibility theorem about acquiring capabilities.

Our contributions are:

A reproducible lexical repair of a VLA: three independent editing sessions, one fixed held-out population, and outcome changes confined to the edited-token instructions.

Controls that separate direction from edit size and full replacement from the editor’s interpolation, together with an explicit account of what a dictionary control already explains.

A 16-session record of retained and declined edits, plus a separate finding that benchmark instruction metadata strongly affects FastWAM but not the evaluated π0.5\pi_{0.5} checkpoint in aggregate.

1. A reproducible lexical repair of a VLA: three independent editing sessions, one fixed held-out population, and outcome changes confined to the edited-token instructions.

2. Controls that separate direction from edit size and full replacement from the editor’s interpolation, together with an explicit account of what a dictionary control already explains.

3. A 16-session record of retained and declined edits, plus a separate finding that benchmark instruction metadata strongly affects FastWAM but not the evaluated π0.5\pi_{0.5} checkpoint in aggregate.

title: Horizon-Coupled Obstacle Guidance for Relative-Action Diffusion Policies
authors: Guangyuan Wang,Haishan Xia,Zitao Zhang,Kejia Chen,Yuanchen Sun,Zhenguo Sun,Donghao Zhang,Yu Zhang,Alois Knoll
abstract:
Real-world robot deployment requires adapting learned policies to unseen obstacles without collecting
new demonstrations or retraining. Existing policy-level guidance often applies obstacle corrections independently at individual horizon steps,
which may address local obstacle violations but fail to coordinate the action sequence into a complete, task-directed detour.
How obstacle responses should be propagated across the
action horizon to coordinate complete, task-directed avoidance motion remains underexplored.
We introduce an inference-time obstacle-guidance framework for pretrained relative-action diffusion
policies. It rolls out cumulative relative actions into a workspace trajectory, evaluates obstacle
interactions along the trajectory with an SDF-based obstacle model, and propagates each obstacle response to all contributing
action increments during denoising. Real-robot experiments across seven obstacle-constrained scenarios spanning
four manipulation tasks show that our method achieves 105/140 (75.0%)
collision-free task successes, compared with 8/140 (5.7%) for
absolute-action point-wise guidance. Ablations show that the relative-action horizon-coupled formulation provides the
larger observed improvement across both obstacle models.
introduction:
Diffusion Policy (DP) [1] has emerged as a prominent
framework for visuomotor manipulation, owing to its ability to model multimodal
action distributions from expert demonstrations and generate observation-conditioned action chunks for
closed-loop control. Recent 3D variants [2, 3, 4, 5] incorporate explicit 3D scene
representations to improve spatial generalization across complex manipulation
tasks. These advances strengthen the potential of DPs for deployment in complex manipulation environments.
However, real-world deployment may introduce obstacles that are absent from the expert demonstrations utilized to train
the policy, and these advances do not by themselves enable the pretrained policy to adapt its motion around
them. Such obstacles can block the learned motion even when
the manipulation objective remains unchanged. A straightforward solution
is to redesign the robot motion for each obstacle configuration, but repeated
redesign requires substantial engineering time, human effort, and deployment cost.
Adapting the sampled actions of a trained DP to deployment-time obstacles without
retraining would avoid these repeated costs and make policy deployment more scalable.

A practical way to address this deployment challenge is to adapt the actions
sampled by the trained DP to newly introduced obstacles. Inference-time policy
steering [6] provides this mechanism without retraining the base
policy. One route learns an auxiliary steering policy over diffusion noise through
reinforcement learning [7], requiring reward signals and
additional interaction for policy optimization. In the reported real-world setting,
this interaction is collected through hardware rollouts, which may involve unsafe actions
and potential collisions. Such interaction makes reinforcement-learning-based steering
less suitable for safety-critical deployment-time adaptation. A second route modifies reverse
diffusion with gradients derived from externally specified robot
objectives [8, 9, 10]. Obstacle
geometry directly defines such a differentiable objective, eliminating
auxiliary-policy training and reward-bearing exploration. We therefore adopt
denoising guidance.

Existing denoising-guidance methods demonstrate that safety constraints can
be incorporated into reverse sampling. Planner-centric methods such as
MPD [11], SafeDiffuser [12],
DPCC [13], and Constrained
Diffusers [14] formulate obstacle avoidance as
constrained state- or joint-trajectory generation under specified state or
goal conditions. Such formulations address state-to-goal motion planning
rather than adapting the action generation of a pretrained visuomotor policy
from evolving visual feedback. Extending obstacle avoidance from this
planner-centric setting to learned manipulation under visual feedback therefore
requires guidance at the policy level.
Lan-o3dp [15] and EmbodiSteer [16]
guide action chunks from pretrained visuomotor policies. Both apply obstacle corrections independently at individual
horizon steps, without explicitly coordinating avoidance responses across the action horizon. Such step-wise corrections
may address local obstacle violations but fail to organize the action sequence into a complete detour that both avoids
the obstacle and continues toward the task goal. How obstacle responses should be propagated across the
action horizon to coordinate complete, task-directed avoidance motion remains underexplored.

To close this gap, we introduce horizon-coupled obstacle guidance for
pretrained relative-action DPs in static environments. Relative end-effector targets are
formed by recursively integrating positional increments from the preceding
target [17]. From this recurrence, we derive a
horizon-coupled guidance structure in which each predicted position depends on all
preceding increments. At each denoising step, our method rolls out the
estimated action chunk into a predicted end-effector trajectory in the
workspace for obstacle evaluation and propagates each response to every
increment contributing to the affected position. This horizon-coupled propagation
coordinates actions across the horizon to form the avoidance motion. The frozen DP supplies the learned
task behavior throughout guided sampling.

In summary, our main contributions are:
(1) a horizon-coupled obstacle-guidance formulation for relative-action diffusion policies that propagates obstacle responses across the action horizon, enabling coordinated, task-directed avoidance motion rather than isolated local corrections;
(2) an inference-time guided-sampling framework that applies this cross-step propagation to predicted end-effector trajectories during denoising, allowing deployment-time obstacle constraints to reshape the action sequence without policy retraining;
(3) real-robot validation across seven obstacle-constrained scenarios spanning four manipulation tasks, achieving 105/140 (75.0%) collision-free task successes compared with 8/140 (5.7%) for absolute-action point-wise guidance.

title: MDF++: Visuo-Tactile World Action Model with End-to-end Representation Learning
authors: Zixuan Huang,Jinhao Yu,Zachary Charlick,Dmitry Berenson
comment: Corl 2026
abstract:
Recently, world-action models (WAMs) have emerged as a powerful framework for robot manipulation. By jointly modeling action generation and future observation prediction, WAMs can act and anticipate the outcomes of the actions. However, existing WAMs typically rely on frozen pretrained encoders trained with reconstruction, which may not produce representations well suited for robot control.
In this paper, we tackle the problem of learning physically-grounded, control-relevant representations for WAMs. We propose MDF++, a visuo-tactile world-action model that learns latent representations of multisensory observations end-to-end with a diffusion backbone. While naive joint training can lead to feature collapse, MDF++ introduces a multi-task learning strategy that leverages cross-modal correlations to learn task-relevant representations. We evaluate MDF++ on a suite of contact-rich manipulation tasks, including real-world bolt screwing and nut mating, and show that it outperforms WAMs built on frozen pretrained representations by up to 50%50\%. Additional videos are available on our website:
jointmdf.github.io.
introduction:
When tightening a screw or mating a nut, vision alone is often insufficient: successful execution depends on subtle contact cues, force feedback, and proprioceptive information. In order to perform such tasks, it would also be useful to anticipate how the robot’s actions affect the world, such as how contact will form, how an object will move, and how force will propagate. This motivates robot models that jointly reason about actions and their consequences. World-action models (WAMs) [7, 30, 51, 52, 22, 26, 31, 40, 61, 24] address this by jointly modeling future observations and actions within a single generative model. Recent work [30, 61, 24] shows that such auxiliary dynamics learning can improve model capability and generalization in robot control.

However, existing WAMs still have two key limitations for robot manipulation. First, most prior WAMs are built primarily around visual observations, leaving tactile and force information largely unexplored. Second, these models typically rely on frozen pretrained encoders, often trained with pixel reconstruction or self-supervised visual objectives. While such encoders provide useful features for image generation or semantic understanding, their representations are not necessarily aligned with robot control. This issue is even more pronounced for tactile, where broadly-applicable pretrained encoders are less established. A natural solution is to finetune the encoders end-to-end with the WAM objective, but we find that naive finetuning leads to feature collapse: the encoder and diffusion backbone co-adapt to produce latents that are easy to denoise but less useful for control.

To address the above limitations, we present MDF++, a visuo-tactile world-action model that learns task-relevant representations end-to-end with a latent diffusion backbone. We build on Multimodal Diffusion Forcing (MDF) [24], but instead of modeling dynamics in a frozen latent space, MDF++ finetunes observation encoders jointly with the world-action model under a mixture of task-oriented objectives, including policy learning, joint action–observation prediction, forward dynamics modeling, and inverse dynamics modeling. To avoid feature collapse during joint training, MDF++ introduces a cross-modal training strategy with selective gradient back-propagation, which encourages the latent space to capture the interplay between different modalities, yielding representations that are better aligned with robot control.

Our key contributions are three-fold. First, we propose MDF++, a diffusion-based visuo-tactile WAM that learns task-relevant multimodal representations end-to-end using cross-modal prediction. Second, we introduce a selective gradient-flow strategy that enables stable joint training of observation encoders and the world-action model while avoiding feature collapse. Third, we evaluate MDF++ on seven contact-rich manipulation tasks, including two real-world threading tasks requiring millimeter-level precision. In simulation, MDF++ outperforms frozen-encoder baselines by 28%\% and naive joint training by 22%\%. In real, it outperforms video-based WAMs [61] by 29%\%.

title: Task-Driven Closed-Loop Design Optimization of Passively Morphing Quadrotors for Contact-Mediated Narrow Gap Traversal
authors: Etor Arza,Luca Girardi,Gabriel Maquignaz,Javier Paez,Stefan Leutenegger,Stefano Mintchev,Kostas Alexis
comment: Video:this https URL. Code:this https URL
abstract:
Aerial robots operating in cluttered environments may encounter openings narrower than their nominal width.
Existing passively morphing drones reduce their width upon traversal, but they typically involve human-made designs, which can struggle to find the right balance among folding ratio, flight efficiency, and control tracking performance.
We introduce a closed-loop design method that jointly optimizes quadrotor geometry and the torque-deflection response of two passively folding arms driven by the success rate in simulation for contact-mediated gap traversal.
An optimization algorithm samples candidate designs that are evaluated in a contact-based simulation of the traversal task, where the task success rate is used as a feedback signal to sample progressively better designs over time.
The resulting prototype passively reduces its width from 31.331.3 to 14.114.1 cm and traverses a 1515 cm wide opening at a 22 m/s reference speed.
It also tolerates gap approach-angle errors of up to 30∘30^{\circ} and folds through a 4040 cm long confined passage.
Compared to a rigid twin, the soft configuration adds only 22 mm of position RMSE and less than 1%1\% electrical power during contact-free flight.
These results show that task-driven closed-loop design optimization can produce passively morphing airframes that are compact under contact, tolerant to approach error, and effectively rigid during nominal flight.
introduction:
The width of an aerial robot can impose a hard limit on the environments it can access.
In cluttered indoor, industrial, and natural settings, an otherwise traversable route may contain openings narrower than the vehicle’s nominal width.
Rigid quadrotors can reduce their projected cross-section through aggressive attitude maneuvers [1, 2], but the opening must still exceed the vehicle’s minimum projected dimension.
Moreover, successful traversal requires accurate perception, state estimation, and timing, making this strategy difficult to deploy reliably in real-world settings.

Morphing aerial robots can overcome this geometric limitation by temporarily reducing their width.
For instance, actuated morphologies [3, 4, 5] can decrease width on demand, but increase system complexity through additional servomotors and adaptive control strategies.
Thrust-triggered quadrotor arm folding through passive joints [6, 7] can achieve large and rapid shape changes, but requires invertible thrust and limiting maneuverability to avoid unintentionally triggering the passive joints.
Contact-mediated passively reconfigurable designs are therefore particularly attractive as they leverage contact with the environment to initiate and maintain shape change [8, 9, 10, 11, 12] without requiring additional actuators or invertible thrust.
However, the geometry and compliance of these existing designs are not specifically optimized for the traversal task, where the trade-off between in-flight rigidity (and consequently tracking accuracy and power consumption) and the maximum achievable squeeze is not specifically addressed.
Aerial robots that achieve contact-mediated in-flight narrow-gap traversal only pass through gaps up to 29% narrower than the drone’s span [8, 9, 10].

A well-designed passively morphing quadrotor must remain effectively rigid under rotor loads during nominal flight and simultaneously easily reduce its width when the opening applies contact forces.
After traversal, it must restore the nominal flight configuration.
A design that is too flexible can deform during normal flight, leading to worse control, while a stiffer structure can be difficult to compress through the gap.
When airframe geometry and compliance are selected by hand, it is particularly difficult to identify which combinations best enable both successful gap traversal and good nominal flight control performance.
Previous works show contact-mediated narrow-gap traversal is possible but generally propose a planar quadrotor architecture and compliance guided by engineering intuition.
To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has jointly optimized airframe geometry and compliance directly driven by closed-loop performance over the complete narrow-gap traversal and recovery task.

In this work, we introduce a task-driven closed-loop design optimization approach for soft quadrotors, optimized for narrow-gap traversal.
Figure 1 summarizes the proposed closed-loop design optimization pipeline and the resulting vehicle’s key capabilities.
We jointly optimize a 22-parameter quadrotor geometry and the programmable nonlinear torque deflection response of two passively folding side arms directly for traversal success.
The compliant response is achieved using elastic rolling cam (ERC) joints [13], whose cam profiles can be synthesized to produce nonlinear restoring torque as a function of the bending angle.
This nonlinearity can be tuned to allow airframes to remain rigid near the nominal configuration, while bending with low effort after contact.
A black-box optimizer evaluates candidate designs using GPU-parallel contact simulation with a nonlinear model predictive controller (NMPC) whose model parameters are instantiated analytically from each candidate morphology.

title: EGT: Execution-Grounded Traversability through Learned Closed-Loop Trajectory Distributions
authors: Chinmay Mundane,Amith Manoharan,Arun Kumar Singh
abstract:
Rough terrain traversability is often estimated through point-wise roll, pitch, or force-angle margins along a planned path. However, these metrics are often inaccurate and overly conservative because they ignore how terrain disturbances and low-level controller corrections can affect the vehicle’s motions. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Execution-Grounded Traversability (EGT), defined as the probability that a vehicle–controller pair can execute a candidate path while meeting trajectory-level tracking and progress requirements.
We estimate EGT by predicting the distribution of closed-loop trajectories using a latent-space flow matching (FM) model conditioned on multi-resolution terrain features and 3D vehicle attitude and wheel-ground contact points prior. Across 650 simulated trials on unseen terrains, EGT reduces safe-path rejection to 2.2% (versus 11.4%–39.5% for pose-margin and force-angle baselines) and unsafe acceptance to 7.7%.
Integrated into a receding-horizon sampling-based planner, EGT reduces navigation failure rates by 24–42 and 30–44 percentage points over [1] and [2], respectively, while cutting goal-reaching time by up to 20.5% and 45%.
Finally, we demonstrate zero-shot transfer of our simulation-trained model to real-world outdoor experiments.
introduction:
Autonomous wheeled vehicles used outdoors for applications such as search and rescue, construction, and forestry must accurately evaluate whether they can follow a reference path over rough terrain without tipping over or getting stuck. Standard traversability methods evaluate safety along this path using tip-over stability margins [3] or limits on terrain-induced roll and pitch angles [4, 5]. However, relying on attitude limits or tip-over margins to evaluate traversability—even dynamic metrics like the force-angle measure [3]—tends to be both overly conservative and inaccurate for three key reasons:

Pointwise limits ignore closed-loop recovery (overly conservative): Checking stability or attitude limits at every point along a path penalizes brief posture excursions. A large transient roll or pitch angle does not make a path infeasible if the vehicle’s momentum and low-level controller can ensure a safe recovery.

Rotational stability does not guarantee traversal (inaccurate): Force-angle and attitude limits only check for rotational tip-over.
Even when a vehicle stays within safe posture limits and tip-over margins, wheel slip can stop forward progress or push the vehicle sideways into obstacles or ditches.

Reference-path checks ignore closed-loop deviation (inaccurate): Calculating posture or tip-over margins along the reference path may provide limited insight because terrain disturbances and subsequent controller corrections can make the vehicle depart substantially from the planned reference.

Therefore, in this paper, we do not define traversability from terrain and posture features alone; instead, we evaluate whether a specific vehicle–controller pair can execute a reference path under closed-loop control.
Formally, we define Execution-Grounded Traversability (EGT) as the probability that a vehicle–controller pair can execute a candidate reference path while keeping the path-tracking error below a set limit and completing a required fraction of its arc length.
This execution-based perspective reshapes how we factor vehicle stability into traversability assessments. Specifically, our core insight is that physical failures—like tipping into a ditch or stalling on a steep slope—directly derail path tracking or halt forward progress. Conversely, satisfying attitude or force-angle bounds alone does not guarantee that the vehicle will complete the path.

To compute EGT, we must predict the distribution of closed-loop path-tracking behavior on rough terrain. One approach, proposed by Wang et al. [6], learns an open-loop, action-conditioned dynamics model and pairs it with a tracking controller at inference time. In effect, the learned model acts as a simulator, generating closed-loop executions through repeated evaluations of the dynamics model and a low-level controller. However, this recursive rollout compounds prediction errors: an inaccurate state prediction alters the controller’s corrective action, which further degrades subsequent predictions. Moreover, these corrections can push the model toward state–action pairs that are poorly represented in the training data, further reducing accuracy. Finally, and most importantly, their learned target is action-conditioned vehicle dynamics,
rather than the complete execution distribution conditioned on a reference path.

In this paper, we bypass the recursive rollouts of [6] by treating the vehicle and its feedback controller as a single closed-loop system. Rather than simulating step-by-step dynamics, we directly learn the distribution of realized trajectories from closed-loop executions in simulation. We model this conditional distribution using a latent-space flow matching (FM) architecture conditioned on multi-resolution terrain features and a 3D kinematic pose–contact prior. Given this context and a candidate path, our learned
FM model jointly predicts the entire sequence of
closed-loop waypoints, without recursive evaluations
of vehicle dynamics and a tracking controller.

Our EGT method provides two main advantages.
First, across 650 simulated trials on unseen terrains, EGT reaches 97.4% classification accuracy.
It is much less conservative and more accurate than the force-angle measure [3] and roll/pitch limit methods [4, 5], cutting the conservative rejection of safe paths from 11.4%–39.5% down to 2.2% and unsafe acceptance down to 7.7%. Second, when we use EGT with conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) execution costs in a simple receding-horizon sampling-based planner, we reduce failure rates by 24–42 percentage points over [1] and 30–44 percentage points over [2].
At the same time, our planner reduces mean goal-reaching time by up to 20.5% and 45% over these baselines.

In summary, the contributions of our work are:

We introduce EGT, a probabilistic traversability
metric based on closed-loop execution requirements.

We introduce EGT, a probabilistic traversability
metric based on closed-loop execution requirements.

We develop a closed-loop trajectory predictor based on latent FM that allows us to estimate EGT along a reference path.

We combine EGT with risk-aware planning and
demonstrate improvements in path classification
and navigation.

1. We introduce EGT, a probabilistic traversability
metric based on closed-loop execution requirements.

2. We develop a closed-loop trajectory predictor based on latent FM that allows us to estimate EGT along a reference path.

3. We combine EGT with risk-aware planning and
demonstrate improvements in path classification
and navigation.

title: SUGARv2: Learning Diverse Visual Humanoid Loco-Manipulation Skills from Synthesized Interaction References
authors: Tianshu Wu,Tianxiang Gui,Yue Chen,Tingxu Liu,Ziye Peng,Guangjie Yang,Xiangqi Kong,Ye Shi,Jingya Wang,Hao Dong
comment: . Project page:this https URL
abstract:
Scaling up visual humanoid loco-manipulation skill acquisition requires reducing the human effort needed as tasks and spatial configurations expand, particularly in demonstration collection and task-specific training design. We present SUGARv2, a unified framework for learning diverse visual humanoid loco-manipulation skills through interaction reference synthesis and a shared training pipeline. To obtain diverse references at low cost, we adapt reusable task templates to different spatial configurations, synthesizing coordinated robot and object motions. To reduce task-specific reward design and training effort, we use reference-based imitation as a common learning objective across tasks. We first train privileged teachers to execute these references, then train visual policies through teacher distillation and reinforcement learning with the same reference-based mimic rewards, using diverse object instances and visual domain randomization to support visual generalization and sim-to-real transfer. Across five humanoid loco-manipulation tasks, SUGARv2 achieves a mean success rate of 91.0% in simulation. Deployment on a real humanoid robot further demonstrates successful sim-to-real transfer for whole-body manipulation. These results demonstrate the framework’s potential for learning diverse visual humanoid loco-manipulation skills.

introduction:
Scaling up visual humanoid loco-manipulation skill acquisition requires reducing the human effort needed for each new task and spatial configuration. Existing approaches rely on manually collected interaction data or task-specific training designs, making it costly to extend skill learning across tasks and spatial configurations. HumanoidMimicGen [23] expands teleoperated demonstrations through whole-body planning, but depends on initial demonstrations and uses decoupled upper- and lower-body control. GRAIL [44] avoids teleoperation and supports whole-body control, but requires video generation and motion reconstruction for every spatial configuration, incurring high costs and potentially producing physically implausible interactions. Task-specific policy learning methods [9, 50, 33] acquire visual loco-manipulation skills through tailored training designs, requiring further engineering for new tasks. These dependencies make scaling skill acquisition costly in data preparation and training design (Table 1). Motivated by this, we present SUGARv2, a unified framework for learning diverse visual humanoid loco-manipulation skills through interaction reference synthesis and a shared training pipeline.

For low-cost reference synthesis, we use GPT-6 Astra [29] to generate reusable task-level interaction templates. These templates specify ordered sequences of key whole-body poses, robot–object and hand–object spatial relations, and intended contact labels. We adapt them to different spatial configurations of the robot, object, and goal to synthesize robot and object trajectories for policy learning.

To reduce task-specific reward design and training effort, we use reference-based imitation as a common learning objective across tasks. We first train privileged teachers to execute these references under physical dynamics, then train visual policies through teacher distillation and reinforcement learning with the same reference-based mimic rewards. Teacher supervision is retained during reinforcement learning to guide policy optimization at states visited by the visual policy. Diverse object instances and visual domain randomization further support visual generalization and sim-to-real transfer.

Across five humanoid loco-manipulation tasks, SUGARv2 achieves a mean success rate of 91.0%, outperforming the strongest baseline by 51.4 percentage points. Deployed on a real humanoid robot, the visual policies successfully perform whole-body manipulation tasks, demonstrating the framework’s potential for learning diverse real-world manipulation skills. Our main contributions are:

We present an interaction reference synthesis pipeline for
humanoid loco-manipulation. By adapting reusable task
templates to different spatial configurations, the pipeline
synthesizes diverse interaction references across tasks, reducing the cost of collecting demonstrations.

We present an interaction reference synthesis pipeline for
humanoid loco-manipulation. By adapting reusable task
templates to different spatial configurations, the pipeline
synthesizes diverse interaction references across tasks, reducing the cost of collecting demonstrations.

We introduce a policy learning pipeline that uses reference-based imitation as a common learning objective across loco-manipulation tasks. Shared mimic rewards connect privileged teacher training with visual policy learning, reducing task-specific reward design effort.

Extensive simulation and real-world experiments validate that our method outperforms strong baselines, generalizes to unseen backgrounds and object instances, and transfers zero-shot to real hardware.

title: TPS-A*: Path Planning for Any-Shape Vehicles with Certified Collision Checking in Trajectory Parameter Space
authors: Jose Luis Blanco-Claraco,Shravan S. Rai,Fernando Cañadas-Aránega,José Luis Torres-Moreno,José Carlos Moreno-Úbeda
abstract:
Global planners for ground vehicles usually approximate the vehicle by
a disk, trading safety against conservativeness, while exact-footprint
checking pays for every candidate motion, pose, and footprint edge. We present
TPS-A*, a lattice planner whose edges are kinematically feasible
trajectories from parameterized trajectory generators, built on certified
collision checking in trajectory parameter space. A grid precomputed per
footprint returns, in one pass over the local obstacles, a certified free
distance along every candidate trajectory, so the per-node collision
cost is independent of footprint complexity and trajectory count. We prove that
this grid never overestimates the free distance of the
continuously swept, possibly non-convex footprint, and state the planner’s
guarantees: collision-free paths and bounded suboptimality relative to its
lattice abstraction. Goals with or without heading are reached exactly by
Reeds-Shepp shots certified as trajectories of the same generators. An exact
independent test finds no collision in its paths. On 300 cluttered worlds, with the true footprint and the same
goal pose for all planners, it solves every query with a collision-free
goal pose in a median of three milliseconds on an AMD Ryzen 7 2700X,
on par with hybrid
A*, 45% of whose paths overlap obstacles, and nearly sixty times faster than
a state-lattice planner, the only other collision-free one; with
position goals, eighty-nine times faster than
hybrid A*. It matches hybrid A* in automated parking and on narrow doorways, docks
a non-convex fork footprint that no convex model admits, and drove a real robot
across a university campus among people.
introduction:
Global path planners for ground vehicles are commonly built on
a simplified vehicle model: the body is approximated by a disk and the obstacles
are dilated by that disk’s radius in a cost
map [1]. For an elongated or irregularly shaped vehicle
this forces a choice between a circumscribed disk, which rejects passages the
true body fits through, and an inscribed disk, which produces paths the true
body cannot follow without collision. Planners that check the exact polygon
avoid this dilemma, but do so pose by pose, so the cost of every candidate
motion grows with the footprint complexity and with the number of poses sampled
along it [2, 3].

This paper addresses global path planning for a single ground vehicle of
arbitrary planar footprint, possibly non-convex, subject to its
kinematic constraints (minimum turning radius, bounded linear and angular
velocity), among static obstacles. Our goal is a planner whose output is
kinematically feasible, whose collision reasoning is certified against
the exact polygon, and whose collision-checking cost does not grow with the
shape of the vehicle.

The approach builds on the Trajectory Parameter Space
(TP-Space) [4, 5]. A Parameterized
Trajectory Generator (PTG) is a family of kinematically feasible trajectories
indexed by a selector kk and a traveled distance dd; mapping obstacles into
TP-Space turns the vehicle into a free-flying point. TP-Space was introduced for
reactive navigation [4, 5, 6]
and later used by our randomized TP-Space RRT planner [7].

Methodological principle. The central observation of this paper is
that, for lattice search, the TP-Space collision model is not merely a faster
pose checker but a different interface between search and collision
checking. A precomputed per-PTG grid stores, for every cell of the
vehicle-local workspace and every trajectory kk, a lower bound on how far the
vehicle may travel along kk before its footprint touches any point in that
cell. One pass of the local obstacles through this grid therefore returns, for
the node being expanded, a certified free distance along every
trajectory of the family at once. The search then selects any number of
successors, at any distance below that bound, without further collision
queries. Consequently the per-node collision cost is independent of both the
footprint complexity and the branching factor, whereas pose-by-pose checking
pays for each successor, each sampled pose, and each footprint edge.

Contributions.

The principle above, stated as a node-batched collision check
for lattices whose successors are PTG trajectories, with a complexity analysis
and measurements against footprint complexity and branching factor
(Sec. IV, VII-B).

A certified construction of the TP-Space collision grid, with a
proof that its free distances never exceed the true ones for the continuously
swept, possibly non-convex footprint, a bound on its conservativeness, and an
extension to region obstacles (Theorem 1); the construction
previously used in TP-Space tools is not conservative.

TPS-A*, a deterministic SE⁡(2)\mathrm{SE}(2) lattice planner built on this check,
with a deferred analytic goal expansion and certified Reeds-Shepp shots that
reach full-pose and position goals exactly, and a precise statement of what it
guarantees: certified collision-free, kinematically feasible paths and
ε\varepsilon-bounded suboptimality relative to its lattice
abstraction, for position goals and, with a Reeds-Shepp heuristic, for
full-pose goals, together with what it does not guarantee (strict resolution
completeness) (Sec. V, VI).

An evaluation on 300 BARN worlds against search-based (Nav2 Hybrid-A*,
SBPL) and sampling-based (OMPL) planners with the true footprint, on narrow
doorways from real floor plans, on the TPCAP automated-parking
benchmark [8] with a passenger car, on docking with a
non-convex footprint, and on a real Husky robot on a university
campus, with every returned path of
every planner checked by an exact, planner-independent test
(Sec. VII). No TPS-A* path collides; on the cluttered
worlds it is as fast in median as the fastest baseline, whose paths often
collide, and much faster than the only other planner whose paths never do.

title: Auditing Grasp Feasibility Predictors with Planner-Verified Counterfactuals
authors: Sajid Ansari,Antony Thomas,Girish Varma
comment: Accepted to WACV 2027. main paper + supplementary
abstract: Grasp-feasibility predictors report near-perfect accuracy on Task and Motion Planning benchmarks, but high accuracy on these benchmarks does not verify that a predictor uses the collision geometry that the motion planner checks. We propose a planner-verified counterfactual (CF) test: holding the grasp pose fixed, we insert a solid obstacle into the approach corridor, add its points to the model input, and let a planner re-derive the label, which flips from feasible to infeasible. Across eight predictors spanning point clouds, voxels, depth, and object tokens, CF-pair AUROC falls from high natural AUROC (0.9200.920–0.9960.996) to chance (0.4700.470–0.5040.504), and the flip holds across four planners, two arms, and a real-object obstacle. Predictors fail at different resolutions, from a bounding box to a 12.512.5 cm voxel. In the point-cloud models we dissect, the obstacle either moves the representation in a direction unrelated to whether it blocks the grasp or is not registered at all. A clearance-aware read of the corridor points, trained on the unmodified benchmark with no counterfactual scenes, reaches 0.9830.983 CF-pair AUROC, but it remains bound to its trained obstacle placements; a placement-invariant clearance representation is still open. We release the counterfactual labels, metrics, datasheet, and relabeling pipeline at https://github.com/codewithsajid/graspfc-cf.
introduction:
Computing grasp poses (grasps) is a fundamental problem in robotic manipulation. Given a grasp on
an object, the end-effector can reach it only if a collision-free path exists from the robot’s
start configuration; motion planning is feasible when such a path exists and
infeasible otherwise. Sampling-based planners [18] commonly used in
manipulation are only probabilistically complete, so they cannot certify infeasibility: they keep
searching until termination or timeout, inflating overall computation time.

Learned predictors [4, 7, 6, 1, 2] that score this feasibility from a scene are now a standard
speed-up for Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) [17, 6, 13, 29], and on point-cloud benchmarks they report near-perfect
accuracy.11
1
            
            
            
            
            
            
            
          TAMP combines discrete actions of task planning with the continuous geometric
motion planning. A task-level action may turn out to be infeasible at the motion-level, e.g.,
objects obstructing a grasp, requiring task-level re-planning. However, these benchmarks evaluate predictor models on naturally sampled grasps, for which the grasp pose is often sufficient to predict the label. A predictor can therefore saturate the benchmark without using the full scene geometry checked by the motion planner. Fig. 1 shows one such grasp: the initial feasible grasp (left) is made infeasible by inserting the cube (right), yet the predictor’s feasibility score remains unchanged.

Collisions are a frequent and significant source of grasp infeasibility (Sec. 3). A natural question is why standard benchmarks fail to reveal collision. Their sampling rarely includes examples near the boundary where a small change in geometry causes a grasp to switch from feasible to infeasible (Sec. 4.1). Consequently, high accuracy on the benchmark does not verify that the model reasons about collisions. The model can achieve high accuracy without actually learning this aspect of grasp feasibility.
This exposes two related issues:
shortcut learning [16] and causal confusion [7], both of which can be measured directly through controlled interventions.

We evaluate different models using their released weights on their original benchmarks and robots. The models do not fail in the same way. Instead, each responds only at the level of detail its supervision, query formulation, and representation support, and stops below it (Sec. 4.3, Tab. 4).
Importantly, the obstacle is present in the input representations. Thus, this insensitivity cannot simply be attributed to PointNet’s critical-point-set theorem [25], which concerns the learned per-point representation rather than the geometric structure of the scene. We verify this directly in Sec. 4.4. Further evidence comes from a clearance-supervised model trained on the same unmodified benchmark, with no counterfactual data at all, which still recovers the collision term (Sec. 4.5).

Together, these results show that the relevant collision signal is present in the input, but standard supervision does not require the model to use it.

Contributions.
We audit eight predictors: three classifiers of a grasp-feasibility
benchmark [3] built on GraspNet-1B scenes [11], and five prior methods spanning
point clouds, voxels, depth images, and object
tokens [4, 7, 6, 1, 2]. For [3, 2, 4, 7], we additionally evaluate the authors’ released weights on their original data and robot platforms. These results leave open a fundamental question: do the predictors actually capture collision-relevant scene geometry? We introduce a systematic test, along with metrics and data, to measure this correspondence.

Benchmark saturation and collision limits.
Predictors that are near-perfect on the natural benchmark score 0.470.47-0.5040.504 once we
insert an obstacle that flips the collision label at the same grasp
(Sec. 4.1, Tab. 1). Natural data almost never places two grasps at the same pose on opposite sides of a contact
boundary, so a predictor can score well without reading the scene (Sec. 4.1).

Planner-verified counterfactual test and metrics.
We define the corridor insertion edit and verify both of its preconditions: every edit
flips the planner’s label, and the inserted obstacle survives the model’s downsampling
(Sec. 3). We report CF-pair and within-grasp AUROC, and release pick-clear accuracy
for auditing new predictors. The planner-swap and real-object controls show the flip is not an
artifact of one planner, arm, or obstacle type (Sec. 4.2).

Predictors fall short in different ways.
Each responds only down to the resolution its representation and supervision support, from a

robot. We therefore report each at its own resolution rather than as one aggregate score.

1. 论文核心任务概括
这篇论文主要关注于评估抓取可行性预测器的准确性，特别是它们是否能够有效地利用碰撞几何信息。通过引入规划者验证的反事实测试，论文展示了在不同的输入条件下，预测器的性能如何变化，并探讨了这些模型在真实场景中可能存在的局限性。

2. 是否属于 World Model：是 + 理由
该论文涉及到对抓取可行性进行预测，核心在于理解和学习环境（即障碍物的存在）如何影响抓取的可行性。这种理解与 World Model 的核心思想相符，即学习环境随动作如何演化，并能够预测未来状态（如抓取是否可行）。

3. 是否属于 VLA：否 + 理由
论文的输入主要是与抓取相关的几何信息（如点云、体素等），而不是视觉和语言的结合。虽然可能涉及到一些视觉信息，但并没有语言输入，因此不符合 VLA 的定义。

4. 是否属于 Humanoid Loco-manipulation：否 + 理由
尽管论文涉及抓取和碰撞检测，但并没有明确提到使用人形机器人或涉及到人形机器人的整体协调控制。任务主要集中在抓取的可行性评估，而不是人形机器人的行走和操控的联合控制。

5. 最终标签总结
该论文属于 World Model，但不属于 VLA 或 Humanoid Loco-manipulation。

6. 如果有歧义，请说明最容易混淆的点
最容易混淆的点在于论文涉及的抓取和碰撞检测可能让人联想到机器人操作，但其重点在于模型如何理解环境的变化对抓取可行性的影响，而不是具体的机器人执行动作或协调控制。

title: Toward the Era of Agentic Embodied Intelligence
authors: Chao Liang,Ke Chen,Fengxiaoxiao Li,Shibo Huang,Yufeng Sun,Zhaokai Yin,Jianhuan Lai,Haozhe Feng,Chenghuan Jia,Zhipeng Zhang
abstract: Frontier foundation models can increasingly guide robot actions, but sustained physical autonomy also requires efficient control and recovery from failures. We introduce A2-MEAS, an embodied multi-agent framework built around code as a scaling interface. Here, a correction code is a learned representation of corrective language, grounded spatial evidence, execution history, and an action proposal. MetaBrain supplies corrective supervision during training and grounded guidance during execution. The correction encoder and adapter learn to turn this guidance into actions, absorbing corrective knowledge into trainable action-policy weights. At deployment, fresh codes adjust behavior while all weights remain fixed. This couples learning from foundation models with using their reasoning when new failures arise. The underlying action model, A2-WLA, augments a vision-language-action policy with motion-aware history and a latent world model. Surprisingly, even before online correction, this simple architecture with action pretraining and task specialization reaches 0.5755 Q-score on the 50-task BEHAVIOR 2026 public subset, approximately 2.21×2.21\times the 2025 winner’s reported public score of 0.2605 across different benchmark editions and training configurations. On the full 100-task BEHAVIOR 2026 public set, the complete system combines MetaBrain, diagnostic agents, and learned correction to achieve 0.6411 Q-score and 45.40% complete-task success. The same action design also supports short-horizon bimanual manipulation, achieving 93.98% average success on RoboTwin 2.0, or 95.05% with the complete system. Real-robot evaluation spans 12 tabletop tasks across five household settings, where A2-WLA achieves 57.92% average success compared with 26.67% for π0.5\pi_{0.5}. Long-horizon pour-over coffee preparation tests recovery during sustained execution. At two filter-handling steps, a history-conditioned Adapter raises post-failure completion from 14.00% to 94.00% and from 8.00% to 82.00%, relative to retries by A2-WLA without the Adapter. To support development at this scale, our training infrastructure reaches 427.1 samples per second, approximately 4.03×4.03\times the throughput of a π0.5\pi_{0.5} reference implementation on matched hardware. We will release the system, models, training scripts, and infrastructure as an efficient, usable framework for embodied learning.
introduction:
General embodied intelligence requires a system to connect its intentions to the physical consequences of its actions. Over a long activity, a robot must remember what remains to be done while responding to changes in objects, contacts, and its own configuration. A successful movement is useful only if the resulting state supports continued progress. A2-MEAS addresses this problem by coupling learned action generation with task-level reasoning and evidence-based diagnosis.

The framework contains three cooperating groups of agents (Figure 1). A2-WLA generates continuous actions from the task instruction and observed history. MetaBrain monitors execution in relation to the full goal and determines when the next attempt should change. Diagnostic agents investigate the physical questions needed to make that decision. All three use a shared record of actions and observations. When execution requires intervention, a learned correction interface converts their instruction and evidence into changes inside the action generator.

Section 1.1 explains how the shared record coordinates these agents. Section 1.2 introduces the action model, its observation and prediction components, and the adapter that accepts corrective guidance. Section 1.3 follows a recovery example from diagnosis through corrected execution. Sections 2 and 3 then develop the interface and action model in detail.

A2-MEAS couples a local control loop with a task-level reasoning loop. The local loop repeatedly generates action chunks from the task instruction and recent observations. The task-level loop uses the resulting evidence to decide whether execution can continue, whether the goal has been achieved, or whether recovery is needed. A shared execution record stores the goal, dispatched controls, and observed outcomes. It gives all agents a common account of what has actually happened without requiring them to share a backbone or run at the same frequency.

The execution layer dispatches only a prefix of each predicted chunk, then obtains fresh observations before the next policy call. Thus, control is closed-loop across chunks even though an uninterrupted prefix executes without a new policy prediction. A2-WLA handles ordinary changes through this repeated observation–action cycle. When monitoring detects an abnormal outcome, the runtime pauses pending controls and asks MetaBrain to review the evidence. Verified recovery returns execution to the nominal loop, and verified completion ends the episode.

Diagnostic agents are invoked when a decision depends on an unresolved physical condition. Table 1 groups their functions into perceptual grounding, spatiotemporal grounding, and interaction assessment. Perception locates objects and regions. Temporal analysis tracks how they move relative to one another. Interaction assessment combines those observations with available robot-state, contact, and geometric evidence. For example, seeing an object between the gripper fingers does not establish a secure grasp. Tracking whether it moves with the hand, together with gripper-state evidence, supports a more informative assessment. Depth or reconstructed geometry can supply additional evidence when available. Each finding retains its observation source and timestamp so that MetaBrain can distinguish a supported conclusion from a missing observation.

The result determines what happens next. Evidence that supports the required condition permits execution to continue. Evidence of a mismatch prompts a correction. Insufficient evidence prompts another observation within the sensing budget. A negative answer and an unknown answer therefore lead to different decisions. Conditional tool invocation keeps ordinary control inexpensive while allowing several diagnostic capabilities to contribute when a correction needs them.

Let gg denote the complete task instruction, retained throughout nominal execution. We index the physical control step at which the policy executes by tt. The policy input xtx_{t} aggregates synchronized multiview visual observations, a finite temporal window of past visual frames, and the current proprioceptive state sts_{t} comprising joint positions and end-effector configurations.

A2-WLA combines three sources of action context. A vision-language backbone encodes the task instruction and visual observations. Its motion-aware history encoder represents changes across recent frames. A latent world model predicts future visual features from a transition representation inferred by the backbone. The action expert uses current context, predicted future context, and proprioception to generate controls. Future observations supervise training but are unavailable at deployment. Section 3 describes these components and the three stages used to train the base policy.

During standard nominal operation, A2-WLA executes with the correction branch deactivated. We designate this default configuration as the base policy πθ\pi_{\theta}, parameterized by θ\theta. At invocation step tt, with sampling randomness suppressed in the notation, it jointly predicts a multi-step continuous action chunk and an auxiliary local-phase progress estimate

The correction branch adds a second way to influence action generation. Its condition encoder combines a recovery instruction, verified spatial evidence, relevant executed history, and an uncorrected proposal from the base policy. The resulting code conditions a residual adapter inside the action expert. The code is computed once per generated chunk, while the adapter recomputes its hidden-state adjustment at each flow-integration step. Later action layers turn the modified representation into a corrected trajectory. This mechanism supplements the policy’s ordinary visual and predictive context without updating its weights (Section 2).

The robot executes only an initial prefix of the generated chunk. Let LtL_{t} be the number of controls actually dispatched at call tt, with 1≤Lt≤Hexec≤H1\leq L_{t}\leq H_{\mathrm{exec}}\leq H whenever execution starts. The BEHAVIOR reference configuration predicts H=50H=50 controls, executes at most Hexec=32H_{\mathrm{exec}}=32, and uses da=23d_{a}=23 control dimensions. After an uninterrupted prefix, the next observation is acquired at t+32t+32, and a new prediction replaces the unused 18 controls. If monitoring interrupts the prefix, the next observation corresponds to t+Ltt+L_{t}. A candidate rejected before dispatch produces no executed controls and is not logged as an action prefix.

The execution record RtR_{t} stores the history available at physical step tt. Each entry links observations before and after a dispatched prefix to its actual controls, executed length, and timestamps. Camera identifiers, coordinate frames, task identifiers, and available local-phase annotations preserve the meaning of those records. Unexecuted proposals are stored separately. The short visual window in xtx_{t} serves immediate action prediction, whereas RtR_{t} supplies a longer history for diagnosis and recovery.

After a dispatched prefix finishes or is interrupted at step t+Ltt+L_{t}, the runtime returns a feedback bundle bt+Ltb_{t+L_{t}} containing the updated execution records, diagnostic findings, progress estimates, and status. The status is RUNNING during nominal execution, TASK_COMPLETE after completion checks succeed, or ABNORMAL when execution requires review. Progress predictions describe the proposed chunk and are interpreted together with the executed controls and observed outcomes. MetaBrain uses this feedback to decide what evidence or corrective instruction is needed next.

The correction interface becomes useful when observing the changed scene is not enough to change an ineffective behavior. Figure 2 illustrates a filter-placement example. The support ring should rest on the cup rim, with the filter hanging inside the opening. If one edge slips below the rim, continuing downward may wedge the ring or disturb the cup. Recovery instead calls for lifting the ring, aligning it above the opening, and lowering it again.

After detecting an anomaly, the framework pauses pending controls and establishes a recovery state. MetaBrain examines the observations and executed controls between the last verified nominal state and the detected deviation. It asks the diagnostic agents to assess contact stability and the spatial conditions required for another placement attempt. Perceptual tools identify the filter and cup regions, while temporal tracking helps bound the interval in which support was lost. Available robot-state and contact evidence informs the recovery assessment. Geometric and kinematic checks assess whether the proposed lifting motion is feasible. The recovery instruction is finalized once its required premises have been resolved. If occlusion leaves a necessary condition unknown, the system requests another observation within its sensing budget. The instruction specifies the adjustment and reference frame, while A2-WLA generates the continuous trajectory.

At the recovery state, the base policy first generates an uncorrected proposal. This proposal shows what the policy would attempt without intervention. The condition encoder combines it with the instruction, spatial evidence, and executed history. In the filter example, “realign the filter” is therefore interpreted in relation to a particular ring orientation, cup opening, and attempted movement. The adapter can then apply different residuals to different action positions, allowing a chunk to lift first and approach again later. These are learned adjustments rather than a prescribed geometric trajectory.

Before dispatch, the runtime checks that the evidence remains current and that the candidate satisfies the available joint-limit and obstacle-clearance checks. It executes a prefix, records the outcome, and checks whether the support condition has been restored. Successful recovery returns the robot to the unfinished task. Otherwise, the new observations and failed attempt inform another recovery pass. The reference configuration allows at most three physical retries and 60 seconds per anomaly, with separate sensing and reasoning limits specified in Section 2.6.

The methodological contribution is code as a scaling interface, a learned connection between grounded recovery context and the action policy’s internal representation. MetaBrain can express what should change, diagnostic tools can establish where and under what conditions, and the action model can translate that context into movement. During training, the condition encoder and adapter learn from MetaBrain-generated guidance, offline-mined candidate deviations, and expert continuations while the original A2-WLA checkpoint remains frozen (Section 2.5). At deployment, fresh guidance and evidence change the correction code, which shapes action generation with all model parameters fixed. The interface thus connects corrective knowledge learned during training with the physical context encountered during execution.
