title: Safe Circumnavigation on Heterogeneous Orbits: A Range-Only HOCBF-QP Framework for Nonholonomic Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Shubham Singh,Anand Singh,Anjali Tiwari,Lara Briñón-Arranz,Katsuki Fujisawa
abstract:
Circumnavigating a stationary target with a team of robots
requires each robot to hold its own standoff distance, to stay evenly spaced from its neighbours, and to avoid collisions with the target and with each other at every instant. The task becomes arduous when the robots are assigned different orbital radii, as their sensors or roles may demand. This paper presents a safety-critical control framework for this problem. Each robot commands both its acceleration and its turn-rate, measures only its distance to the target, and exchanges information only with its two ring neighbours. The design has three features. First, a structural property of the model lets one control law serve every robot regardless of its assigned radius. Second, the acceleration drives each radius exactly to its target, while the turn-rate balances the formation with the neighbours. Third, a higher-order control-barrier-function quadratic program enforces target, geofence, and inter-robot safety on both inputs at once; it leaves the nominal controller untouched away from the constraints and stays valid while the unmeasured range rate is still being estimated. Simulations confirm these guarantees. In a comparison, the closest existing multi-orbit design, even with full state information, violates both the target standoff and the inter-robot margin, whereas the proposed controller does not.
introduction:
Coordinated circumnavigation of a stationary target
by autonomous robots underlies persistent surveillance of critical
infrastructure [1], monitoring of
hazardous sites [2], offshore
inspection [3], standoff
reconnaissance [4], and oceanographic
sampling [5, 6]. In each
setting the robots must converge to prescribed orbits, hold a
balanced formation with their neighbours, and never collide with the
target or with each other, at every instant and not merely in the
limit. The task is harder when robots are assigned distinct orbital
radii, as platforms differing in sensor resolution, payload, or role
naturally require: satellite constellations place high-resolution
imaging units inside relay units [7], and
firefighting UAV teams place suppression platforms inside monitoring
platforms [8].

A single scalar input cannot meet these requirements: if only the
turn-rate is commanded, one degree of freedom must drive orbit
convergence, maintain safety, and coordinate the formation at once,
and these objectives compete for the same
channel [4]. Commanding both acceleration
and turn-rate, the two-input model standard in collective
circular-motion studies [9], removes this
competition: the turn-rate serves the formation and the
acceleration serves radial convergence. Two difficulties remain.
First, the obstacle and inter-agent constraints have relative degree
two in the inputs, so hard, instantaneous safety requires a barrier
formulation solved jointly across both channels. Second, the target
is uncooperative, so each robot senses it through a single range
measurement, with no bearing, range rate, or absolute position; such
range-only sensors are also inexpensive, lightweight, and low-power,
making this a design choice as much as a
limitation [10, 11]. Teammates, by
contrast, are cooperative and exchange local information, so the
relative displacement to a neighbour is available. Any safety
certificate must therefore survive the error incurred while the
unmeasured range rate is being reconstructed. Addressing both
difficulties, together with heterogeneous orbit assignment, is the
subject of this paper.

Stable circular orbits were first established for single unicycle
agents [4, 12] and
later extended to multi-agent
formations [13, 14]; cyclic
pursuit [15, 16] supplied
foundational stability results for ring-coupled formations, and
circular formations for distributed source seeking under
communication constraints [17] illustrate
the breadth of the problem. These designs, however, either decouple
orbit tracking from coordination without formal coupling
guarantees [12] or rely on potential fields
that carry no safety certificate [13]. On
heterogeneous multi-orbit circumnavigation specifically, the closest
work [18] uses virtual-agent normalization
with circulant-matrix diagonalization, but requires orbit-dependent
tuning and full velocity access and offers no hard safety guarantee;
the alternatives are time-varying switching
strategies [19, 6] or are
restricted to homogeneous radii [20].

Where safety is treated at all in this literature, it draws on
control barrier functions (CBFs) [21], barrier
certificates [22], or the asymmetric
barrier Lyapunov function (ABLF) of [23]. Our own
prior work certified hard geofencing for a single unicycle via a
Möbius-transformed ABLF [24], but that construction
folds safety into one tracking Lyapunov function and does not extend
to an obstacle constraint and pairwise inter-agent
constraints acting jointly on two inputs [25]. The
CBF-QP paradigm [26] is the natural fit instead:
it certifies forward invariance as a minimally invasive filter on
any nominal controller and has been applied to multi-robot collision
avoidance [27], though not to heterogeneous
ring circumnavigation, and the relative-degree-two constraints of
our problem lie beyond standard CBF-QPs. The higher-order CBF
(HOCBF) construction of [28] resolves exactly
this, and solving it jointly across acceleration and turn-rate is
the central technical device of this paper.

What remains is the sensing side. Range-only circumnavigation has
been studied for localization and
pursuit [1] and for target
following [29], but these works pursue
convergence, not certified safety: to our knowledge, no existing
design makes a hard, instantaneous safety guarantee survive the
transient of the estimator that range-only sensing necessitates.
This is where the convergence-oriented and safety-oriented lines of
work fail to meet, and it is the gap this paper closes: a framework
combining two-input unicycle actuation, heterogeneous orbit
assignment, and hard obstacle and inter-agent safety enforced
through a jointly solved HOCBF-QP that remains valid under range-only
sensing of the target and local communication between neighbours.

Against this backdrop, the paper makes three contributions:

The body-frame radial error is shown to be algebraically
independent of the assigned orbital radius. As a result, one control
law serves every agent, whatever its orbit, and no orbit-dependent
normalization or tuning is needed.

The body-frame radial error is shown to be algebraically
independent of the assigned orbital radius. As a result, one control
law serves every agent, whatever its orbit, and no orbit-dependent
normalization or tuning is needed.

A cascaded backstepping law in the
acceleration channel drives each orbital radius to its target
exactly and exponentially, rather than practically or in
time-average. The turn-rate channel is thereby freed for a
gradient-based formation law that uses only ring-neighbour data.

Safety is then delegated to a single HOCBF-QP. It enforces the obstacle, geofence, and
inter-agent constraints, all of relative degree two in the inputs. Because the range rate is unmeasured, a
super-twisting differentiator reconstructs it in finite time, and an
explicit constraint tightening keeps the safety guarantee valid
throughout the estimation transient, not only after it settles. In
simulation, the heterogeneous multi-orbit design
of [18], granted full state access, violates
both the target standoff and the inter-agent margin during its
transient, whereas the proposed controller keeps both margins

title: Robust Readout of Cross-Point Resistive Arrays via Time-Domain Optimization
authors: Taro Tako,Hiroshi Kaminaga,Taisuke Kobayashi
comment: IEEE Sensors 2026 accepted
abstract: Cross-point resistive arrays are attractive for high-density tactile sensing because they reduce wiring complexity. However, conventional frequency-based readout methods can become inaccurate in robotic sensing environments, where long interconnects and measurement and environmental noise degrade the observed signals. We propose a time-domain optimization method for robust readout of cross-point resistive arrays. The method determines resistance values by fitting a time-domain observation model to the measured waveform over the interval, rather than relying solely on spectral amplitudes. By exploiting the full waveform, the proposed method improves robustness under noisy observation conditions. In simulations of a 16×16 array, the proposed method reduced the mean readout error by 20% compared with the baseline method. Furthermore, validation over 1,000 trials showed that the proposed method achieves more robust estimation than the conventional method, reducing the mean error and standard deviation by 24.6% and 77.6%, respectively. The improvement was also confirmed in cross-point array simulations with resistance distributions emulating tactile sensor responses.
introduction:
Robot-embedded tactile sensors require large-area and dense coverage for accurate environmental perception and full-body coverage of the robot [1, 2, 3].
Cross-point resistive arrays are widely used to realize large-area sensing in robots [4, 5, 6].
In general, a cross-point resistive array is configured using switches for each row and column, and the readout target resistor is determined by the switch configuration.
Since the number of switches increases linearly with the number of resistors, the time required to read all resistances also increases, along with the readout error caused by the parasitic resistance of the switches.
Many previous studies on cross-point resistive arrays have focused on reducing readout errors [4, 7, 8, 9, 10].
Alternating-current (AC) measurements [11, 12, 13] are promising because they eliminate switches in the circuit and enable simultaneous readout of multiple sensors, thereby avoiding timing mismatches among sensors and allowing simultaneous readout independent of array size.
Existing AC measurement methods for cross-point arrays distinguish element responses by assigning different frequency components to different channels and recovering the corresponding responses using spectral analysis.
However, these methods rely on frequency-domain information to recover individual sensor responses, and their accuracy can degrade significantly in the presence of noise and limited sampling conditions.
To address this limitation, we propose a time-domain optimization method, as illustrated in Fig. 1.
The proposed method determines them from time-domain signals.
This improves robustness to noise and enables accurate measurement even under partially degraded signal conditions.
We evaluate the proposed method in simulation using two circuit types and three conditions, including resistance distributions designed to emulate tactile sensor responses, and demonstrate its effectiveness.

title: When to Trust the BIM: Identifiability-Aware LiDAR-Inertial--BIM Fusion under As-Built Deviations
authors: Yujie Zhang,Yuxuan Guo,Xinbao Sun,Chunlei Zhao,Langqi Miao,Xiaohui Jia,Jinyue Liu
comment: (including appendices)
abstract: Building information models (BIM) can provide a global geometric reference for robot localization with LiDAR-inertial odometry (LIO). However, as-built deviations from the as-designed model mean that a disagreement between a scan and the BIM may arise from a pose error, an offset wall surface (an as-built deviation or an unmodeled object in front of the wall), or a shifted room, and in some geometries these explanations produce identical observations. In this paper, we formalize this attribution problem as fault identification over three fault classes and derive a geometric criterion for when attribution is possible. Building on it, we propose an identifiability-aware method that reports an attribution only when the fault is attributable; otherwise, it retains the candidates, defers BIM updates and BIM-based pose corrections in the ambiguous directions, and recovers once new references arrive. In the pre-registered two-dimensional study, on cases whose fault is detectable but not attributable, the method’s conditional error rate was 0.83%, against 31.67% for a baseline with uncertainty-based abstention at the same answer rate. On the 5,600 attributable cases, the method reported a unique attribution 5,574 times, with no incorrect attributions. In paired fault injections in a laboratory room with its IFC model and on three floors of the SLABIM dataset, it raised no off-target attribution (0 of 168 conditions in the laboratory; 0 of 1,302 on SLABIM) and attributed all eight laboratory faults predicted to be attributable, whereas both reproduced baselines raised off-target structural flags in every setting.
introduction:
BIM is increasingly used as a global geometric reference for robot localization with LiDAR-inertial odometry. What a BIM records, however, is the building as it was designed, and the building as constructed can deviate from that design. When a LiDAR scan disagrees with the model, a robot that takes its global reference from the BIM [39, 47, 54] therefore has to decide which of three things moved: its own pose, the surface at one wall, or a whole room. In some layouts the scan looks the same in all three cases.

Consider a robot that sees a single room (Fig. 1). In world A, the room was built 20 cm away from its position in the BIM, and the LIO pose is correct; in world B, the room matches the BIM, and the LIO pose is 20 cm off. The two worlds give the same scan and the same LIO pose, so no method can tell them apart from these data or be right in both. We call such a pair paired worlds. This ambiguity matters because scans are already used to update the BIM toward the as-built state [46, 38], and a wrong revision pollutes that model. A pose pulled toward an unverified BIM sends navigation to the wrong place and then hides the deviation once the map is laid over the BIM.

Even so, current LiDAR–BIM systems return one answer on this pair. Localization against a floor plan or a BIM treats the model as the reference [9, 28, 20, 49]. LIO-BIM adds a BIM factor only after the scan-to-BIM match passes a quality test [39], and BIM-Loc admits only structure it has judged consistent [54]. diS-Graphs estimates wall and room deviations in stages, starting from an alignment on walls without deviation, and its authors show that a single joint optimization confuses pose error with structural error [36]. These methods answer three different questions: where the robot is, whether the match is good enough to use, and how large the deviations are once an alignment has been fixed. Each method returns one pose, and diS-Graphs also returns one set of deviations, so in the paired worlds, each can be right in at most one world. Reporting a covariance with that pose does not close the gap, because a covariance computed on the assumption that the map is correct cannot reflect an error in the map. Localization, gating and staged estimation take the BIM as the reference they measure against; the fusion below treats it as one more source of evidence and checks that evidence whenever the scan disagrees with it.

Before a conclusion is reported, or the pose is corrected with the BIM, the explanations have to be tested, because they are not always separable. An LIO bias offsets the absolute pose in xx, yy and yaw. A wall-surface offset moves the surface observed at one BIM wall along its normal, and a room translation shifts a whole room in the plane relative to the coordinates at which the run started. The test is decided by the witnesses, that is, the walls and references that independently constrain the offset direction. In the single room the walls of the room together count as one witness against the prior, so those two witnesses detect a conflict, but a pure translation still fits a room translation and an LIO bias alike. In this single-room translation, the cause can be attributed only once the wall outside the door, the third witness, is seen. Whether the explanations can be told apart is set by the geometry of those witnesses, and more data in the same geometry does not change it. Where the geometry separates them, whether a given stretch of the trajectory can tell them apart also depends on the size of the offset relative to the noise. When applied to the fault classes defined by a BIM, this geometric test is the identifiability criterion of the detection–identification–adaptation (DIA) framework [41, 50].

In addition, LiDAR-inertial odometry is kept free of the BIM, so it remains an independent witness. At each conflict, every single-fault explanation is fitted. Any explanation that leaves part of the data unexplained, leaving it for another explanation to account for, is dropped. If the cause can be uniquely attributed, the attribution is reported and the pose is corrected from it. Where several remain, the candidates are kept and the pose follows the odometry wherever they disagree on a BIM-anchored position, until a new witness separates them. Here, we call those directions ambiguous, and the rule deferred BIM anchoring. If the LIO is wrong, the error in an ambiguous direction is about the difference between the candidates until the cause is attributed. With no explanation left, the position is withdrawn.

In the framework of this paper, withholding an attribution is allowed when the witnesses cannot separate the explanations, and fewer answers then mean fewer recorded errors. The errors are therefore compared at the same answer rate, an answer being a reported attribution to a wall, a room, or the LIO. Because the specification was fixed before the runs, this is a pre-registered simulation. Its baseline is a diS-Graphs-style reproduction of [36] that withholds an answer where its own covariance is large. Where the noise model labels a fault detectable but not attributable, the method almost always withholds an attribution.

On the 7,200 simulated cases with that label, the conditional error rate at the same answer rate was 0.83% (1 of 120 answers) for our method, against 31.67% (38 of 120) for the abstaining baseline. The difference meets the pre-registered criterion for a clear improvement. On the 5,600 attributable cases, our method reported a unique attribution 5,574 times and made no wrong attribution. In a separate demonstration with a strong prior, a new reference resolved the paired worlds in all 200 room-world trials and in 194–195 of 200 LIO-world trials, with no wrong unique attribution. Our method raised no off-target attribution in 168 injected conditions in a laboratory room with its IFC model, nor in 1,302 conditions on SLABIM [23], and it attributed all eight laboratory faults predicted to be attributable.

The main contributions are summarized as follows:

Identifiability criterion. A geometric criterion for when a scan–BIM conflict can be uniquely attributed to an LIO bias, a wall-surface offset, or a room translation. The criterion follows from the observation that a narrower explanation contained in a broader one can never be confirmed on its own; in a single room, a room translation and an LIO bias form such a pair (Section 4).

Identifiability criterion. A geometric criterion for when a scan–BIM conflict can be uniquely attributed to an LIO bias, a wall-surface offset, or a room translation. The criterion follows from the observation that a narrower explanation contained in a broader one can never be confirmed on its own; in a single room, a room translation and an LIO bias form such a pair (Section 4).

Deferred BIM anchoring. A fusion method that reports an attribution only when the cause can be uniquely attributed, and that otherwise retains the candidates and defers BIM anchoring in the ambiguous directions (Section 5).

Evaluation under known faults. An evaluation that compares errors at a fixed answer rate in pre-registered simulation, together with paired fault injections on a laboratory room and on three floors of SLABIM, where the ground-truth fault is known because it was inserted (Sections 6 and 7).

The criterion answers the question in the title: the BIM can be trusted where the geometry makes the fault attributable and the offset is large relative to the noise. Trusting the BIM means correcting the pose with it, except for the wall or room that was attributed, whose change is only proposed for a person to check. Where the explanations cannot be separated, the BIM is left unchanged and anchoring is deferred in the ambiguous directions. Where no single fault explains the data, the BIM is left unused and the position is withdrawn.

title: DobotTrack: Target-Grounded Vision-Language-Action Learning for Embodied Person Tracking
authors: Shengjun Deng,Yinghan Zhang,Chengrui Wei,Liu Liang,Songyuan Liu,Pengkun Zheng,Yajun Zheng,Ying Zhang,Yuan Tian,Xi Li,Teng Wang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Language-guided embodied person tracking requires a mobile agent to identify a target from a referring description and consistently follow the target under egocentric observations. We present DobotTrack, a target-grounded vision-language-action (VLA) framework that integrates auxiliary grounding supervision with efficient temporal modeling. We systematically investigate five auxiliary tasks—person segmentation, bounding-box grounding, visual-spatial classification (VSC), future DINO feature prediction, and future-frame prediction—and adopt complementary mask and bounding-box supervision to enhance target delineation and localization. We introduce Q-identity, a target-conditioned historical visual compression module that leverages target-grounding predictions to selectively preserve identity-discriminative appearance features and spatial cues in compact historical tokens. On EVT-Bench, our 0.8B-parameter model achieves an average success rate of 77.9%, exceeding OmTrackVLA by 16.9 percentage points across the three tasks. We further construct a real-world person-tracking dataset collected using a quadruped robot, comprising 126 episodes and 596,323 mask-annotated frames. The target masks enable automatic derivation of bounding boxes and visual-spatial labels encoding horizontal position and apparent image scale, providing additional grounding supervision without separate manual annotation of these labels. Together, our framework and annotation pipeline support learning target-grounded tracking policies from simulated and real-world data. Code is available at https://github.com/Dobot-Team/dobot_track.
introduction:
Tracking a person specified in natural language requires an embodied agent to determine whom to track while continually deciding how to move. Unlike tracking in a recorded video, the agent’s actions change its viewpoint and the target’s visibility, coupling visual recognition with motion generation [1, 2]. Appearance variation, occlusion, and nearby distractors make this coupling particularly important: a plausible trajectory is insufficient if the agent tracks the wrong person. Language-guided embodied tracking therefore calls for representations that connect the referring description, the intended target’s image location and the agent’s future motion.

Vision–language–action models provide a way to learn these capabilities within a shared model. Uni-NaVid unifies several embodied navigation tasks, including person tracking [3], while TrackVLA shares a language-model backbone between target recognition and trajectory planning [4]. Subsequent work introduces explicit spatial reasoning, target-identification memory, and image-grounded referring decisions [5, 6]. During sustained tracking, changes in illumination and viewpoint can substantially alter the same person’s visual appearance, making target association and re-identification after occlusion difficult [7, 8]. These variations motivate retaining target-discriminative information across observations. These challenges, illustrated in Fig. 1, raise two complementary questions. First, how can a tracking policy be encouraged to represent the specified target explicitly, rather than relying on trajectory imitation alone? Second, how can historical visual observations be efficiently compressed while preserving target-discriminative appearance cues and scene context essential for reliable person tracking?

We address these questions through target-centric perceptual supervision and identity-aware history compression. We present DobotTrack, a target-grounded VLA framework built on InternVL3 [9]. We systematically investigate person segmentation, bounding-box grounding, visual-spatial classification, future DINO feature prediction, and future-frame prediction as auxiliary tasks to improve tracking policy learning. The final model combines mask and box supervision to couple fine-grained foreground delineation with explicit target localization. Building on this grounding, Q-identity compresses historical observations into compact tokens that retain identity-discriminative appearance and spatial context. The language model captures temporal dependencies for trajectory prediction from the chronological sequence of compressed historical and current-frame tokens.

The model processes an appearance-based instruction together with a temporal window of RGB observations. The learned mask token and box token precede the waypoint tokens in the causal sequence, allowing the waypoint states to attend to their target-related representations. Task-specific heads decode the resulting hidden states into the target mask, bounding box, and future trajectory in one forward pass.

A second consideration is the alignment between policy-learning objectives and real-world annotations. EVT-Bench supports simulated embodied-tracking research [4], and TPT-Bench provides robot-egocentric tracking sequences with target boxes and synchronized sensor streams, including odometry [10]. Complementing these resources, we construct a quadruped-collected dataset with 126 tracking episodes and 596,323 mask-annotated RGB frames. The recordings combine target descriptions, visual observations, and robot motion information. Target masks yield boxes and structured VSC labels, while temporally continuous recordings provide observation histories and future waypoint supervision. Episode-level partitioning keeps samples from the same recorded episode within a single data subset.

This report makes three contributions:

A target-grounded tracking framework with systematic auxiliary supervision analysis.
We develop DobotTrack, a vision-language-action framework for embodied person tracking, and systematically investigate five auxiliary tasks: person segmentation, bounding-box grounding, visual-spatial classification, future DINO feature prediction, and future-frame prediction. Based on our empirical findings, we adopt complementary mask and box supervision to improve target delineation and spatial localization.

Identity-aware historical visual compression.
We introduce Q-identity, a target-conditioned historical visual compression module that leverages target-grounding predictions to preserve identity-discriminative appearance information and essential spatial cues in compact visual tokens, providing target-aware temporal context for subsequent trajectory prediction.

A real-world tracking dataset and annotation pipeline.
We construct a quadruped-collected person-tracking dataset comprising 126 episodes and 596,323 mask-annotated frames. We develop an annotation pipeline that derives bounding boxes and structured VSC labels for horizontal target position and apparent image scale from target masks, and organize the data into temporally structured learning samples with episode-level partitioning.

title: ToolDex: An Ego-Exo Human Demonstration Dataset for Creative Physical Tool Use
authors: Mohamed Elmoghany,Kehan Li,Ruoqu Chen,Tarun Chiruvolu,Shutong Zhang,Ryan Wang,Stephen Tian,Yaru Niu,Michelle Guo,Ding Zhao,Weiyu Liu,Mengdi Xu,Li Fei-Fei,Jiajun Wu
abstract:
Creative tool use is a fundamental human capability and an important step toward general-purpose embodied intelligence. It requires agents to reason about object affordances, physical constraints, and manipulation strategies, especially when standard tools are unavailable. However, progress in this area is limited by the lack of real-world datasets that capture human tool-use behavior with sufficient scale, fidelity, and diversity. Existing benchmarks are often simulation-based, focus on simplified interactions, or lack detailed observations and annotations.
We introduce ToolDex, a large-scale egocentric-exocentric (ego-exo) human demonstration dataset for creative physical tool use. ToolDex captures scenarios in which humans select, adapt, and repurpose available objects as tools. Using synchronized egocentric cameras and eight exocentric cameras, the dataset provides high-fidelity multi-view observations and rich annotations for hands, tools, target objects, and their deformable interactions. Beyond data collection, we establish a benchmark suite characterizing three core capabilities: physical tool-use reasoning, sparse-view 3D and 4D reconstruction, and robot policy learning. ToolDex provides a foundation for studying human tool-use behavior and developing embodied agents that can adaptively use tools in complex real-world environments.
Dataset visualizations and benchmarking results are available at https://tooluse-dataset.github.io/.
introduction:
Tool use is a fundamental human capability and a key step toward general-purpose embodied intelligence (Goodall, 1964, Hunt, 1996, Shumaker et al., 2024, Fitzgerald et al., 2021). In everyday environments, humans do not rely solely on a fixed set of predefined tools; they also flexibly repurpose available objects based on their physical properties and functional affordances. For example, when a knife is unavailable, a person may use a spoon, chopsticks, or another nearby object to divide a cake. This form of creative tool use requires more than recognizing object categories. It demands physical reasoning about contact, geometry and task constraints. As such, physical tool use provides a natural testbed for evaluating whether embodied agents can generalize beyond memorized object-action associations and adapt to novel physical scenarios.

Despite recent progress in robotic manipulation (Black et al., 2024, Black et al., 2025, Kim et al., 2026), learning generalizable tool-use behavior remains difficult (Shi et al., 2023, Wang et al., 2024). Task and motion planning methods can solve structured tool-use problems when
symbolic task descriptions are carefully specified, but often struggle in open-ended real-world settings (Garrett et al., 2021). Recent large language models and vision-language models have shown promising reasoning ability for selecting or describing tools, yet they remain limited in grounding such reasoning into physically executable manipulation (Fang et al., 2024, Xu et al., 2023, Lin et al., 2025, Gao et al., 2026). This gap is especially pronounced in tasks involving deformable target objects (such as sand or cake), non-rigid contacts,
and long-horizon interactions,
where success depends on fine-grained hand-object-tool dynamics rather than high-level semantic reasoning alone.

A major obstacle is the lack of datasets and benchmarks that capture human physical tool-use capabilities at sufficient scale, fidelity, and diversity.
Existing robot tool-use benchmarks are often simulation-based or focus on simplified object interactions, making it difficult to evaluate the complexity of real-world manipulation (Xu et al., 2023, Gao et al., 2026, Bakhtin et al., 2019, Zhang et al., 2025).
Meanwhile, recent egocentric human manipulation datasets have greatly expanded the coverage of hand-object interactions (Hoque et al., 2026, Punamiya et al., 2026, Li et al., 2026, Liu et al., 2024).
Among them, TACO explicitly captures tool-action-object compositions for hand-object manipulation (Liu et al., 2024).
However, it does not explicitly model the target objects manipulated by the tools, such as cakes to be cut or water to be stirred.
As a result, existing datasets either contain limited tool-use instances or lack the full hand–tool–target-object interactions and annotations needed to study physical tool use.

In this paper, we introduce ToolDex, a large-scale ego-exo human demonstration dataset for learning and benchmarking creative tool-based manipulation (Figure 1).
Our dataset is designed around everyday tool-use scenarios in which humans creatively solve manipulation tasks by selecting, adapting, and repurposing available objects.
A key feature of our dataset is its explicit coverage of deformable target objects, such as dough, fluids, and sand, where success depends on fine-grained contact and material interactions.
To capture these behaviors with high fidelity, we use a synchronized multi-view capture system consisting of two egocentric cameras and eight exocentric cameras. Egocentric views capture local interaction context, while exocentric views enable accurate multi-view tracking and reconstruction.
The resulting dataset provides rich annotations for studying both high-level tool-use reasoning and low-level physical manipulation.

Beyond data collection, we use ToolDex to establish a benchmark suite for evaluating tool-use capabilities across three levels.
First, we evaluate physical tool-use reasoning, testing whether vision-language models can identify appropriate tools, infer object positions, and provide plausible manipulation strategies.
Second, we evaluate 3D and 4D reconstruction, focusing on the recovering hand, tool, and deformable scene states from multi-view observations.
Third, we evaluate robot policy learning, where human demonstrations are used to train robot policies for tool-based manipulation.
Together, these benchmarks characterize semantic reasoning, spatial perception, and embodied control, offering a comprehensive evaluation protocol for physical tool-use.

Our contributions are threefold.
First, we present a real-world ego-exo dataset centered on creative physical tool use spanning diverse tools, deformable target objects, tasks, and interaction strategies.
Second, we provide rich multi-view annotations that support hand tracking, tool tracking, object interaction analysis, and scene reconstruction.
Third, we introduce a benchmark suite that evaluates embodied agents from reasoning to reconstruction to policy execution.
We hope this dataset will serve as a foundation for studying human tool-use behavior and for developing robots that can creatively use tools in complex, open-world environments.

title: A Controlled Study of Models, Skills, Feedback, and Curriculum in Agentic Robotics
authors: Kaiyuan Chen,Xinyue Zhu,Shuangyu Xie,Uksang Yoo,Thi Thu Phuong Luong,Marcus Gualtieri,Christian Juette,Liu Ren,Spencer Huang,Ken Goldberg
abstract:
Agentic robotics asks coding agents to implement and iteratively improve robot policies from simulated and real-world physical interactions. We study the self-learning loop of agentic robotics through a controlled simulation study spanning nine manipulation tasks, 631 different experiment configurations, and 28K coding agent rollouts, systematically varying model capability, skill priors, feedback structure, and curriculum. The experiment data suggests that the bottleneck is often not the access to sufficient information, but interpreting it into the right policy update.
Across these factors, a successful self-learning loop depends on how effectively agents attribute failures, reason task-relevant spatial and geometric structure, and selectively restructure code to improve policies.
introduction:
Recent coding agents, such as GPT Astra  (OpenAI, 2026a) and Claude Fable  (Anthropic, 2026a), have become increasingly capable of generating and iteratively repairing executable programs, motivating a growing class of Agentic Robotics (AR) systems in which LLM- and VLM-based agents write code that composes perception, planning, and control skills into robot policies (Liang et al., 2023b; Singh et al., 2023; Fu et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a).
However, self-improvement in robotics differs fundamentally from software debugging. In software, failures, such as compiler errors, are often exposed through symbolic feedback that is already closely aligned with the program; but in robotics, the evidence to improve a policy is instead embedded in physical interactions: object geometry, spatial relationships, contact, motion, and changes in the scene over time. As illustrated in Figure 1, a failed placement can be attributed to an earlier incompatible grasp and a collision requires reasoning about the geometry of an object after it becomes part of the moving robot.
In this paper, we ask: what determines whether an agent can interpret physical interaction and convert it into effective robot-policy improvement?

We design a controlled simulation study of agentic robot self-learning across five contact-rich VABAR manipulation tasks Xie et al. (2026b) and four longer-horizon MimicGen tasks Mandlekar et al. (2023). Holding the overall self-learning harness fixed, we systematically vary four components of the learning loop: model capability, skill prior, feedback structure, and curriculum, as illustrated in Figure 2.
Across these studies, we find that self-learning is limited less by the availability of useful information than by the agent’s ability to turn the information into effective policy updates. More execution feedback is not necessarily more useful: feedback is most effective when aligned with semantically meaningful policy decisions rather than reported at the finest temporal resolution. Similarly, world-frame states contain all the information needed for manipulation, yet agents often fail to recover task-relevant object-relative and functional relationships unless these are made explicit. Even when agents identify local geometric errors, they often struggle to translate them into coherent collision-aware motion plans. We find that this limitation can also affect curriculum design: agents tend to preserve and patch policy structure inherited from earlier stages rather than fundamentally reorganize it, so privileged learning can either provide a useful initialization or constrain later learning when the inherited policy depends on privileged precision or brittle manipulation strategies.
Our results further suggest that progress in agentic robot self-learning comes from the better structures of skills, feedback, and state representations and the learned physical reasoning ability from the underlying models.

This paper makes three contributions:
(1) A controlled study design for Agentic Robotics that isolates four important components of simulation-guided self-learning, (2) Experiment data from 631 implemented experiments with 28 thousand simulation rollouts on Agentic robotics policies, (3) Six findings on model capability, skill priors, feedback structure, and curriculum.

title: FASTFUNNELS: Agile Multi Robot Navigation in Narrow Spaces via Adaptive Dynamic Funnels
authors: Vignesh Rajagopal,Rohan Chandra
abstract: In this paper, we focus on the problem of high-speed multi-robot navigation in cluttered spaces with tight spatial constraints. A key technical challenge that the literature today faces is to balance safety with agility, often trading one for the other (slowing down near a bottleneck to avoid a collision versus failing to swerve in time at high speeds) especially in car-like dynamic systems. The approach presented in this paper aims to solve this problem and belongs to the family of formation control methods where Ackermann-steering agents coordinate with each other when navigating tight spaces. Formation control techniques today, however, rely on rigid, pre-defined shapes and adaptations, initial conditions, environmental conditions, and vehicular dynamics, that are typically impractical to maintain at high speeds. For e.g. agents going through a small gap can ONLY first form a square that eventually transforms into a line using analytical equations, and then back into a square. Our approach, on the other hand, draws inspiration from a smoothly flowing droplet of water that adapts its shape continuously and dynamically through whatever space its flowing without slowing down. We propose a hierarchical algorithm that, at the high level, trains a reinforcement learning policy to produce a fast, dynamic “blob-like” elliptical patch that can morph its shape in real-time and can squeeze, stretch, and orient itself fluidly around obstacles and through tight spaces. At the lower level, the agents or robots are optimized via distributed model predictive control (DMPC) to stay inside the patch (which acts as a soft forcing function for the agents) and not collide with each other. We evaluate our approach, FastFunnels, using simulated F1TENTH racing cars and show that FastFunnels surpasses the baselines and achieves a completion rate of 89% at 7.737.73 m/s across N=1N{=}1 to N=6N{=}6 robots in 14 different scenarios averaged over 20 trials each, while all baselines either fail to complete the track or succeed at extremely low speeds (0.070.07–1.791.79 m/s,  40% completion rate). Supplementary code, videos, and additional results can be found at https://autonavbot.github.io/Fastfunnels/.
introduction:
Agile (defined as high-speed mobility in narrow spaces) multi-robot autonomous navigation in tight, cluttered environments has become essential for applications such as search and rescue, warehouse logistics, and exploration in dense environments[1, 2]. The fundamental hardness of this problem is the conflict between continuously making progress towards the goal and satisfying dynamic environmental constraints at high speeds. To solve this problem, there has been significant interest in developing decentralized solutions that typically frame multi-agent navigation as a joint trajectory optimization problem [3]. However, solving joint optimization problems in real time is very computationally expensive [4, 5, 6]
Literature in multi-robot coordination suggests that part of the computational complexity can be mitigated by leveraging adaptive formation control to improve spatial coordination [7, 8, 9, 10]. By operating with a shared spatial consensus, a team of robots can collectively adapt to environmental constraints as a unified entity, preventing deadlocks, bottlenecks, and team fragmentation (e.g., stragglers) that otherwise occur when individual agents greedily optimize their own localized trajectories.

However, current formation control methods [7, 8, 9] rely on rigid formations or ad hoc/rule-based protocols for coordination, which is overly conservative and unsafe in high-speed multi-agent navigation especially in narrow spaces. For example, if the passage geometry is narrower than the formation’s fixed shape, boundary violations can occur and the team loses its safety. To mitigate this, rule-based methods and discrete shape libraries enforce a narrower, predefined shape (e.g., switching from a wedge shape to a line shape) before entering a tight corridor. However, predefined shapes are overly conservative, as they often force the team to drastically decelerate or halt entirely before the bottleneck, destroying the fluid momentum required for high-speed mobility.

Novelty: This work extends the current state-of-the-art in formation control [7]: going beyond pre-defined formations for unicycle dynamics and implementing real-time, continuously adapting, high-speed formations for Ackermann steering agents. Our approach also differs in the way the multi-robot system moves through narrow spaces–unlike the rigid motion of prior methods [7, 8, 9], our system mimics the smoothness and agility of water droplets as it flows around bends and corners. The core technical insight of our underlying algorithm is to separate multi-agent interaction, safety, and fluid agility—because integrating all three together in a multi-robot system is extremely challenging and is the primary reason for the rigidity and conservativeness of prior methods. By delegating fluid agility to a high-level object (a virtual “blob-like” deformable elliptical funnel patch), the multi-robot system only needs to satisfy basic safety and containment constraints—something which is far easier.

Main Contributions: This paper proposes a novel hierarchical algorithm that enables high-speed adaptive formation control for F1TENTH vehicles with real car dynamics with Ackermann steering. A reinforcement learning leader policy guides a team of follower distributed MPC agents. Formally we contribute:

A reinforcement learning policy that trains a “blob-like” deformable elliptical patch that can morph its shape in real-time and can squeeze, stretch, and orient itself fluidly (like a water droplet) around obstacles and through tight spaces. (Section IV-A).

A real-time distributed model predictive control (DMPC) optimization solver for each ackermann-steering agents such that they stay inside the patch and not collide with each other (Section IV-B). The patch serves as a spatial guide (or a soft forcing function) for the agents, instead of requiring the agents to assume a specific shape as is done in typical formation control methods, which is what allows the system (patch + agents) to continuously change its shape at high speeds.

To test the limits of FastFunnels, we chose the state of the art F1TENTH racing simulator that has extremely fast racing car agents (up to 20m/s). We compared with the state of the art formation control baseline (DEFORM [7]), velocity obstacles-based collision avoidance [11], multi-agent graph-based method with control barrier functions [12], and a multi-agent reinforcement learning baseline (Section VI).

Real world experiments are conducted on 1/7th scaled Traxxas UDR vehicles which use Ackermann steering (Figure 4). They are deployed with lidar sensing on a cluttered narrow corridor with static obstacles along the way.

Main Result. Our main result is that FastFunnels completes all 20 trials of 14 scenarios at an average of 40% higher completion rate while being 7.69×\times faster than the fastest baseline. Also, even when FastFunnels slows down around the bottlenecks, it is still 1.2×\times faster than DMPC, 2.3×\times faster than ORCA and 6.5×\times than GCBF+.

title: VLA Handover: Failure-Prediction-Based Switching from On-Robot to Server VLA Models
authors: Takayuki Nishio
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Networking and Internet Architecture (cs.NI)
comment: . Submitted to IEEE ICC 2027
abstract:
Large vision-language-action (VLA) models generalize well but are difficult to run in real time on a
robot, and small VLAs that run there fail more often. Remote inference over beyond-5G and 6G
networks lets a robot use a large VLA on a server, but querying the server for every action chunk
limits the number of robots per server. We propose VLA handover: the robot runs a small VLA (S-VLA)
and switches to a large VLA (L-VLA) on a server only when the S-VLA is likely to fail. We formulate the switching as minimizing the request cost under a
required success probability and, since this problem cannot be solved directly, propose a heuristic
framework that retrains neither VLA. In simulation with SmolVLA and π0.5\pi_{0.5} on three of the four LIBERO
suites, VLA handover raised the success rate by 11–22 percentage points over the S-VLA alone and
sent 49–77% fewer requests than server-only control at a 2–4 percentage-point lower success rate, and its
completion time grew less with the network latency.
introduction:
Robot foundation models have shown strong
performance in robot manipulation, in particular vision-language-action (VLA)
models [1, 2], which map camera images and a natural-language instruction directly
to robot actions. These models rely on vision-language models with billions of parameters and are
therefore difficult to run in real time on the computer mounted on a robot. Small VLAs such as
SmolVLA [3] are designed to be deployed on consumer-grade GPUs or CPUs, but they
generalize less well: on the LIBERO-Long suite [4], SmolVLA succeeded in 35.0% of the
episodes in our evaluation, whereas π0.5\pi_{0.5} [2] succeeded in 93.2% (Sec. IV).

Remote control of robots over low-latency, high-reliability beyond-5G and 6G
networks [5] allows a robot to use a large VLA: the robot sends the
information required for inference, such as images and its state, to a VLA on an edge or cloud
server, and the server returns the output actions. As the number of robots grows, however, the
communication traffic and the server load become the bottleneck and limit the number of robots that
one server can accommodate. In our setting (π0.5\pi_{0.5} on an NVIDIA GB10 without batching), a
server accommodates only about two robots when every action chunk is inferred on the server; the
number depends on the server but is inversely proportional to the requests per robot. In
addition, the communication and computation latency delays each action; in dynamic scenes, or when
the robot cannot hold still while waiting, it can also lower the task success rate.

Existing schemes that combine an on-robot model with a server VLA involve the server in the
inference of every action chunk. RoboECC [6], RAPID [7], and
ComVLA [8] partition the inference of one VLA between the edge and the cloud, adapting the
split point to the network bandwidth or the number of transmitted visual tokens to the channel
capacity. AsyncVLA [9] runs a large VLA on a workstation and an on-robot edge adapter
asynchronously, and CloudEdgeVLA [10] combines delayed cloud features with current
local vision; both train the server and on-robot models jointly. The requests of these schemes do
not decrease when the on-robot model would succeed, and the latter two cannot be applied to existing
VLAs without retraining. Using the server only when it is needed raises the question of when to
switch, which is a trade-off: a switch that is too early sends requests in episodes that the small
VLA would complete alone, whereas a switch that is too late comes after a critical mistake of the
small VLA or too close to the deadline, so that even the large VLA cannot complete the task.

Related decisions have been studied in other settings. In cloud robotics, Chinchali et
al. [11] learn when to offload perception inference from the uncertainty of the
on-robot model and the network cost, and Penmetcha et al. [12] predict whether to
offload an application from the execution time; these works decide per inference of a perception or
application module, whereas our decision concerns which policy controls the robot for the rest of a
closed-loop episode. In interactive imitation learning, a robot requests a human supervisor when it
is at risk, under a budget of interventions [13], with fewer
switches [14], or from a limited pool of remote supervisors shared by a
fleet [15]; the helper is a human, and the communication and computation latency of
the help is not modeled.

In this paper, we propose VLA handover: the robot runs a small VLA (S-VLA) and switches to a
large VLA (L-VLA) on a server only when the S-VLA is likely to fail.
Fig. 1 illustrates the system and an example episode. This paper makes the following contributions.

Formulation and framework. We formulate VLA handover, i.e., deciding when to switch from an on-robot S-VLA to an L-VLA and to which of the L-VLAs on multiple servers, as the minimization of the expected request cost
subject to a required task success probability (Sec. II). Since this problem
cannot be solved directly, we propose a heuristic single-server framework in which a handover manager
estimates failure scores of the S-VLA, decides from them when to switch, and resets the arm and
switches the model (Sec. III); neither VLA is retrained.

Proof-of-concept experiments. In a proof of concept with SmolVLA and π0.5\pi_{0.5} on four LIBERO suites under an emulated
latency, we evaluate the requests, the success rate, and the completion time against the alert
threshold and the latency, and report both the suites where VLA handover reduces requests at a small
loss of success and the suite where it falls well short of server-only control (Sec. IV).

title: RevoSim: Scalable Multimodal Tactile Simulation for Dexterous Manipulation
authors: Ke Zhang,Lixin Xu,Ziyi Wang,Xiyue Dong,Jie Tan,Lianghu Shao,Xianpeng Wang,Chuanyu Li,Renjing Xu
abstract:
We present RevoSim, a scalable and high-fidelity multimodal tactile simulator
for the BrainCo Revo3 hand that jointly models 285 piezoresistive taxels and
five visuotactile fingertips. RevoSim efficiently generates synchronized
pressure, depth, RGB, and marker-displacement observations; on a single RTX
5090, its depth-conditioned marker-displacement configuration supports up to
4,096 parallel environments. We train in-hand manipulation and grasping
policies entirely in simulation, establishing a foundation for future
sim-to-real transfer.
introduction:
Dexterous manipulation is fundamentally contact-rich. Vision and proprioception provide estimates of object and robot states, but cannot directly observe local interaction phenomena such as incipient slip, contact migration, or hidden contact. Tactile feedback is therefore crucial once contact occurs. However, scaling tactile reinforcement learning remains challenging: physical hardware wears during data collection, tactile observations are high-dimensional and device-specific, and fast, transferable simulation is still unavailable for many tactile embodiments [1, 2].

Existing tactile simulators can synthesize fingertip images and marker motion,
model compliant deformation, or provide efficient tactile approximations for
parallel reinforcement learning [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 2, 8].
Distributed-array simulators further support force fields, configurable taxel
layouts, and sensor non-idealities [2, 1]. However, most methods focus on a single sensor family
or generic taxel layout. Accurately reproducing heterogeneous whole-hand
tactile sensing while maintaining the throughput required for parallel
reinforcement learning therefore remains challenging.

To address this gap, we present RevoSim, a scalable multimodal tactile
simulator for the BrainCo Revo3 hand [9]. Revo3
combines vision-based tactile fingertips, which capture local contact geometry
and elastomer motion, with piezoresistive arrays that measure contact locations
and loads across the palm and finger pads. To the best of our knowledge,
RevoSim is the first framework to jointly simulate these two modalities,
generating synchronized high-resolution fingertip observations and whole-hand
taxel measurements in parallel environments, as shown in
Fig. 1. Both modalities are calibrated against real
sensor responses, including their geometry, sensitivity, temporal behavior,
drift, hysteresis, dead taxels, and crosstalk. Qualitative comparisons show
consistency between simulated and real sensor responses. The simulator
supports policy training in simulation and provides a basis for future
sim-to-real transfer studies.

title: Wellness Robots and the Path to Full Autonomy
authors: Mohammad H. Mahoor,Matthew Hessler,Lombe Chileshe,Ola Alsaadi,Eshrat Emamian,Kerstin S. Haring,Richard M. Voyles
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
The convergence of demographic, workforce, and economic pressures has produced a senior care system that is unable to meet the needs of the people it serves. Understanding why traditional models cannot scale is the prerequisite for understanding why a new paradigm — and a new category of robot — is needed.

The global population aged 65 and over is projected to more than double by 2050, reaching approximately 1.6 billion. In the United States alone, the Alzheimer’s Association estimates that the population living with Alzheimer’s disease and AD-related dementias (AD/ADRD) could reach 16 million by mid-century [12], with annual direct care costs exceeding $1 trillion. AD/ADRD is not the only driver: depression affects roughly 30–40% of older adults in long-term care, while loneliness — independently associated with accelerated cognitive decline, depression, and mortality — has reached pandemic proportions. The COVID-19 era exposed how thin the margins are: facility-wide social distancing, already against a backdrop of severe staffing shortages, transformed loneliness from a quality-of-life concern into a measurable mortality risk factor.

The supply side of senior care has been deteriorating for over a decade and is now in critical condition. PHI National projects a shortfall of roughly 1.2 million direct care workers in the United States by 2030 [13]. A 2024 LeadingAge survey of 759 facility operators found that 60% feared closure [14] due to staffing pressures. Median direct-care wages remain near minimum wage in many states, while turnover rates of 60–100% per year compound the problem: each new caregiver requires onboarding, builds resident relationships from scratch, and is statistically likely to be gone within a year. The result is a workforce structurally unable to deliver the relational, longitudinal care that older adults — and especially those with cognitive impairment — require.

This workforce reality produces a measurable engagement gap inside the facility itself. The average assisted-living resident receives fewer than 18 minutes of structured wellness programming per day. The typical activities staff-to-resident ratio is approximately 1:47, which makes systematic individual programming structurally impossible. Group activity formats — bingo, sing-alongs, exercise classes — are inherently constrained: they happen at fixed times, address two or three wellness dimensions at most, and are not personalized. Residents who decline to attend, sleep through morning sessions, or simply prefer one-on-one interaction are largely unserved. The 16+ hours each day outside of programming time — evenings, weekends, holidays — are essentially uncovered. For residents with cognitive impairment, this lack of structure is itself a clinical risk factor.

Several technology categories have been positioned, by various vendors, as solutions to this crisis: medication reminder apps, telehealth platforms, fall-detection wearables, voice assistants, tablet-based engagement programs, and emotional companion robots. Each addresses some piece of the problem. None, individually or collectively, addresses the central issue. The reason is that the senior care crisis is not primarily a healthcare automation problem. Reminding someone to take a pill, escalating a fall, or asking “how are you feeling today?” on a tablet are point interventions; they do not in themselves constitute care. Healthcare automation is not wellness autonomy. A reminder is not a relationship; a detection is not an intervention; a generic conversation prompt is not adaptive engagement. A robot that delivers any one of these in isolation is a useful appliance, not an autonomous wellness robot.

What is required is something different in kind: a system that continuously assesses an individual’s state across multiple dimensions of wellbeing, adaptively plans interventions, remembers who the person is over weeks and months, escalates appropriately when concerns are detected, and does so while respecting the resident’s autonomy and dignity. That is not automation. That is a new category of system, requiring its own paradigm, its own standards, and its own measurable autonomy framework. Establishing those is the project of this paper.

title: HOC2R: Hand-Object Contact Trajectories for Human-to-Robot Motion Transfer
authors: Hongkun Yu,Francisco M. López,Francisco Cruz
comment: . Accepted for oral presentation at the Australasian Conference on Robotics and Automation (ACRA 2026)
abstract:
Human videos contain abundant object-manipulation demonstrations, but they do
not directly provide motion cues that a robot can follow. We present HOC2R, a
Hand-Object Contact trajectory extractor for
Robot motion that combines frozen DINOv3 and SAM 2.1 features with
learned heads for hand-object association and contact localization. HOC2R
supports two modes: count-aware automation that detects, counts, and
localizes visible contacts in untrimmed videos, and fixed-two localization for
two-finger grippers when contact frames are known.
On a 30-task point-annotated benchmark, count-aware
automation improves contact-count accuracy from 58.1% to 71.4% and
reduces mean localization distance from 19.81 to 10.46 pixels relative to an
adapted VRB2 baseline. On seven unseen RGB-D rollouts, a five-task fixed-two
checkpoint reduces mean localization distance
from 67.67 to 27.02 pixels.
Across six robot evaluation sequences, the 30-task fixed-two checkpoint produces
four feasible trajectories and succeeds on three tasks, compared with two
feasible trajectories and one successful task for each adapted baseline. HOC2R is
competitive in the evaluated single-hand scenes, robust to the
hand-color shift, and strongest in the evaluated multi-hand scenes. These
results support HOC2R as a practical pseudo-labeling method for extracting
robot-usable contact trajectories from human demonstrations.
introduction:
Large-scale robot learning is limited by the cost of collecting diverse robot
demonstrations, while human videos contain abundant examples of grasping and
object manipulation. Prior work learns from human play, predicts visual affordances,
or transfers motion across embodiments
[11, 2, 13]. A persistent
gap is the interaction geometry connecting observed human demonstrations to
robot actions. Boxes and masks identify participants, but not the contact
locations needed to derive a robot-gripper trajectory.

We study hand-object contact trajectories: visible contacts linked
across frames of a human demonstration. They provide an interaction-centered
cue for downstream robot learning without requiring paired robot actions.
Extraction is difficult because fingertips are small or occluded, background
corners produce competing responses, and multiple hands and objects create
association ambiguity. Changes in hand color and appearance, viewpoint,
illumination, background, and camera setup further challenge transfer from
limited point annotations.

HOC2R addresses these failures by combining complementary frozen visual
representations. A proposal head over DINOv3 features identifies likely hand-object interaction
regions, while a learned heatmap head predicts contact likelihood from
whole-image SAM 2.1 features. Proposal-box touch scores rerank heatmap candidates. Count-aware
automation distinguishes contact from no-contact frames and predicts how many
contacts are visible. For downstream robot control with a two-finger gripper,
fixed-two localization assumes that consecutive frames containing hand-object
contact have already been identified. We call these frames the active contact
segment. Fixed-two then returns two proposal-constrained points. This separation is
important: count-aware automation is strongest on held-out in-domain tasks,
while fixed-two localization is more
reliable after domain shift.

HOC2R provides a practical starting checkpoint for extracting robot-usable
contact trajectories from human manipulation videos. Its principal advantage
appears under multi-hand ambiguity, where adapted baselines can follow a
resting or non-manipulating hand. We further test whether the extracted
contacts remain useful for robot control after RGB-D lifting to 3D and
geometric safety filtering.

Our contributions are:

HOC2R, a hand-object contact-trajectory extractor that combines
proposal geometry learned from DINOv3 features with point localization
learned from SAM 2.1 features for count-aware automation and fixed-two
localization.

evaluations across held-out tasks, domains, and model components that expose
multi-hand robustness, domain sensitivity of contact-presence and contact-count prediction, and the effect of
small but diverse adaptation sets.

calibrated RGB-D robot evaluation showing that the extracted
contacts can produce feasible post-contact trajectories for grasping,
pushing, and two-hand pen motion.

localization.

title: PRISM: Primitive Routing via In-context Skill Mixing for Retentive VLA Adaptation
authors: Jiachen Tao,Gengyu Zhang,Haoxuan Wang,Bing Liu,Yan Yan
comment: . Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models promise a single language-conditioned policy adaptable to many manipulation behaviors, yet deployment additionally requires skill retention and long-horizon composition: a policy must retain previously acquired skills and reuse them inside composite tasks whose behavior changes across phases. The standard recipe absorbs every new task into one shared update, which provides neither a parameter-level locus for reusable skills nor a mechanism for invoking each skill along the trajectory. We observe that this missing structure is latent rather than absent: per-skill low-rank updates of a pretrained VLA occupy a robustly distinguishable, low-dimensional subspace, and a single composite-task LoRA concentrates roughly half of its Frobenius energy in this subspace, against a near-zero matched random-rotation control. Building on this geometry, we introduce PRISM, which represents reusable skills as parameter-level primitives: each skill family is stored as a dedicated low-rank action-expert adapter in a primitive bank, primitives are augmented with skill-specific low-rank residuals and composed at inference by a per-chunk VLM-conditioned router that reads the prefix representation to track task progress, and the router is supervised by per-chunk labels from a deterministic, task-conditioned, action-derived oracle. During composite training, the vision encoder, the language LoRA, the skill residuals, the router, and the shared action projections and time MLP are updated; every primitive is held frozen, so the base per-skill action-expert adapters are preserved by construction. On RoboCasa365, PRISM achieves 56.43%\mathbf{56.43\%} atomic-skill success and reaches 20.00%\mathbf{20.00\%} on long-horizon composite tasks, while a standard π0.5\pi_{0.5}-LoRA two-stage fine-tune reaches 17.86%17.86\% atomic and 17.50%17.50\% composite success. We additionally validate PRISM on an AgileX PIPER real-robot setup.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models [6, 5, 20, 36, 4, 3, 35] are emerging as a general substrate for language-conditioned robot manipulation: a single pretrained policy, steered by natural-language instruction, can in principle be adapted toward a broad range of downstream behaviors. Yet deployment exposes two failure modes of the standard single-policy adaptation paradigm: sequentially fine-tuning the policy on a new behavior degrades performance on previously acquired ones, forcing a choice between retraining from scratch and losing capabilities; and long-horizon tasks that recombine known sub-skills must still be fit end-to-end as if their constituent skills had not already been mastered—an object-washing task, for instance, requires end-to-end training even though it chains a lever-like interaction (to activate a water source) with a pick-and-place-like interaction (to move the object through the stream). We refer to the two requirements that address these failures as skill retention and long-horizon composition, and ask how a VLA should be parameterized to support both.

The standard adaptation paradigm is monolithic: a downstream task is absorbed into a shared set of model parameters, with no explicit representation of which part of the update corresponds to which reusable behavior. This parameterization may be adequate for mastering one task in isolation, but it lacks two handles required for deployment. The first is where: where is a previously learned skill localized in the model update? Without such a parameter-level locus, later updates can interfere with the directions that supported earlier behaviors. Common defenses either allocate additional task-specific parameters, which limits reuse, or constrain updates globally, which can slow acquisition without identifying the skill-specific directions that require protection. The second handle is when: when during a long-horizon trajectory should the policy invoke each skill? A composite task cycles through distinct phases of object interaction, motion, and sub-goal. Without a mechanism for switching behavioral regimes, an undifferentiated policy must fit each composite end-to-end as if it were a fresh task. Long-horizon demonstrations are not merely longer action sequences but reflect the selection and recombination of behaviors the policy has already acquired, and a policy with no parameter-level skill identity has no way to interpret such a trajectory in relation to its prior skills.

We find that this missing structure is more latent than absent. When each primitive skill family is adapted on its own through a small low-rank update [17], the family of per-skill update tensors does not diffuse uniformly throughout parameter space: it occupies a robust, semantically clustered subspace that reproduces across independently trained checkpoints (Section 3.3)—low-dimensional relative to the full action-expert parameter space, while remaining nearly full-rank across primitive families. Moreover, when a single LoRA is fit on a composite-task dataset, a substantial fraction of its update tensor lies in the linear span of the per-skill update tensors (Section 3.3): composite-task behavior is, to a first approximation, partially expressible as a combination of per-skill primitives. However, when atomic and composite behaviors are absorbed into a single shared adapter trained sequentially, the skill-specific directions learned during atomic adaptation are no longer separately addressable, and atomic-skill performance degrades as composite training proceeds. We refer to this loss of per-skill addressability as primitive collapse.

This observation suggests a constructive parameterization. If reusable skills occupy distinguishable low-dimensional update directions, then mixture weights over these updates can be trained to serve as skill-level control variables rather than arbitrary adapter coefficients. Later adaptation need not rewrite a shared update; it can preserve skill-localized slots while learning to route over them. Likewise, long-horizon execution need not fit composite behavior as an independent policy; it can select or mix primitives over time as the task progresses. Under this view, retaining and composing skills reduce to routing over preserved primitives: once a skill is represented as a primitive slot, executing a long-horizon behavior activates the appropriate primitive or mixture at each phase.

Building on this observation, we introduce PRISM, a VLA adaptation framework that turns reusable skills into first-class parameter-level objects. PRISM has three coupled components: a primitive bank that stores each skill family as its own low-rank adapter over the action expert, augmented with a skill-specific residual during composite training; a prefix-conditioned router that emits a per-chunk mixture over these primitive–residual branches; and a deterministic action-derived labeler that supplies per-chunk supervision for the router. The bank gives a direct parameter-level answer to the where question—adding a new skill amounts to adding a new slot, while every existing primitive remains parametrically untouched.

The router answers the when question. At every action chunk it reads the VLM prefix—a contextual feature fusing the current instruction with the current visual state—and emits a distribution over the bank, so the active mixture varies along a long-horizon trajectory. Conditioning on the prefix rather than on the instruction is essential: the instruction is fixed across the trajectory, while sub-goal placement depends on how far the robot has progressed. Training the router from composite demonstrations is nontrivial because behavior cloning alone exerts little pressure for mixture weights to align with skill semantics; PRISM therefore supervises it with per-chunk labels produced by a deterministic, action-derived labeler that requires no learned parameters or per-trajectory human labels once the rule is fixed.

In summary, PRISM makes three contributions.
(i) Structural finding. Per-skill low-rank updates of VLA action experts span a near-NN-dimensional, semantically clustered subspace that is reproducible across independently trained banks; a composite-task LoRA places ∼\sim56%56\% of its Frobenius energy in this span, versus ≈0%\approx 0\% under matched random rotations.
(ii) Framework. PRISM couples a primitive bank with skill-specific residuals, a per-chunk VLM-conditioned router, and a deterministic action-derived labeler; during composite training, the vision encoder, language LoRA, residuals, router, action projections, and time MLP are updated, while primitives remain frozen.
(iii) Evaluation. On RoboCasa365, PRISM achieves 56.43%\mathbf{56.43\%} atomic success after composite training and reaches 20.00%\mathbf{20.00\%} composite success, against 17.86%17.86\% atomic and 17.50%17.50\% composite success for a standard π0.5\pi_{0.5}-LoRA two-stage fine-tune. We further validate PRISM on an AgileX PIPER real robot.
