title: HomeLoop: A Simulation Framework and Benchmark for Robot-IoT Coordination in Everyday Domestic Assistance and Safety
authors: Ramy ElMallah,Marc Bishara,Hyegang Kim,Yuxi Zhang,Chongyu Zhu,Chi-Guhn Lee
abstract: Recent progress in embodied robotics is bringing robots closer to deployment in homes, as vision-language models (VLMs) are demonstrating significant advances in reasoning, making VLM-driven robots promising home assistant agents. These agents will often be introduced into homes that already have cameras, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, and residents with wearables. To fulfill their potential, they need to integrate with existing smart infrastructure and reason through ambiguous scenarios: a smoke alarm may come from a pan about to ignite, a pan already on fire, a resident cooking or a faulty sensor, and each calls for a different response. To that end, we introduce HomeLoop, a simulation framework and benchmark built on Isaac Sim that combines robot bodies, networked devices and wearables, simulated residents and visitors, faulty sensors, and hazards that evolve over time. Our benchmark is composed of 20 tasks across five families grounded in real-world household hazards and needs, and designed so that the same alert can have different causes. A runtime monitor scores each episode with temporal-logic checks on the final outcome and the actions along the way, and every action carries a predefined cost. We evaluate six open-weight and proprietary VLMs. The best achieves a family-balanced score of 61.9%, and across models we see a pattern of over-reaction: failed episodes involving prohibited interventions outnumber those involving missed required interventions by more than two to one, with models often shutting off the stove before investigating the alarm’s cause. HomeLoop is an extensible foundation intended for use in research on robot–-IoT coordination, long-term memory, proactive assistance, and privacy–-safety trade-offs as VLM capabilities improve. HomeLoop will be released with 2,100 home layouts that can be automatically furnished in diverse configurations, five robot bodies and 20 networked device types which can be combined into a myriad of customized episodes.
introduction:
Consider a home assistant robot with access to data from the home’s Internet of Things (IoT) devices including sensors and cameras. A smoke alarm sounds in the kitchen, and the cause may be a pan approaching ignition, a pan already on fire, the resident cooking, or a faulty sensor. The robot could react in several ways: recheck the sensor, inspect the scene through a home camera, physically enter the kitchen to turn off the stove, contact the resident, or call emergency services. These actions have consequences that depend on the underlying situation. Turning off the stove can prevent a pan overheating, and calling emergency services can help when a fire has started. However, turning off the stove during normal cooking interrupts the resident’s meal, while calling emergency services when there is no fire is a costly mistake, illustrating how nuanced reasoning is needed for a home assistant agent to successfully react.

We have grounded our task selection in HomeLoop in common hazards that occur in homes. For example, cooking is the leading cause of residential building fires in the United States (U.S. Fire Administration, 2025). Beyond that, water damage and freezing damage generated 1.5 claims per 100 insured homes annually in 2019–2023 (Insurance Information Institute, 2026). Seniors falling is another common hazard that assistive robots have to respond to, affecting more than one in four adults aged 65 and older each year (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2026). The agent could also assist with everyday tasks such as shopping, housework, and meal preparation, which are commonly supported by family caregivers (AARP and National Alliance for Caregiving, 2025).

Existing works that combine benchmarks and simulation frameworks capture different aspects of home assistance, but lack a shared environment for IoT interaction and embodied robots across everyday assistance and safety tasks. In HomeBench (Li et al., 2025) and SimuHome (Seo et al., 2026), language models issue calls to device application programming interfaces (APIs) in a non-rendered simulation of IoT sensors and actuators without robots. In BEHAVIOR-1K (Li et al., 2023), embodied agents perform household tasks in rendered homes, but without networked IoT devices. SafeAgentBench (Yin et al., 2024) and IS-Bench (Lu et al., 2026a), tested in the AI2-THOR (Kolve et al., 2017) and OmniGibson (Li et al., 2023) simulators respectively, evaluate whether language-model planners refuse hazardous instructions or mitigate hazards, but both lack IoT capabilities. In HAZARD (Zhou et al., 2024), embodied agents act amid simulated fires and floods without connected devices. Robot–IoT integration has been explored in systems such as RiSH (Do et al., 2018), CBASH (Zhu et al., 2023), a system built on SF2D (Azghadi et al., 2025), and IndoorR2X (Yang et al., 2026b). These systems demonstrate connections between robots and household sensors, but do not provide a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating agents across everyday assistance and safety tasks. Among the 37 works we compared (Table 1, Appendix E), none provides such a benchmark and simulation framework with networked sensing and control, house cameras, embodied action, and outcome-based evaluation. To address this gap, we present HomeLoop, a benchmark and simulation framework that brings a robot, networked devices including house cameras, and residents into a shared household environment for everyday assistance and safety tasks (Figure 1). Built in Isaac Sim (NVIDIA, 2025a), HomeLoop allows homes, robot bodies, scenarios, tasks, and access to connected devices and cameras to be configured independently. Scenarios define resident activities, device faults, and timed events, while tasks specify required outcomes and time and cost limits. A runtime monitor evaluates task completion and safety conditions on the world state and robot and device actions throughout and at the end of the episode, using finite-trace linear temporal logic.

We make three contributions:

A simulation framework in which homes, scenarios, tasks, robot bodies and service access are composed from independent configuration files, with 2,100 furnished homes built from real floor plans, five robot bodies and 20 networked device types available (Section 3 ).

A benchmark of 20 tasks in five families chosen from household needs and grouped so that tasks starting with the same alert require different responses (Section 4).

An evaluation of six open-weight and proprietary VLMs; ablations of price visibility, service access and images; an analysis of when they intervene; and a run of one model in ten further homes, all recomputable from the released episode records (Sections 5 and 6).

Across the six models (Appendix A), the best, Astra, fully succeeded on 12 of the 20 tasks in each of two runs, and Gemma 4 31B, which has public weights, reached 69% of Astra’s overall score at 3% of its API spend. In total, wrongful interventions outnumbered missed ones by more than two to one. For example, Astra, Gemini and Luna switched off the stove or the water main before capturing any image, even when the alarm had a benign or faulty cause.

title: Polarization calibration of fisheye cameras using skylight in the wild
authors: Shuo Wang,Shiqi Che,Dianze Dong,Wenxin Liu
comment: submitted to ICRA 2026
abstract: Skylight polarization provides directional cues for robotic navigation, but fisheye lens effects and analyzer imperfections can degrade polarization measurements across the field of view. We present a joint lens–analyzer calibration method that explicitly models incidence-dependent lens transmission together with analyzer gains and angular offsets in a unified eight-parameter formulation. Given known geometric calibration, rotations between camera frames can be estimated using visual features and cross-frame directional polarized light consistency can be used for polarization calibration. Therefore, our calibration approach requires only a short handheld outdoor sequence under natural skylight, without dedicated polarization calibration equipment or a predeﬁned sky polarization model. On real-world outdoor sequences, the proposed method achieves a weighted cross-frame angle-of-linear-polarization (AoLP) mean absolute error below 0.5° across all incidence angles, with a 73.4% reduction in the 80°–90° incidence angle region, and generalizes to an independent sequence with an overall mean absolute error of 0.466° without refitting. Preliminary solar-azimuth experiments using a camera mounted on a quadruped robot further show improved alignment with the visible solar center, supporting the potential of calibrated AoLP measurements for relative-heading estimation and future polarization–inertial navigation. The calibration software tool will be released upon acceptance of this paper.
introduction:
Skylight polarization provides a natural compass for robotic navigation by encoding heading relative to the solar meridian. Atmospheric scattering creates a polarization pattern tied to the sun’s position, which insects such as bees exploit through specialized receptors in their compound eyes [1]. This directional cue has recently been incorporated into visual-inertial localization frameworks to constrain heading drift [2] and shown significant improvement in GPS-denied conditions. Beyond navigation, polarization sensing has shown promise in transparent object reconstruction [3], further expanding its role in robotic perception.

Current polarization navigation systems often employ point-source polarization sensor or compound-eye-inspired configurations that sample a small set of viewing directions [4]. Clouds and weak polarization can easily compromise the available directional cues [5], while sparse sampling restricts the ability to recover reliable information from other sky regions. On the other hand, a key limitation of image-based polarization navigation is the lack of effective full-field calibration for fisheye polarization cameras. Although fisheye optics provide broad angular coverage of skylight polarization [6], conventional DoFP calibration methods primarily correct analyzer response errors [7], leaving substantial polarization distortions in peripheral image regions due to incidence-dependent lens responses [8, 9]. Existing image-based navigation approaches typically assume a horizontally mounted, upward-facing camera and estimate heading from zenith-centered polarization patterns or manually selected image regions [10]. This reliance on observations near the optical axis limits the use of peripheral information and makes heading estimation sensitive to camera orientation changes caused by platform motion, potentially reducing navigation accuracy.

We propose a joint lens–analyzer calibration framework that combines the incidence-dependent relative transmission of orthogonal polarization components with analyzer gains and angular offsets in a unified forward model. Under the axial-symmetry assumption, we model the lens response in a single incidence plane and extend it across viewing azimuths by rotating the local polarization basis (Fig. 1). The resulting calibration effectively eliminates lens-induced polarization distortions and corrects analyzer imperfections, enabling accurate polarization measurements across the entire image, including peripheral regions.

In addition to the newly proposed model for full-field polarization calibration, we combine the advantages of image-based polarization sensing with visual motion estimation to develop a practical, low-cost calibration procedure. Our method requires only a short handheld outdoor video sequence capturing the sky and surrounding structures near the horizon, without any expensive dedicated laboratory equipment or complicated experimental setup.

The main contributions of this work are:

A unified eight-parameter lens–analyzer response model for fisheye polarization cameras, enabling joint calibration of lens transmission, analyzer response, and angular misalignment.

A practical handheld outdoor calibration framework requiring neither dedicated polarization calibration equipment nor predefined sky polarization models.

An open-source software package, to be released upon acceptance, that enables convenient use of the proposed calibration system and supports practical deployment.

1. A unified eight-parameter lens–analyzer response model for fisheye polarization cameras, enabling joint calibration of lens transmission, analyzer response, and angular misalignment.

2. A practical handheld outdoor calibration framework requiring neither dedicated polarization calibration equipment nor predefined sky polarization models.

3. An open-source software package, to be released upon acceptance, that enables convenient use of the proposed calibration system and supports practical deployment.

title: FATHOM: World-Model-Guided Diffusion Action-Trajectory Selection for Sparse-Marker AUV Tracking
authors: Xiaorui Wang,Zeyu Sha,Mingyang Yang,David Chen Wang,Feitian Zhang
abstract: Reliable relative tracking is fundamental to cooperative autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs), yet remains challenging under nonlinear vehicle dynamics and degraded underwater visual conditions. Active light markers improve robustness to appearance variation, but provide deliberately sparse observations that can become incomplete or corrupted by occlusion, reflections, and detection noise during dynamic motion. To address the resulting partial-observation control problem, this paper proposes FATHOM, a world-model-guided diffusion action-trajectory selection framework for sparse-marker AUV tracking. FATHOM first integrates structured marker observations, inertial measurements, action history, and temporal dynamics into a predictive tracking belief using a multimodal task-supervised recurrent state-space model. A diffusion action prior then generates multiple expert-like multi-thruster trajectories, whose future tracking consequences are predicted through the learned latent dynamics. Rather than directly executing a generated trajectory, FATHOM selects the most favorable candidate under an explicit receding-horizon objective and continually updates the decision from onboard observations. Extensive offline analyses verify the learned predictive belief, multi-step world-model prediction, diffusion trajectory generation, and predictive selection. More importantly, comprehensive real-AUV experiments, including strong pose-based comparisons and component ablations, demonstrate robust autonomous tracking across nominal and challenging motions with naturally occurring partial marker visibility, while maintaining real-time onboard operation without motion-capture feedback.
introduction:
Autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) are increasingly moving from isolated operation toward cooperative autonomy, enabling persistent observation, distributed exploration, target following, inspection, and intervention over extended underwater environments [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]. A fundamental capability in such systems is close-range relative tracking, where a follower must regulate its motion with respect to a moving leader. Unlike waypoint regulation against a static reference, relative tracking continuously couples perception, target motion, nonlinear vehicle dynamics, and multi-axis actuation. Underwater operation further complicates this loop through hydrodynamic coupling, external disturbances, and strongly variable visual conditions.

Optical sensing is attractive for close-range tracking because of its high spatial resolution and low latency. Its reliability, however, is affected by wavelength-dependent attenuation, scattering, turbidity, nonuniform illumination, and reflections [8, 9, 10, 11, 12]. Active light markers provide a purposeful alternative to relying solely on natural appearance. Their controlled spectral and geometric structure produces distinctive observations and has been successfully used for underwater and robotic relative localization [13, 14, 15]. The resulting sensing is robust but deliberately sparse. During dynamic relative motion, only a subset of markers may remain visible, while image noise, reflections, occlusion, and spurious detections further perturb individual observations. The controller therefore cannot always infer the interaction state reliably from the current frame alone.

A common solution is to reconstruct an explicit six-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) relative pose and feed it to a conventional or learned controller. Modern active-marker estimators provide accurate and temporally consistent pose estimates even under partial observations [13, 14, 15]. Yet pose estimation and feedback decision making are not identical problems. For dynamic tracking, information useful for predicting the next control consequence is distributed across recent marker observations, vehicle motion, and previously executed actions. Compressing this history immediately into a single geometric estimate risks discarding task-relevant temporal and dynamic information. This motivates maintaining a compact representation of how the relative interaction evolves rather than estimating only the leader’s current pose.

Latent world models provide a natural basis for such reasoning. Recurrent state-space models summarize incomplete observation histories into latent states and predict their evolution under candidate actions [16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22]. This capability is particularly relevant to sparse underwater sensing because temporal memory and action-conditioned prediction address different aspects of the same partial-observation problem. A useful control representation should therefore not only explain the current tracking condition, but also support short-horizon prediction under hypothetical thruster commands.

Prediction alone, however, does not determine which commands should be considered. Direct regression to a single action sequence is restrictive when different multi-thruster behaviors are valid for the same tracking condition. Diffusion models provide an expressive way to represent high-dimensional and multimodal action distributions [23, 24, 25, 26, 27]. Recent work has extended this idea from direct imitation toward trajectory generation and model-guided planning [28, 29, 30, 31]. This suggests a complementary view of generative control. Rather than committing immediately to one action, a learned policy generates multiple plausible trajectories whose predicted consequences are evaluated before execution.

These observations lead naturally to the framework proposed in this work. We introduce FATHOM, short for Feedback Action Trajectory selection with Hidden-state Outcome Modeling. The name also reflects the physical and conceptual setting of the problem. A fathom is historically associated with measuring underwater depth, while to fathom means to understand something that is not directly observable. In our setting, the controller must similarly infer a hidden tracking condition from sparse underwater observations and reason about the consequences of future actions.

FATHOM organizes closed-loop decision making as Believe–Generate–Predict–Select, as illustrated in Fig. 1. A Structured Sparse-Marker Encoder (SSME) extracts a compact representation from unordered and partially missing LED observations. A Multimodal Task-Supervised Recurrent State-Space Model (MT-RSSM) then integrates this representation with inertial measurements, previous actions, and temporal dynamics to form a predictive tracking belief. Conditioned on this belief, a Diffusion Action Prior (DAP) generates multiple expert-like trajectories of eight-thruster commands. MT-RSSM predicts their future tracking consequences, and a World-Model Predictive Selector (WMPS) chooses the trajectory with the lowest receding-horizon control objective. Only its first command is executed before the belief is updated from the next onboard observation.

This design gives each learned component a distinct role. The recurrent world model captures what cannot be inferred reliably from a single sparse observation and predicts how the interaction may evolve. Diffusion represents multiple plausible control behaviors without collapsing them into a single conditional action. Predictive selection then converts this diversity into an online advantage by choosing among those behaviors according to their anticipated closed-loop consequences. The resulting controller operates from onboard sparse LED observations and inertial sensing, without requiring motion-capture feedback during deployment.

The main contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we develop a control-oriented representation for AUV tracking under deliberately sparse active visual sensing, where SSME and MT-RSSM integrate incomplete marker observations, inertial motion, action history, and temporal dynamics into a predictive tracking belief that supports both hidden-state inference and future prediction. Second, we propose FATHOM, a world-model-guided diffusion control framework that treats diffusion as an action-trajectory prior rather than the final decision maker. Multiple expert-like thruster trajectories are evaluated through learned latent dynamics, and a finite-error analysis relates world-model prediction accuracy to the quality of predictive trajectory selection. Third, we demonstrate fully onboard sparse visual–inertial tracking on real AUVs and systematically evaluate FATHOM against privileged and pose-based controllers, showing the benefits of predictive belief and trajectory selection under challenging motion and naturally occurring partial marker visibility while retaining real-time execution.

title: Localizing and Editing the Goal Representation of a Vision-Language-Action Model
authors: Sudhanshu Srivastava,Faisal Aqlan
abstract:
Operators can state safety constraints for robots as prohibitions such as “do not put the bowl on the stove”. We study whether OpenVLA follows such prohibitions and where it represents the goal it executes. The 10 tasks of LIBERO-Goal share one scene, so we can label the goal that each rollout executes. We combine closed-loop rollouts with activation patching, linear probes, activation steering and runtime monitors.
On LIBERO-Goal, negation had no detectable effect on which task OpenVLA executed. The model executed the forbidden task in 79% of negated rollouts and completed 78% of plain tasks. A goal probe gives similar read-outs under “not X” and “X”.
Activation patching shows that the first action depends mostly on the instruction tokens before layer 12 and on the last prompt token from layer 16 onward.
A fixed steering vector at the instruction tokens at layer 8 redirected 12 of 18 rollouts. Fixed vectors and prefill patches at layers 12 to 20 redirected none of 158. From layer 16, only patches at every decoded action token redirected the robot (15 of 18 rollouts at layer 24).
When the instruction changes during a rollout, the layer-32 goal read-out detects non-compliance better than failure detectors, and an external probe on image and instruction features performs comparably.
These results support enforcing prohibitions outside the instruction and monitoring goal read-outs against the specification. Goal edits in OpenVLA should act before layer 12 or patch every action token.
introduction:
People use language to specify and correct robot tasks, and vision-language-action models (VLAs) [1, 2, 3] take this language directly as input. Many safety requirements are prohibitions. An operator may forbid contact with a hazardous object or entry into a restricted zone. Such an instruction names no goal. It removes behaviors from the set that the robot may execute, so a robot that executes an excluded behavior violates a safety constraint.
Audits show that VLAs under-use language [4, 5, 6]. A VLA whose actions do not change under a negation or a correction can competently execute a task that the operator excluded. This is an embodied instance of goal misgeneralization [7, 8].
Runtime monitors for VLAs predict whether the instructed task will fail [9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15]. They are not designed to flag a robot that competently performs a forbidden task.
We ask where OpenVLA [2] encodes its goal and whether this representation can be edited. We also test whether goal read-outs help runtime oversight. In LIBERO-Goal [16], 10 tasks share one scene, so the instruction alone selects the goal. We evaluate all 10 goal predicates at every step to label the executed goal of each rollout.

Contributions.
In this simulated scene, negation had no detectable effect on which task OpenVLA executed. We locate the goal, show where it can be edited and compare goal read-outs with failure detectors as monitors.

title: Lodos: A Lightweight Simulator Designed for Contact-Rich Interactions with Detailed Meshes
authors: Onur Beker,Andreas René Geist,Georg Martius
abstract: In recent years, massively parallelized rigid-body simulation has played a central role in robotics research, enabling rapid progress in areas such as reinforcement learning, stochastic optimal control, and randomized smoothing-based trajectory optimization. Particularly in contact-rich settings, the scalability of such simulations in large part depends on well-optimized representations of collision geometry, often requiring a coarse approximation of the underlying surfaces using primitives such as spheres, capsules, cylinders, and boxes. Whenever the complexity of the surfaces or the precision demands of the application render such approximations insufficient, it is instead necessary to employ mesh-mesh collisions, which impose a significant reduction in throughput. This paper proposes a simulation framework designed from scratch to address this bottleneck, with novel routines for broadphase and narrowphase collision detection as well as the subsequent contact dynamics computation. As experimentally validated, the framework matches existing well-established simulators in terms of physical faithfulness, and can achieve approximately an order of magnitude higher throughput in the detailed mesh-mesh collision setting that it specializes in. The source code is available at https://github.com/martius-lab/lodos.
introduction:
What makes a good simulator for solving control problems that involve contact-rich interactions? Let us build the desiderata by focusing on the control and contact-rich interaction parts of the question separately.

A good simulator for control: Sampling-based control approaches that leverage massively vectorized simulation [1, 2] have proven to be very proficient at solving contact-rich manipulation tasks. A common pattern shared by such approaches, whether it is domain randomization with RL [3, 4], risk-aware control with stochastic MPC [5], or randomized smoothing [6] with gradient-based optimization, is that actions are selected such that they remain “approximately correct” with respect to metrics averaged over randomized ensembles of contact parameters generated via artificial (and oftentimes non-physical) perturbations (e.g. adding virtual forces, noisy friction coefficients and haptic sensing, approximate or domain randomized collision geometry). And a main argument of this paper is that in such a setting, perturbations and averaging already introduce a “convex-hull” effect on how much the physical faithfulness of each ensemble member can reflect on (or matter for) the selection of the common actions facing the ensemble. Therefore, there should be room for using simplified versions of contact dynamics (that can still sufficiently preserve the “convex-hull”) to achieve drastically increased ensemble sizes instead, resulting in a net benefit for the downstream control algorithm.

A good simulator for contact-rich interactions: Most of the commonly used simulators in robotics research [7, 8, 9, 10] use a combination of convex polytope based collision detection [11, 12] with a numerical optimization routine to solve the regularized non-linear complementarity (NCP) or cone-complementarity (CCP) systems of equations describing contact dynamics [13, 14, 15, 9, 16, 17]. While this battle-tested recipe certainly has its merits, it suffers from the following drawbacks particularly in contact-rich settings:

The regularization introduced to the NCP/CCP equations scales frictional contact forces down from the exact value needed to maintain complete staticity in a rigid-body system (e.g. zero velocity and acceleration), meaning all contacts eventually slip under constant forces such as gravity.

Applying GJK-EPA algorithms [11, 18] to convex polytope collisions produces a single contact point, which is occasionally further extended into a sparse set of contact points lying at the corners of a 2D polygon [12]. Neither mechanism can faithfully implement contact forces distributed over a patch, meaning torsional friction is emulated in an ad hoc manner by introducing artificial constraints to the optimization routine that oppose motion around the contact normal.

Convex-polytope-based collision routines scale poorly with parallelization, particularly under contact-rich configurations involving complex non-convex meshes.

Contributions. We present a novel simulation routine designed from scratch to facilitate research on developing control algorithms in contact-rich settings. In particular:

We propose a new collision detection routine built upon sphere - SDF collisions as the axiomatic interaction, which can represent arbitrary non-convex (closed) surfaces at arbitrary levels of precision, and scales much more favorably with massive parallelization compared to the traditional convex polytope based approach. Specifically, this includes a novel hierarchical broadphase routine to logarithmically cull potential sphere-SDF interactions, and a novel narrowphase routine using 3D-spline-based SDF and surface normal representations whose evaluation time is independent of geometry complexity.

We propose a new model of contact dynamics based on rescaling spring-damper forces via a staggered fixed-point iteration scheme, derived from a lumped parameterization of the traditional SOCP-based contact models employed in most common simulators [16, 7]. The main benefits are that it: i) scales much more favorably under massive vectorization compared to standard approaches, ii) does not exhibit a slipping artifact, iii) allows patch-patch contacts and therefore faithful torsional friction simulation.

1. The regularization introduced to the NCP/CCP equations scales frictional contact forces down from the exact value needed to maintain complete staticity in a rigid-body system (e.g. zero velocity and acceleration), meaning all contacts eventually slip under constant forces such as gravity.

2. Applying GJK-EPA algorithms [11, 18] to convex polytope collisions produces a single contact point, which is occasionally further extended into a sparse set of contact points lying at the corners of a 2D polygon [12]. Neither mechanism can faithfully implement contact forces distributed over a patch, meaning torsional friction is emulated in an ad hoc manner by introducing artificial constraints to the optimization routine that oppose motion around the contact normal.

3. Convex-polytope-based collision routines scale poorly with parallelization, particularly under contact-rich configurations involving complex non-convex meshes.

1. We propose a new collision detection routine built upon sphere - SDF collisions as the axiomatic interaction, which can represent arbitrary non-convex (closed) surfaces at arbitrary levels of precision, and scales much more favorably with massive parallelization compared to the traditional convex polytope based approach. Specifically, this includes a novel hierarchical broadphase routine to logarithmically cull potential sphere-SDF interactions, and a novel narrowphase routine using 3D-spline-based SDF and surface normal representations whose evaluation time is independent of geometry complexity.

2. We propose a new model of contact dynamics based on rescaling spring-damper forces via a staggered fixed-point iteration scheme, derived from a lumped parameterization of the traditional SOCP-based contact models employed in most common simulators [16, 7]. The main benefits are that it: i) scales much more favorably under massive vectorization compared to standard approaches, ii) does not exhibit a slipping artifact, iii) allows patch-patch contacts and therefore faithful torsional friction simulation.

title: Lodos-v2: An Efficient Primal Formulation of the Exact Frictional Contact Problem
authors: Onur Beker,Andreas René Geist,Georg Martius
abstract:
Lodos-v2 is a GPU-based simulation framework for massively parallel rigid-body dynamics with contact. It is specifically designed to achieve high throughput in scenes involving collisions among large numbers of detailed meshes.
Its predecessor, Lodos-v1, had two main limitations. First, it solved the standard convex relaxation of cone-complementarity-based contact dynamics, thereby inheriting well-known physical artifacts, including lift-off and artificial compliance in the normal direction, as well as creep in the tangential direction. Second, its contact-group reparameterization scheme, which rescales spring-damper forces using a single factor per collision pair, could not be integrated with other constraints required by a full-fledged simulator, such as joint limits and welds.
Lodos-v2 addresses both limitations through two main contributions. First, it introduces an efficient algorithm for solving the exact frictional contact problem by sequentially solving a cascade of convex relaxations in primal form within an outer proximal minimization loop. Second, it extends the contact-group reparameterization scheme of Lodos-v1 to the primal formulation of cone-complementarity-based contact dynamics, enabling its integration with the other constraints of a full-fledged simulator.
Experiments demonstrate that these contributions result in throughput improvements over established rigid-body simulation frameworks. The source code is available at https://github.com/martius-lab/lodos.
introduction:
Massively vectorized simulation of rigid-body dynamics with contact (Makoviychuk et al., 2021; Google DeepMind and NVIDIA, 2025; The Newton
Contributors, 2025) is essential for a range of robotics applications, including reinforcement learning (RL) (Hwangbo et al., 2019; Allshire et al., 2022), sampling-based model-predictive control (MPC) (Kurtz, 2024; Li et al., 2024), and randomized smoothing (Suh et al., 2022; Pang et al., 2023) for gradient-based optimization. Lodos-v1 (Beker et al., 2026) was developed to support such applications by enabling high-throughput simulation of scenes that contain large numbers of collision pairs between geometrically detailed meshes. Its two main contributions were (i) efficient broadphase and narrowphase collision routines for vertex-SDF contacts and (ii) a “contact-group reparameterization” scheme that scales spring-damper contact forces using a single factor per collision pair, thereby making the number of solver decision variables and constraints independent of the number of contacts. Lodos-v2 preserves the collision detection framework of Lodos-v1 while substantially extending its treatment of contact dynamics. In particular:

Lodos-v1 lacked a mechanism for integrating contact constraints with other constraint types commonly supported by general-purpose physics simulators, such as MuJoCo (Todorov et al., 2012), including joint limits, weld constraints, and friction-loss constraints. Lodos-v2 overcomes this limitation, enabling it to reproduce MuJoCo’s contact dynamics at higher simulation throughput.

Lodos-v1 solved the convex relaxation of cone-complementarity-based contact dynamics introduced by Anitescu et al. (Anitescu, 2006), which is also employed by MuJoCo. As a result, it inherits the known physical artifacts of this relaxation, including sliding contacts lifting-off, normal-direction compliance, and tangential creep that prevents contacts from remaining stationary under zero velocity and acceleration. Lodos-v2 addresses these limitations by introducing a novel primal-form solver for the exact cone complementarity problem, building on the work of Carpentier et al. (Carpentier et al., 2024). This enables Lodos-v2 to reproduce the contact dynamics of Kamino (Tsounis et al., 2026) at higher simulation throughput.

title: What Limits mmWave Human-State Sensing for Robot Perception?
authors: Shuntian Zheng,Guangming Wang,Hongyang He,Shuai He,Yu Guan
abstract:
Assistive robots and search-and-rescue platforms require reliable human-state sensing in smoke, darkness, and privacy-sensitive environments, where cameras and LiDAR may be unreliable.
Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar offers an alternative that works without ambient light, penetrates smoke, and does not capture visual appearance.
However, the compact arrays that fit robot size, power, and cost budgets have limited apertures, producing joint-localization errors on the order of decimeters at a few meters, large enough to compromise the safety margins and tracking accuracy a robot depends on.
Existing pipelines reduce pose error through frame fusion, multiple viewpoints, return selection, or stronger estimators, but examine one technique at a time, without relating its effect to a shared measurement limit or separating gains from added information from gains from estimator completion.
We address this gap with a framework that models the human and environment as one time-varying scattering field and states a Cramér–Rao-type error floor for joint localization as a function of bandwidth, aperture, signal-to-noise ratio, fused frame count, phase coherence, and visibility of retained returns.
We then use existing frame-fusion, multi-viewpoint, return-selection, and pose-estimation methods as matched probes of this floor rather than as competing pipelines.
Under the evaluated conditions, experiments on three datasets and a live deployment show these strategies move joint-localization error in the predicted directions, for example lowering mean per-joint position error from about 97 to 65 mm with a second viewpoint, while a stronger estimator mainly lowers overall error by completing joints the measurement cannot resolve.
These results give the robotics community a principled basis for deciding whether to prioritize observation design or estimator capacity when deploying reliable mmWave human sensing.
introduction:
Human-aware robots need reliable estimates of where a person is and how the body is articulated, so that standoff distances, tracking covariance, and contact or avoidance plans remain trustworthy [2, 13].
Cameras and LiDAR supply dense geometry under favorable optics, but steam, smoke, darkness, and privacy-sensitive indoor layouts routinely break that assumption, as in the factory scene of Fig. 1.

Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar is a complementary front end for these settings because radio returns remain usable without ambient light, penetrate fog and steam, and do not archive visual appearance [16].
This promise is strongest on the compact single-chip arrays that fit on-robot size, power, and cost budgets.
Yet those arrays resolve human joints far more coarsely than optical range sensors: a representative 3​T×4​R3\mathrm{T}{\times}4\mathrm{R} front end already yields near-14∘14^{\circ} azimuth beamwidth [8], which maps to decimeter-scale lateral uncertainty at a few meters and can erode interactive margins even when a downstream network outputs a plausible skeleton.
Throughout, pose localization accuracy therefore denotes the accuracy with which the radar measurement itself can locate body joints, as distinct from the visual fidelity of an estimated mesh or pose sequence; joints the measurement does not constrain remain not identifiable (Fig. 1, top right).

This paper asks: How accurately can mmWave locate human joints, and which sensing quantities set that limit?

A growing literature already reduces pose error without answering that question.
Temporal and spatial aggregation fuse successive frames or additional viewpoints to enlarge the observation and average noise [15, 1].
Learned human-state estimators map sparse radar features onto dense joint or mesh outputs [5, 6].
A further line retains static environmental reflections instead of discarding them as clutter [17]; we treat this choice as return selection, parallel to multi-frame and multi-view enrichment.
These families typically keep a conventional preprocessing chain fixed, report gains under a single reconstruction metric, and leave unspecified both how accurately the measurement can locate the body and which sensing quantities remain responsible for the residual gap.
Empirical improvements therefore accumulate as pipeline scores, without a shared criterion for whether the next gain should come from more frames, additional viewpoints, a different return policy, or a larger estimator (Fig. 1, right).

We attribute this bottleneck to a missing measurement characterization: enhancements alter different stages of the sensing chain without a shared error floor on pose localization accuracy.
Three structural mismatches follow.
First, multi-frame and multi-view aggregation often proceeds under implicit assumptions that phase stays aligned across the fused frames (coherence) or that the combined viewpoints are geometrically calibrated, so apparent gains may reflect favorable phase alignment or geometry rather than a controlled information increase.
Second, reconstruction metrics do not separate measurement information, structure already constrained by the observation, from estimator completion of coordinates the radar never rendered identifiable.
Third, return selection changes which scatterers enter the observation, yet rarely quantifies the resulting information about the human state once the unknown environmental geometry is marginalized, that is, averaged out as a nuisance rather than estimated.
Absent a common formalism that separates these effects, existing results do not state an error floor on human-joint localization imposed by the radar measurement itself, independent of which enhancement is applied.

We therefore close that missing measurement characterization instead of adding another reconstruction network.
We model human and environment as one time-varying scattering field and state a Cramér–Rao-type error floor on pose localization, so that the sensing quantities altered by existing enhancements can be compared under one reference.
Those enhancements then serve as controlled probes of the floor, which we label Fuse, View, Est, and Vis, in one-to-one correspondence with the mismatches above:
Fuse and View isolate temporal and spatial aggregation;
Est separates measurement information from estimator completion;
and Vis tests when retaining weak or reflected returns is informative about the human state.

Concretely, under matched conditions and varying one probe at a time on complementary public benchmarks:
Fuse lowers error on the joints the measurement itself renders identifiable with a log–log slope of −0.28-0.28 in the fused frame count, while mean per-joint position error (MPJPE) over all joints improves more slowly, consistent with estimator completion;
View lowers MPJPE from 96.696.6 to 64.8​mm64.8\,\mathrm{mm} once a second viewpoint is added;
and Vis lowers error on identifiable joints by 10.4%10.4\% and MPJPE by 9.3%9.3\%, with a larger margin in high-multipath scenes and no resolved effect under near-stationary motion or severe phase drift.
A live deployment reproduces the multi-frame and visibility trends under real sensor noise, including indoor captures with up to three concurrent subjects.
These probe-level trends anchor the following contributions.

The main contributions are as follows:

(C1) Measurement-limit diagnosis.
We identify the core limitation of lightweight mmWave human-state sensing for robots as a missing measurement characterization of pose localization accuracy, and we separate this sensing limit from estimator completion.

(C2) Measurement-imposed error floor.
We state a Cramér–Rao-type error floor on human-joint localization as an explicit function of the sensing quantities that front-end choices alter, providing a common reference for comparing those choices; the experiments vary the subset those choices can change at deployment time, namely fused frame count, coherence, viewpoint count, and visibility.

(C3) Factor probes via existing enhancements.
We recover multi-frame, multi-view, return-selection, and estimator pipelines as matched probes, yielding falsifiable, factor-level predictions without a new end-to-end architecture.

(C4) Public and live validation.
We test these predictions on complementary datasets and on a live prototype with up to three concurrent subjects, quantifying where measurement-type error follows the predicted trends, most directly through the fusion slope of −0.28-0.28 on identifiable joints, and where estimator completion accounts for the remaining gain.

title: STRIDE: Learning Humanoid Locomotion in Minutes with Acceleration-Based Rewards
authors: Nico Bohlinger,Jan Peters
abstract:
Learning locomotion directly on a humanoid robot is a promising direction to avoid the sim-to-real gap.
However, locomotion rewards in Reinforcement Learning (RL) typically track the base velocity, which cannot be measured onboard without an external motion capture system or well-calibrated state estimator.
This is why we introduce STRIDE, which learns humanoid locomotion from minutes of samples with a reward that only requires the onboard Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU).
Instead of tracking the base velocity, STRIDE rewards the robot for following a commanded acceleration profile.
To learn efficiently from this reward, we use the off-policy RL algorithm XQC and combine a high gain setting for the joint position controllers with left-right symmetry augmentation.
In simulation, STRIDE learns to walk on the Unitree G1 and Booster T1 humanoids within 14 minutes of samples.
Compared to learning without these two components, it reduces the falls during training by 81%, while without them the robot learns only in over an hour.
introduction:
Reinforcement Learning (RL) has become the standard approach for legged locomotion [1, 2, 3], where policies are trained in thousands of parallel environments in simulation and then transferred to the real robot [4, 5, 6, 7].
This transfer requires accurate models, extensive domain randomization and often an adaptation to the physical robot [8, 9].
Learning directly on the robot avoids this gap, and quadrupeds already learn to walk within minutes of real-world interaction [10, 11].
Yet, two properties of humanoids make learning on the robot especially difficult.
First, the locomotion rewards typically used in prior work track the base velocity, which has to come from a motion capture system or from a well-calibrated state estimator [12].
But even such a state-estimator can still introduce errors and delays, or systematically underestimate the velocity [11].
Second, bipeds are inherently unstable, so they need large amounts of samples to learn from and fall frequently.
Every fall on a real robot requires a reset and wears down the hardware.

This is why we propose STRIDE, which learns humanoid locomotion from minutes of samples with a reward that only requires the onboard Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU).
Instead of tracking the base velocity, STRIDE rewards the robot for following a commanded acceleration profile and for holding the velocity that it estimates by integrating its own acceleration.
To learn efficiently from this reward, we use a high gain setting for the joint position controllers and train an off-policy RL algorithm on symmetry-augmented copies of the collected transitions.
In simulation, STRIDE learns to walk on the Unitree G1 and Booster T1 humanoids within 14 minutes worth of samples.
Compared to learning with a low gain setting and without symmetries, it reduces the falls during training by 81%, while only half of the runs without these two components learn to walk within 83 minutes at all.

title: ActPrune: Action-Grounded Visual Token Pruning for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Sungwon Moon,Minji Kim,Hyemin Boo,Daeun Song,Jiyoung Lee
abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models perform versatile manipulation tasks from language instructions, but their inference cost limits how fast a robot can respond in closed-loop control.
Visual token pruning reduces this cost; however, prior methods estimate token redundancy from encoded visual embeddings or attention, only after the visual encoder has processed the entire observation.
We propose ActPrune, a training-free token pruning method that moves the pruning decision ahead of the vision encoder by grounding it in a geometric prior derived from the robot’s own action.
The action chunk predicted at the previous control step is already available before the current observation is encoded, and it specifies the end-effector and camera motion between consecutive observations.
The same action affects the two standard camera views asymmetrically: in the fixed third-person view, ActPrune retains patches along the projected end-effector trajectory together with semantic anchors, while in the wrist view, it prunes patches that remain unchanged after compensating for the action-induced camera motion.
Extensive experiments on two simulation environments (LIBERO and VLABench) and four real-robot tasks demonstrate that ActPrune achieves up to 1.61 ×\times speedup and 59.5% FLOPs reduction with negligible degradation in success rates.
introduction:
A long-standing goal in robotics is to develop a single policy that can perform diverse manipulation tasks from natural language instructions.
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have made progress toward this goal. Many of them build on pretrained vision-language models and generalize to new objects and instructions by inheriting web-scale representations. However, this capability comes with high inference cost. VLA models rely on large vision-language backbones that process hundreds of visual tokens at every control step. In closed-loop control, this computation is repeated for every new observation. As a result, inference latency can limit how fast the robot can respond.

Recent methods have explored different ways to reduce the inference cost of VLA models [1, 2, 3, 4]. Visual token pruning instead reduces computation by removing redundant visual tokens during inference.
Existing pruning methods identify redundant tokens from encoded visual features [5, 6], attention [7, 8], temporal changes [9, 10], or action information [11, 10].
In these approaches, redundancy is mainly determined from the visual observations themselves, after the vision encoder has processed every token.

A robot in closed-loop control, however, does not simply observe a sequence of images. Between two observations, the robot executes an action that changes its state and interaction with the scene. The action therefore provides information about where and how the next observation may change. More importantly, this action is already available before the next observation arrives. Unlike visual features or attention scores, it does not require the current observation to be encoded first. The previous action can therefore provide an early signal for identifying visual redundancy before visual encoding.

The effect of the action on the observation depends on the camera viewpoint.
A standard manipulation setup pairs a fixed third-person camera with a wrist-mounted camera [12, 13, 14].
In the fixed third-person view, the scene stays stable across steps.
Change is confined to the region the manipulator occupies.
In contrast, the wrist view changes globally and dynamically across steps.
These changes arise from camera motion and viewpoint shifts induced by the actions.
The action therefore implies contrasting patterns of new information across camera views.

Based on these insights, we propose ActPrune (Fig. 1), a training-free framework that exploits the closed-loop structure of robot manipulation to reduce visual computation.
Specifically, the action chunk predicted at the previous step is available before the current observation is processed in the visual encoder.
It provides a physically grounded prior on where visual computation should be spent without requiring a vision encoder forward pass.
ActPrune leverages this prior to prune visual tokens, projecting the anticipated end-effector trajectory onto the fixed third-person view to mark newly visualized information, while removing motion-compensated redundant patches for the wrist view.
The remaining budget is applied after the encoder, where encoder attention ranks the retained tokens.

We summarize our contributions as follows:

We introduce ActPrune, a training-free framework that derives geometric priors directly from robot actions, enabling visual token pruning before the vision encoder.

We identify that the same action induces distinct redundancy patterns in fixed and wrist-mounted views, and exploit this asymmetry with view-specific pruning.

ActPrune achieves state-of-the-art efficiency on LIBERO [13] and VLABench [14], with up to 1.61×\times speedup and 59.5% FLOPs reduction while preserving competitive performance. We further validate its real-world advantage on a 7-DoF Franka Research 3.

title: It Takes Two to Tangram: Multi-Agent Object Centric Reinforcement Learning for Assembly
authors: Paul Knaußt,Kay Pompetzki,Nico Bohlinger,Niklas Funk,Cristiana de Farias,Rolf Findeisen,Jan Peters
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
abstract:
Geometric assembly requires fine spatiotemporal coordination to place parts without causing collisions or deadlocks under tight clearances.
To address this, we present an object-centric reinforcement learning framework that treats each part as an agent and learns a shared policy for continuous assembly control.
A graph neural network represents the pieces, their target poses, and their spatial relationships, and predicts translational and angular velocities for each component.
Per-agent proximal policy optimization with a centralized graph critic directly learns motion and temporal coordination within a single feedback policy.
We study this formulation through planar Tangram assembly, where pieces must slide and rotate into a given configuration while remaining on the assembly surface.
Procedural generation of target configurations and randomized initial arrangements support training and evaluation across diverse assembly problems.
Our experiments isolate the roles of relational structure and multi-agent optimization, and compare learned control with sampling-based planning.
We demonstrate concurrent assembly in simulation and transfer the policy to sequential execution on a real robot, as our object-centric formulation decouples learned assembly coordination from low-level physical control.
Project page: https://tangrambench.org/
introduction:
From arranging or assembling furniture in a home to fitting components together on a production line, many tasks require moving multiple objects into precise spatial relationships, often within cluttered or confined spaces [1, 2, 3].
In such cases, even when every object’s destination is known, its motion cannot be considered in isolation.
To illustrate the problem, consider sliding puzzle pieces across a table to form a given shape.
As one piece approaches its target, it may narrow or block the path of another.
Once the desired configuration is known, the challenge becomes coordinating the pieces’ motions toward their targets while accounting for the space they need along the way.

One approach to the coordination problem is to jointly plan which objects to move and how to move them.
Task and motion planning (TAMP) methods couple these decisions by searching for action sequences whose associated motions satisfy geometric and robot constraints [4].
In robot assembly, this involves selecting part sequences and assembly configurations together with feasible manipulation motions [5].
In nonprehensile rearrangement, object-centric approaches guide planning through actions directed at individual objects [6], or compute desired object motions that are realized through closed-loop pushing [7].
This abstraction organizes manipulation around changes to the objects whose configurations define the task.
Learning-based approaches also address multi-object rearrangement through hierarchical policies [8], while assembly methods exploit structured representations of parts and their relationships to select placements [9, 10]
or generate object motions [11].
These approaches establish objects and their relationships as useful units for reasoning about manipulation.

Multi-agent pathfinding offers another perspective on coordination, studying how agents can reach their respective goals while avoiding conflicts during concurrent movement [12].
Coordinating these movements requires reasoning about interactions between agents and the space they share.
Graph representations provide a way to encode these relationships, supporting learned policies for decentralized path planning [13], multi-agent navigation and collision avoidance [14], and coordinated motion, task allocation, and scheduling in multi-robot reaching [15].
This perspective naturally extends to object-centric assembly and rearrangement, where individual objects can be represented as agents acting toward a shared target configuration.

Thus, we introduce Graph networks for Object-centric Multi-agent Assembly (GOMA), a graph-based multi-agent approach to geometric assembly.
GOMA represents each part to be assembled as a cooperative agent and uses a shared policy trained with Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization (MAPPO) [16] to predict continuous object motions from a relational representation of the assembly state.
A graph neural network (GNN) encodes interactions between parts, combining an object-centric representation with multi-agent learning toward a shared assembly objective.
Our central question is whether an object-centric multi-agent formulation provides an effective basis for learning coordinated assembly.
We further investigate which aspects of the representation and learning formulation matter for coordination, including how information about other parts informs each agent’s actions.

To study this problem, we also introduce TangramBench, a procedural benchmark suite for planar geometric assembly based on the game of Tangram.
The classical Tangram puzzle consists of seven geometric pieces (see Fig. ) that must be arranged to form a target silhouette.
Despite its small set of simple parts, tightly packed configurations create strong geometric dependencies between their motions, making Tangram a compact setting for studying coordinated assembly.
Tangram has previously served as a robot testbed for collaborative pick-and-place [2] and sequential assembly from silhouette prompts [17], while recent benchmarks study geometric reasoning over valid piece configurations [18, 19].
In contrast, TangramBench provides the target pose of each piece and constrains its motion to the support plane, isolating the problem of coordinating feasible object motions toward a known assembly.
We procedurally generate three levels of geometric difficulty, from loosely packed configurations to compact assemblies in which interactions between pieces become increasingly important.
The benchmark supports large-scale training and evaluation and includes simulation-ready models together with physical pieces and a compatible manipulation tool for real-robot experiments.

In summary, our contributions are:

An object-level multi-agent formulation of geometric assembly that learns simultaneous part motions and temporal coordination through a shared continuous-control policy.

An empirical investigation of relational state representations and per-agent policy optimization, with comparisons against joint-action learning and sampling-based planning.

TangramBench, a procedural benchmark suite for geometric assembly, with physical pieces and evaluations of concurrent simulation control and sequential robot execution.

1. An object-level multi-agent formulation of geometric assembly that learns simultaneous part motions and temporal coordination through a shared continuous-control policy.

2. An empirical investigation of relational state representations and per-agent policy optimization, with comparisons against joint-action learning and sampling-based planning.

3. TangramBench, a procedural benchmark suite for geometric assembly, with physical pieces and evaluations of concurrent simulation control and sequential robot execution.

title: VICTR: Value-Informed In-Context Learning for Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Luca Macesanu,Tianluo Zhang,Aditya Patil,Archit Sharma,Kevin Angers,Christopher M. Clark,Chen Feng,Juexiao Zhang
comment: . Project page:this https URL
abstract:
Recent advances in robot foundation models have highlighted the potential of in-context learning (ICL) for adapting robot behavior from demonstrations without further fine-tuning.
Previous work has used retrieval-based post-training to equip pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models with the capability for ICL by teaching them to condition action predictions on retrieved visually-relevant demonstration chunks. However, the effectiveness of retrieval hinges on selecting context relevant to the current execution stage, which visual similarity alone may not capture.
We introduce VICTR, a framework enabling in-context learning in VLAs via progress-informed context retrieval built around an In-Context Value Function Estimator (IC-VFE). IC-VFE conditions on a reference demonstration video, a language instruction and the current observation to estimate task-relative progress.
By conditioning progress estimation on a reference demonstration, IC-VFE can align the current state with a demonstrated execution even for tasks unseen during training.
VICTR uses the estimated progress to select demonstration chunks at corresponding stages of execution and supplies them to a π0.5\pi_{0.5} policy post-trained for in-context action generation.
On unseen out-of-domain real-world manipulation tasks, VICTR raises the success rate from 6.2% for a fine-tuned π0.5\pi_{0.5} baseline to 23.8% and more than doubles the task progress rate, from 28.9% to 55.5%.
Project page with code, data and videos: https://ai4ce.github.io/VICTR/
introduction:
In-context learning (ICL) enables robot policies to adapt their behavior from demonstrations supplied as context, without repeatedly fine-tuning parameters for new tasks at deployment – mirroring large language models, which can infer new tasks from examples in their context without updating model parameters [1]. The emergence of this capability in large pretrained models motivates an analogous question for robotics: whether generalist policies can similarly adapt their behavior from demonstrations supplied at inference time.
This form of adaptation can potentially address a persistent challenge for robotics foundation models. Despite substantial progress through training on diverse datasets [2] and reinforcement learning [3], reliable out-of-the-box performance across diverse tasks and environments remains challenging [4, 5].
Adapting a policy to a new domain often requires additional demonstration collection and fine-tuning, leading to a recurring cost as deployment requirements change.
Recent industry systems have begun to demonstrate the promise of ICL, either as an emergent capability of large-scale pretraining [6] or through pretraining objectives that explicitly use demonstration videos to specify tasks [7].
Alongside these advances, RICL [8] demonstrates that pretrained VLAs can acquire ICL capabilities through retrieval-based post-training without retraining from scratch with extensive resources, learning to generate actions in-context conditioned on selected demonstration chunks.

Retrieval-based ICL relies on selecting demonstration chunks that provide useful guidance for the robot’s next action. Existing retrieval methods rely on visual similarity [8, 9], but visually similar observations often occur at different execution stages, making appearance an ambiguous selection signal.
We argue that task-relative progress provides an important retrieval signal beyond visual similarity, aligning the current observation with demonstration chunks at corresponding stages of execution.
A related notion appears in RECAP [3], whose value function estimator (VFE) predicts the negative number of steps remaining until success as a distribution over discretised bins, and forms advantages from it for reinforcement learning. Normalised by the episode horizon, that value runs from −1-1 at the start of an episode to 00 at success—the scale on which we define task-relative progress, a unitless quantity in [0,1][0,1] comparable across tasks of different lengths. We keep RECAP’s formulation and this support, but supervise it with semantic progress annotations rather than elapsed time, and use the estimate to retrieve demonstration chunks at inference rather than to optimise the policy.
However, RECAP is conditioned on the current observation and language instruction without a reference demonstration, meaning that adaptation to new tasks depends on the VFE’s prior knowledge of the new language instruction.
We seek a progress estimator that can directly use demonstration context to interpret task-specific execution progress, without requiring task-specific fine-tuning.

To this end, we make progress estimation itself an in-context learning problem. We introduce an In-Context Value Function Estimator (IC-VFE) that jointly conditions on the current observation, a language instruction, and a reference demonstration video. The demonstration provides a task-specific reference in-context for the task goal and how it unfolds, supplying execution information beyond the language instruction. IC-VFE uses this reference to assess the current state’s progress relative to a demonstrated execution, enabling adaptation through context without task-specific fine-tuning. This estimator forms the core of VICTR, our Value-Informed Context Retrieval framework for in-context VLA policies.

In VICTR, we instantiate IC-VFE with a Gemma-based [10] vision-language architecture to predict task-relative progress, and post-train a π0.5\pi_{0.5} policy to generate actions conditioned on demonstration chunks retrieved by progress alignment. Both models’ weights remain fixed at deployment. In real-world evaluations, IC-VFE agrees with human progress
annotations more closely than existing online value estimators on both seen and unseen tasks, and this advantage carries through to control: on unseen out-of-domain tasks, VICTR raises the success rate of a fine-tuned
π0.5\pi_{0.5} baseline from 6.2% to 23.8% and more than doubles
the task progress rate, from 28.9% to 55.5% (Figure 1).

In summary, this work makes three primary contributions:

An In-Context Value Function Estimator (IC-VFE) that uses a reference demonstration video to estimate task-relative progress without task-specific fine-tuning.

VICTR, a π0.5\pi_{0.5}-based ICL framework that retrieves demonstration chunks by progress alignment to guide action generation.

Real-world evaluations on 8 in-domain and 8 out-of-domain tasks, where progress-informed retrieval raises out-of-domain success from 2.7% for a fine-tuned π0.5\pi_{0.5} and 15.0% for a visual-similarity retrieval baseline to 25.0%.

title: ForPC: Force-Aware Whole-Body Control for Precise Humanoid Cart Pushing
authors: ZhenYu Zou,Xing Liu,ShiChuang Wang,YunLong Dong,LiNan Deng,Feng Hua,Jun Wan,Cheng Cheng
comment: . Project website:this https URL. Corresponding author: Cheng Cheng
abstract:
Humanoid robots are expected to take over strenuous material handling in manufacturing, logistics, and healthcare, where operating existing wheeled carts would let them move heavy loads without modifying the workplace.
However, humanoid cart pushing remains challenging because the bimanual grasp closes a force-coupled loop in which the contact wrenches that drive the cart also disturb the robot’s balance, and payload changes alter the coupled dynamics.
We propose ForPC, a force-aware whole-body control framework that regulates cart velocity through two-stage reinforcement learning.
A locomotion prior is first trained under varied hand loads and upper-body postures to provide balance support.
A force latent and a state latent are then inferred from onboard observations, without external force sensors, and fed to a residual policy that coordinates bounded arm, waist, and leg adjustments with base-velocity commands.
Multi-objective rewards penalize bimanual internal opposition, grasp slip, and actuator saturation, encouraging the policy to apply contact force on demand without human demonstrations.
Sim-to-sim experiments show that ForPC reduces cart-velocity RMSE by up to 68.2% relative to a locomotion-only baseline (Loco-only) and cross-track RMSE by up to 74.2% on the multi-bend route.
Trained solely in simulation, the policy also transfers to a physical Unitree G1 without real-world training or fine-tuning and, with no payload-specific adjustment, pushes a cart carrying up to 30 kg30\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{g} at 0.5 m/s0.5\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{/}\mathrm{s}.
These results suggest that humanoid robots could eventually replace humans for efficient material handling in daily life.
introduction:
Humanoid robots possess an anthropomorphic morphology and whole-body dexterity, enabling them to directly operate human-centric equipment, including manual wheeled carts designed for human workers [Tong et al., 2024, Gu et al., 2026, Kheddar et al., 2019].
By autonomously taking over repetitive and strenuous hauling tasks, humanoid robots could enhance operational productivity and transport efficiency, and thus hold broad application prospects.

Despite early progress in humanoid cart transport [Hawley and Suleiman, 2017, Rioux and Suleiman, 2018], achieving precise and dependable pushing remains challenging.
Sustained contact establishes a bilaterally coupled physical system, in which hand forces drive the cart while its motion inertia and rolling resistance transmit reaction loads back to the robot and disrupt its locomotion balance.
Under payload variations, the robot must accurately regulate both the magnitude and the direction of its contact effort to maintain a steady heading and forward cruise.
Grasping the same handle makes uncoordinated arms prone to working against each other.
This mutual opposition produces internal forces that do not contribute to propulsion [Yoshikawa and Nagai, 1991] and consumes the joint torque margin needed for heading corrections and steering maneuvers.

Model-based formulations coordinate motion and force tasks with balance objectives but require explicit models of the contact and the object [Sentis and Khatib, 2005, Wensing et al., 2024, Sleiman et al., 2021], whereas learning-based methods obtain whole-body coordination from simulated interaction, demonstrations, or motion tracking [Dao et al., 2024, Ze et al., 2025, Zhao et al., 2025, Liao et al., 2026].
Recent controllers further accommodate manipulation loads [Ben et al., 2025, Zhang et al., 2026b, Xiao et al., 2025] or infer contact forces and object motion from the robot’s own signals [Portela et al., 2024, Zhi et al., 2025, Li et al., 2026a, Liu et al., 2026, Wan et al., 2025].
However, Portela et al. [Portela et al., 2024] and Zhi et al. [Zhi et al., 2025] estimate contact forces without object motion, whereas HAIC [Li et al., 2026a] predicts object motion without an explicit hand-force estimate, so none of them closes the feedback loop on both the cart velocity and the bimanual hand wrenches.
Without such feedback, a policy can neither assess the cart’s actual dynamic response nor detect whether the two arms are fighting against each other on the handle.
Although wrist force/torque sensors could provide direct feedback, such sensing is not always available for control, so recent methods estimate these forces from proprioception [Portela et al., 2024, Zeng et al., 2026].
Precise cart pushing under varying payloads, which requires feedback on both the cart motion and the hand forces without external force sensors, therefore remains an unresolved challenge.

Addressing this challenge requires treating the humanoid and the cart as a tightly coupled dynamic system rather than decoupled motion primitives.
Effective payload transport depends on closing the feedback loop around the physical interaction, so the controller must perceive both the cart’s real-time motion response and the contact loads at the hands.
Because everyday carts have no built-in motion sensors and the hands provide no direct force measurement, these quantities must be inferred from signals available on the robot itself.

We propose ForPC, a force-aware whole-body control framework that uses two-stage reinforcement learning for dynamic cart pushing, as shown in Figure 2.
In the first stage, an interaction-resilient locomotion prior is pre-trained under severe, randomized external hand disturbances and bounded posture offsets, and is then frozen so that the task policy can reuse its support response.
In the second stage, a teacher–student estimator infers force and state latents from histories of joint kinematics, upper-body torques, and the visually observed relative cart heading, and the task policy uses these latents to output bounded waist–arm and leg joint residuals and modulate robot base velocity commands.
Without relying on external force sensors or human demonstrations, our framework effectively coordinates bimanual effort and transfers zero-shot across varied payloads.
We evaluate ForPC against a locomotion-only baseline (Loco-only) in Isaac Sim and MuJoCo on velocity tracking, force estimation, and route following, and then deploy the policy, trained solely in Isaac Sim, zero-shot on a physical Unitree G1 humanoid to accomplish the transport of parts and workpieces along complex paths ().

The main contributions of this paper are threefold.

We propose ForPC, a two-stage whole-body control framework for coupled humanoid cart pushing that combines a locomotion prior, interaction estimators, and a residual policy.

We design a force-guided interaction inference module that infers a force latent from onboard signals and uses it to guide the estimation of a state latent, allowing the policy to perceive contact loading and cart motion without external force sensors.

We transfer our policy zero-shot to a real Unitree G1 humanoid, which achieves precise cart-pushing control along complex paths under a 30 kg30\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{g} payload.

1. We propose ForPC, a two-stage whole-body control framework for coupled humanoid cart pushing that combines a locomotion prior, interaction estimators, and a residual policy.

2. We design a force-guided interaction inference module that infers a force latent from onboard signals and uses it to guide the estimation of a state latent, allowing the policy to perceive contact loading and cart motion without external force sensors.

3. We transfer our policy zero-shot to a real Unitree G1 humanoid, which achieves precise cart-pushing control along complex paths under a 30 kg30\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{g} payload.
