title: CS-Pi: Constraint-Satisfying Flow Policy Sampling
authors: Soumojit Bhattacharya,Oliver Kroemer,Shubham Tulsiani
comment: Accepted to CoRL 2026. Project page:this https URL
abstract:
A flow-matching policy deployed in the field must often satisfy a constraint
that was absent from its demonstrations, such as avoiding an obstacle it has
never seen. Retraining for every new constraint is impractical, so the
constraint must be enforced at inference time. Enforcing it must not discard
what the policy learned: an action the policy would rarely sample may avoid the
obstacle yet fail the task. We therefore want actions that are both
safe, satisfying the constraint, and plausible, remaining likely
under the policy. Gradient guidance, the most common approach, steers noisy
states, so it must evaluate its cost on the policy’s running estimate of the
clean action; when the policy is uncertain between passing left or right of an
obstacle, this estimate is their average and can pass straight through it. We
instead build on rejection and projection. Rejection redraws actions until one
is safe: every output is plausible, but the wait is intractable when safe
actions are rare. Projection moves an action to the nearest safe one: it is
efficient, but the result need not be plausible. Our key insight is that
flow-matching sampling lets us combine the two, keeping projection’s efficiency
and rejection’s plausibility. CS-Pi, our draw-project-renoise sampler,
projects each draw to the nearest safe action, adds noise back scaled to how
far the projection moved it, and re-runs the unmodified policy until a draw is
safe. Replacing only the projection step extends CS-Pi to continuous costs.
Across a 2D diagnostic, a 7-DoF shelf pick-and-place, an orientation
preference, and a zero-shot Franka deployment, CS-Pi reaches 81%81\% safe
success on the shelf and 55%55\% on hardware, against 55%55\% and 40%40\% for
projection, while staying plausible.
introduction:
Large-scale flow-matching and diffusion policies have become capable generalist priors for robot manipulation[1, 2]: trained once on broad demonstrations, a single model can pick and place objects, open drawers, and fold clothes. Yet no training set anticipates every deployment, and such a policy will inevitably meet safety-critical scenarios its demonstrations never contained, for example: a wine glass left beside the drawer it must open, which the arm must not touch. This requirement is a constraint, supplied only at deployment. It defines a safe set: the set of actions that satisfy it; in our example, every action that does not touch the glass. Our goal is to sample actions that both come from the policy and lie in the safe set, without retraining the policy for each new constraint. The natural approach is to correct the policy’s output: sample an action and project it onto the safe set, moving it to the nearest safe action, or steer the denoising trajectory using a function of the constraint. Such corrections address the second half of this goal, moving the action into the safe set. They can lose the first: the correction can move the action somewhere the policy would rarely sample. This matters because the policy is what captures the task. An action it considers unlikely may clear the wine glass yet no longer reach the drawer handle. Such an action also loses what the policy learned from the demonstrations, beyond the task itself: smooth, kinematically feasible motion. We therefore require the sampled action to be both safe, satisfying the constraint, and plausible, remaining likely under the policy.

Among such training-free samplers, the most common is gradient guidance [3, 4, 5], which nudges each denoising step along the gradient of a cost on the action. Guidance has two shortcomings. First, safety constraints are typically hard constraints: an action either satisfies them or violates them, with no degree in between. An action either touches the wine glass or it does not; this yes-or-no answer says nothing about which way to move the arm, so a hard constraint offers no gradient to follow. Guidance must instead use a smooth cost, such as a collision cost that grows as the arm nears the glass, which discourages contact but does not rule it out. Second, even a smooth cost is meaningful only on a clean action, while guidance acts on noisy intermediate states. Guidance therefore evaluates the cost at a proxy: the policy’s running estimate of the clean action, an average over every clean action the noisy state could still become. This proxy is reliable only when the cost changes slowly across those actions, so sharpening the cost toward the true constraint makes guidance less reliable, not more. The proxy fails when the policy is uncertain between distinct modes, such as passing left or right of the glass. The average of the two can pass straight through the glass, an action the policy would never sample. The gradient evaluated there may point towards neither mode (App. E).

We instead build on rejection and projection, two classical mechanisms that act only on the final sampled action rather than guiding the intermediate noise levels. Rejection sampling redraws complete actions from the policy until one satisfies the constraint: every output is plausible, but the wait is intractable when safe actions are rare. Projection maps a sampled action to the nearest constraint-satisfying point: it is efficient, but the projected action need not be plausible and can be jerky or task-irrelevant. Our key insight is that flow-matching sampling lets us combine the two, keeping projection’s efficiency and rejection’s plausibility. When a projected action is implausible, we need not take rejection’s drastic step of restarting sampling from pure noise; we can instead resample from a reduced noise level around the projection, so the policy returns a safe and plausible action near the projection.

We operationalize this insight in CS-Pi, a draw-project-renoise sampler (Fig. 2). CS-Pi starts from a single draw from the policy and refines it in a loop. Each iteration projects the current draw onto the safe set and, rather than executing the possibly implausible projection, adds noise back to it, scaled to how far the projection moved the draw. It then re-runs the unmodified policy from that noise level to obtain the next draw. The loop ends once a draw is safe. Each draw comes from the policy and tends to land closer to the safe set than the last, so the draws approach the safe set while remaining plausible, at a compute cost far below rejection and with no constraint gradient at any noisy state.
We first present CS-Pi for hard constraints, then extend it to continuous costs, such as an orientation preference, by replacing only the projection step. The same change lets CS-Pi combine hard constraints with costs. Across a 2D diagnostic, a 7-DoF shelf pick-and-place with deployment-time obstacles, the orientation preference above, and a zero-shot Franka deployment, CS-Pi is the only sampler that satisfies the constraint while staying plausible wherever the constraint permits; on the shelf it reaches 81%81\% safe success (completing the task without collision) against 55%55\% for projection and 32%32\% for gradient guidance.

title: Meituan-Robotics-0: A Vision-Language-Action Foundation Model for Desktop Manipulation
authors: Meituan Robotics Team:Caicheng Wang,Chen Zhao,Chengpeng Jin,Duo Xu,Fengjiao Chen,Guanglu Wan,Heqing Yang,Jia Wang,Jiacong Zhou,Jie Hu,Jiyuan Ru,Lingfeng Zhang,Linjiang Huang,Manyuan Zhang,Ningchu Liu,Shijie Zhou,Si Liu,Shuo Li,Tianyi Zhang,Xi Zhang,Xin Chen,Xuezhi Cao,Xunliang Cai,Yanbin Zeng,Yang Yang,Yang Yi,Yanli Tan,Yifu Xu,Yimeng Jia,Yuchen Tang,Yuchen Xie,Yuxiang Zheng,Zerwei Chng,Zilong Huang,Zipeng Ye,Ziyuan Qin,Ziqin Wang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: . Project page:this https URL; Code:this https URL
abstract:
General-purpose desktop manipulation requires an embodied system that can acquire broad behavioral priors from heterogeneous data, transfer them across robot embodiments, recover from closed-loop execution errors, and preserve task-relevant state over extended horizons. We present Meituan-Robotics-0 (MR0), a vision-language-action foundation model and embodied-agent system for stationary-base desktop manipulation. Its data foundation combines 147 million vision-language samples with 15,060 hours of curated robot trajectories spanning 12 embodiments.
MR0 converts this heterogeneous experience into executable control through a three-stage training recipe. Discrete action-token pre-training first aligns multimodal representations with robot behavior. Continuous flow-matching mid-training then transfers these priors to fine-grained cross-embodiment control. Real-world post-training further adapts the policy using successful demonstrations, human-gated corrections, and outcome-labeled autonomous rollouts.
We introduce Rollback, a data collection mechanism that pairs replaced policy segments with human corrections for CFG-DAgger training. A unified end-effector interface supports learning across heterogeneous embodiments, while asynchronous action-chunk merging maintains smooth execution under variable inference latency. Because the low-level policy is reactive, an event-driven agent converts visual observations into persistent task events and invokes task-level reassessment only when task progress or feasibility changes. This separation preserves continuous motor control while enabling cross-task retrieval and conditional task resumption.
Evaluated as a standalone policy, MR0 achieves 93.6% success on RoboTwin 2.0 and ranks fifth in the RoboDojo VLA track. Under matched HG-DAgger post-training, MR0 achieves higher average success rate and progress score than π0.5\pi_{0.5} across the three tasks.
On Ethernet insertion, CFG-DAgger trained with Rollback data reaches 70% success and a progress score of 0.90 without value learning or advantage labeling.
Qualitative agent deployments further demonstrate cross-task event retrieval and recovery from temporarily unsatisfied task conditions. These results show that aligned heterogeneous data, real-world post-training, and event-level memory provide complementary foundations for transferable and long-horizon desktop manipulation.
introduction:
Vision–language–action Cai and others (2026); Ding and Wang (2026); Ma et al. (2026); Qwen Team (2026a); StarVLA Community (2026b); Wu and others (2026); Zheng et al. (2025) models provide a general interface for mapping visual observations and language instructions to robot actions. Their increasing data and model scales have substantially broadened the range of manipulation behaviors that can be learned within a single policy. Deploying such policies on desktop manipulation, however, exposes several limitations that cannot be addressed by scaling the action model alone. Robot datasets AgiBot-World-Contributors and others (2025); Jiang et al. (2025); Khazatsky et al. (2024); Tian et al. (2025); Wu and others (2025); Zhang et al. (2026a); Wang et al. (2026) collected from different sources use inconsistent observation formats, action spaces, embodiments, and task descriptions, which prevents them from providing coherent supervision without careful alignment. Even after data alignment, policies trained primarily on successful demonstrations receive little guidance for recovering from the error states induced by their own closed-loop behavior. Moreover, a reactive policy conditioned only on the current observation cannot preserve task information once it leaves the observation window. A practical desktop-manipulation system must therefore connect aligned heterogeneous data, robust real-world policy learning, and persistent task-level memory.

We present Meituan-Robotics-0 (MR0), a desktop-manipulation framework built around a large-scale data foundation, a generalist VLA policy, and an event-driven embodied agent, as summarized in Figure 1. The data foundation combines 147 million vision–language samples with 15,060 hours of curated robot trajectories spanning 12 embodiments. The vision–language corpus provides general visual-semantic knowledge together with embodied supervision for grounding, scene understanding, affordance prediction, and task reasoning.
The robot corpus comprises three complementary components:
RoboDesk, a curated collection of open-source real-robot
trajectories totaling 3,235 hours; 7,530 hours of
licensed real-robot data spanning seven robot configurations; and
4,295 hours of open simulation data. The complete corpus is
processed through temporal and visual filtering, kinematic-consistency
checks, cross-embodiment action canonicalization, and hierarchical task
alignment. RoboDesk and the simulation data broaden task, environment,
and embodiment coverage, while the licensed real-robot data provide
task-focused manipulation experience.

Building on this aligned data foundation, the MR0 policy follows a three-stage training recipe that separates the acquisition of broad action priors from continuous-control learning and real-world adaptation. A shared multimodal backbone is first paired with a discrete action head and pre-trained jointly on vision-language data and tokenized robot actions. Continuous mid-training then introduces an MMDiT Esser et al. (2024) action head and optimizes flow matching over a unified end-effector representation, transferring the pre-trained features to fine-grained control across single-arm and bimanual embodiments. Real-world post-training Li et al. (2026a); Li et al. (2025); Ye et al. (2025) starts with supervised finetuning on successful demonstrations. HG-DAgger Kelly et al. (2019) adds human corrections from policy-induced error states, while RECAP (RL with Experience and Corrections via Advantage-conditioned Policies) Amin et al. (2025) derives advantage labels from outcome-labeled autonomous rollouts. We further introduce Rollback, a collection mechanism that returns to a historical anchor to collect a human replacement while retaining the original policy segment. These paired segments supply direct positive and negative labels to CFG-DAgger and remove the need for value learning and advantage labeling. At deployment, asynchronous action-chunk merging integrates new predictions with commands already being executed, maintaining smooth control without blocking on policy inference.

The VLA policy does not explicitly maintain task state across subtasks. MR0 therefore adds an event-driven embodied agent Huo et al. (2026); Li et al. (2026b); Zhang et al. (2026b) to retain relevant context, track task progress, and revise plans as conditions change. A Monitor summarizes short visual windows into task-relevant events, and a Memory Manager consolidates these events into a persistent record of task progress and environmental conditions. The Planner updates the active subtask only when a new event changes task progress, reveals a failure, or alters whether the current objective is feasible. Motor execution consequently remains with the VLA policy, while the Planner is invoked only when task-level reassessment is needed. This separation enables the system to retrieve information acquired in earlier tasks, suspend an objective whose prerequisites are temporarily unavailable, and resume it after the required conditions are restored.

We evaluate the policy and agent under protocols matched to their respective roles. MR0 achieves 93.6% average success on RoboTwin 2.0 Mu et al. (2025). On RoboDojo Chen et al. (2026), the history-augmented policy ranks fifth in the VLA track by average success rate.
With approximately 13.6k hours of embodied training data, MR0 achieves
competitive performance across the evaluated manipulation capabilities.
Human-intervention data improve both MR0 and π0.5\pi_{0.5} across three real-robot tasks.
Under matched HG-DAgger post-training, MR0 achieves higher average success rate and progress score than π0.5\pi_{0.5} across the three tasks.
In a separate comparison on Ethernet insertion, MR0 trained with CFG-DAgger reaches 70% success and a progress score of 0.90, outperforming HG-DAgger and RECAP on the same Rollback data.
Qualitative agent deployments further illustrate cross-task event retrieval and task resumption following temporary interruptions.
Together, these evaluations show how aligned data, continuous policy learning, real-world post-training, and event-level memory address complementary requirements of general-purpose desktop manipulation.

title: Q-OIL: Optimistic Exploration in Learning from Human Interventions
authors: Pranav Teegavarapu,Sriyash Poddar,Rico Qi,Cleah Winston,Krisha Khandelwal,Aykut Onyol,Natasha Jaques,Abhishek Gupta
comment: Project website:this https URL
abstract: As robots are deployed in the real world, they will inevitably make mistakes. Human interventions provide valuable feedback for improving their behavior, enabling them to adapt online to new scenarios. However, studying human-in-the-loop robot learning is difficult: real-world experiments are slow and expensive, so most algorithm development relies on simulated human models. We show that common human modeling assumptions do not match how real people intervene in practice. Through analyzing intervention data from human participants, we find that humans tend to intervene when agent progress stalls, and that their corrective actions are often suboptimal. Motivated by these findings, we introduce a progress-based model of human intervention that achieves higher rank correlation with real-user algorithm rankings, enabling realistic algorithm benchmarking and development in simulation. Building on these insights, we propose Q-OIL, a method that adds optimistic bonuses to intervention transitions in reinforcement learning and softly guides exploration toward human corrections. We find that decoupled critics are critical for stability because they prevent the bonuses from backing up to pre-intervention states. As a result, Q-OIL learns more efficiently than competitive baselines, achieving 10–50% higher success in simulation and on real robots, and improving pretrained VLAs on two bimanual manipulation tasks. As we ground both evaluation and algorithms in realistic human behavior, this work provides a practical path toward scalable robot learning from interventions.
introduction:
Robot policies trained offline on large-scale datasets are brittle [1], often struggling to generalize beyond their training distributions [2] and failing across diverse testing conditions. For robust deployment, robots must adapt online from feedback [3, 4, 5, 6]. As robots fail around human observers, we can rely on human feedback through corrections [7, 8, 9], where humans intervene when the robot gets stuck or makes mistakes. Such signals arise organically in the real world; for example, users may physically steer a manipulator toward the goal [10, 11, 6] or take over in self-driving systems [12]. Interventions can be viewed as more than resets or recovery actions [12]. Corrective actions convey implicit preference signals, i.e., information about failures in the robot’s behavior and potential ways to improve [13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20].

Despite recent progress in robot learning from interventions, algorithm development remains difficult because real-world interaction is slow and expensive. Simulation offers a scalable alternative [21]. For intervention learning, we also require synthetic human models to determine when and how to intervene [16]. These enable repeatable evaluation and systematically guide algorithmic components (e.g., how to incorporate corrections, the exploration-safety trade-off, robustness to noise) before deployment. However, common synthetic human models and learning algorithms are insufficiently grounded in real-world behavior. They make assumptions that we show are not reflective of real human intervention data. This creates a gap between methods trained on synthetic human models and their performance when exposed to real users. We need a principled understanding of when and how humans intervene, both to guide our algorithmic design choices and to evaluate these methods. We first analyze real human interventions in robot manipulation. Our analysis suggests both how to better model human interventions and how to learn from them.

First, we find that rather than reacting to instantaneous suboptimality, humans intervene when the robot’s progress stagnates over a horizon. This pattern aligns with cognitive models of caregiving: humans act on the agent’s ability over time rather than on isolated states [22]. Given this finding, we propose a progress-based synthetic intervention model that accounts for value improvement over a horizon, better matches observed humans, and yields algorithm rankings more consistent with real human evaluation (Fig. 4). Second, this analysis shows that real corrections are suboptimal and can diverge from the learner policy during training, which suggests that algorithms for learning from interventions must be robust to noisy, divergent interventions, i.e., use feedback to adapt robot behavior without compromising asymptotic performance. This motivates our key algorithmic insight: use interventions as optimistic guidance for exploration, rather than optimal supervision. This speeds up training without compromising asymptotic performance.

Building on these insights, we introduce Q-OIL (Q-Optimistic
Intervention Learning), a simple online RL framework that learns from real human corrections and efficiently handles diverse users and suboptimal interventions.
We start by providing an additional positive reward, i.e., an optimism bonus, to intervention transitions.
Intuitively, the optimism bonus uses interventions to guide exploration toward potentially successful behaviors.
The influence of optimism naturally decays as interventions become less frequent, shifting learning back to the original task reward. To make this stable, we introduce a critical decoupling of optimism from TD learning [23]: the optimistic critic drives exploration and policy updates, while a task-only critic provides TD targets, preventing catastrophic bonus propagation to non-intervention states. Importantly, Q-OIL is agnostic to the underlying off-policy RL algorithm, allowing it to be incorporated into different policy learning frameworks. We demonstrate this across simulated and real-world robot manipulation tasks with human participants, and further scale Q-OIL to improve pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies on challenging manipulation tasks.

In summary, we make the following contributions:

We analyze real data to ground synthetic human models for realistic simulation evaluation and informed algorithm design. Our findings show that interventions occur when robot progress stagnates, motivating a progress-based model that promotes improved experiment design.

Based on human analysis, we propose Q-OIL, a simple algorithm that treats interventions as optimistic guidance for exploration rather than optimal supervision targets.

Across diverse real and simulated robot manipulation tasks with human participants, Q-OIL learns faster, reduces human effort, and remains robust to suboptimal and diverse interventions. We further scale it to improve pretrained VLAs on two bimanual manipulation tasks.

title: Computer-Use Agents Are Embodied Generalists
authors: Pranjal Aggarwal,Sean Welleck
abstract:
In many areas of AI, general-purpose models have increasingly replaced handcrafted methods and specialized architectures. We argue that embodied AI is poised for a similar shift. Our key claim is that embodied tasks can be formulated as interaction with digital software. Specifically, we build software that renders an agent’s view of a physical environment on a screen and provides controls for acting in it. A computer-use agent (CUA) can then perform embodied tasks through the same screenshots and keyboard and mouse actions that it uses to operate ordinary software. Using a single CUA design and changing only the software, our entries win first-, second-, third-, and sixth-place prizes across four ECCV workshop competitions, without any competition-specific agent tuning. These results suggest that the skills CUAs learn on software, such as visual grounding, precise clicking, and exploration, already carry over to embodied tasks, giving CUAs a far broader scope in embodied AI than previously realized. We therefore advocate that computer-use agents can be embodied generalists. Further, we advocate that, by following the training strategy that made computer-use agents general, embodied AI can converge on a single general model as well, ushering in a new era of general embodied AI.11

introduction:
In many areas of AI, general-purpose models have increasingly replaced handcrafted methods and specialized architectures (Sutton, 2019; OpenAI et al., 2025; Luong and Lockhart, 2025). We argue that embodied AI, which studies agents that perceive and act in physical environments, is poised for a similar shift (Open X-Embodiment Collaboration et al., 2024; Gemini Robotics Team et al., 2025). In particular, we explore connecting embodied AI with computer-use agents: general-purpose digital agents that operate diverse software applications through screenshots, mouse clicks, and keyboard inputs. Although operating a computer and acting in a physical environment may seem quite different, we observe that both involve similar challenges, including visual grounding, exploration, and adapting actions based on feedback from the environment (Yang et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2025a; Huang et al., 2022).

Our key insight is that embodied tasks can be formulated as interaction with digital software. Specifically, we construct software that renders observations on a screen and provides controls for acting in the physical environment (Figure 1). A computer-use agent can then observe the environment, take actions, and inspect their consequences using the same interface that it uses to operate ordinary desktop software. Task-specific functionality resides in the software rather than the agent design, allowing us to use existing computer-use agents across different embodied tasks without developing specialized models.

To investigate our approach, we develop software applications for four embodied AI tasks: vision-language navigation, dialogue-driven navigation, language-guided 3D segmentation, and referring video segmentation. We use a single, minimal computer-use agent harness across all four applications, without competition-specific agent tuning, and enter 4 ECCV 2026 workshop competitions. Our entries place first in OpenSUN3D, second in MeViSv2-Text, third in DialNav, and sixth in the VLNVerse competitions. These results demonstrate that computer-use agents can achieve strong performance across diverse embodied tasks by interacting with task-specific software through a shared agent design.

Beyond these results, we argue that embodied AI can follow the same path that computer use has already taken. Only two years ago, computer-use agents faced the challenges that embodied AI faces today. They struggled to click precisely and relied on overlays or separate grounding models to locate targets (Yang et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024; Gou et al., 2025), much as most VLAs today add a dedicated action head for continuous control (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025; NVIDIA et al., 2025). They also lagged far behind agents with task-specific APIs (Xie et al., 2024; Aggarwal and Welleck, 2026c; Song et al., 2025). Today, the same model that writes code and solves mathematics problems can also operate computers by writing click coordinates as ordinary text (Anthropic, 2024; Quiros, 2026), and the strongest agents perform comparably whether they act through the screen or through APIs (NeoCognition, 2026). This progress came from training for precise visual grounding, building environments for reinforcement learning, and making interaction fast enough for real-time use (Gou et al., 2025; Aggarwal et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026; Aggarwal et al., 2026a). Each of these has a direct counterpart in embodied AI. Simulators can generate grounding data at scale (Yuan et al., 2024), embodied environments can be used for reinforcement learning (Li et al., 2026), and faster inference can enable real-time control (Black et al., 2025b). Since our approach exposes embodied environments through software, advances in computer-use agents can also transfer to embodied AI directly, and embodied tasks can become part of the training of future general-purpose agents. We therefore believe that embodied AI will converge on a single general model, just as computer use did (OpenAI, 2026c; Anthropic, 2026).

title: Augmentron: Scalable Multi-View Visual Augmentation for Robot Learning
authors: Tanay Tandon,Aseem Doriwala,Jade Choghari,Catherine Weaver,Pragna Mannam
comment: Accepted to the 8th Robot Learning Workshop (WRL), NeurIPS 2026
abstract:
Robot policies trained on visually narrow demonstrations can become sensitive
to environmental features that are unrelated to the task. Existing generative
augmentation methods can introduce visual diversity, but processing every frame
and camera view independently is computationally expensive and may produce
inconsistent observations across cameras and timestamps. We introduce Augmentron, a geometry-aware
pipeline that generates reusable scene representations and renders them through
recorded camera poses. This produces temporally and multi-view consistent
environment and workspace variations while preserving the robot, task objects,
actions, and annotations. Across three physical manipulation tasks, replacing
half of the real world training dataset with Augmentron data improves model success across three tasks for both in out-of-distribution distractor objects, and out-of-distribution workspace variation evaluations. In a separate comparison against alternate augmentation techniques, Augmentron achieves the highest pooled success in all three conditions. The results show that introducing augmented data to a data training recipe can help policies generalize to dynamic real-world settings.
introduction:
Robot demonstration datasets are often visually narrow: the same environments,
surfaces, and distractor configurations recur across many trajectories, even
though many of these visual features provide little information relevant to
the task. Policies trained on such data can fail when these details change
while the underlying task remains constant. In our evaluation, a real-only
policy fine-tuned from π0.5\pi_{0.5} [2] achieves 66.7%
success on three in-distribution (ID) tasks, but success rate falls to 18.0% with out-of-distribution (OOD) distractor objects. This
failure occurs despite broad vision-language-action pretraining
[3, 9, 12].

Collecting new demonstrations across diverse settings is expensive and
difficult to scale, making visual augmentation an attractive way to expand the
coverage of existing data. Augmenting robot trajectories, however, is more
difficult than editing individual images. The robot and task objects must be
preserved, and visual changes must remain consistent over time and across
camera views. Per-frame generative methods repeat segmentation and generation
for every observation, while video-generation costs grow with trajectory
length and camera count. Additionally, non-stationary robot wrist cameras introduce an additional
challenge due to their continuously changing viewpoints.

To address these challenges, we introduce Augmentron, a geometry-aware
pipeline that generates a reusable representation of a visual domain that avoids editing frames independently. Augmentron uses robot state and camera
calibration to initialize robot masks and amortizes segmentation across the
trajectory. Synthetically generated cubemaps and top-down scene images are then
reused across fixed and wrist camera views to create consistent environment
and working-surface variation. This design preserves the robot and task objects
while avoiding repeated per-frame generative inference.

We evaluate Augmentron across three physical manipulation tasks and
three visual conditions. In a controlled replacement experiment, substituting
half of the real world dataset with Augmentron data improves model performance across all tasks in
all three visual conditions. In a separate comparison of complete training volumes,
Augmentron achieves the highest overall task success rate in every condition,
including consistently stronger results than
RoboEngine [15]. Augmentron also
processes four-view demonstrations in 0.93×0.93\times their source-video duration,
compared with 16.28×16.28\times for RoboEngine on the same source set and hardware.

title: Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents
authors: Jingdong Zhang,Jionghao Wang,Zhengming Yu,Yancheng Cai,Wei Chow,Chris Choy,Zhiyang Dou,Hang Hua,Jiachen Li,Zhixuan Liu,Chen Wang,Songlin Wei,Siyuan Yang,Yu Yuan,Xiaohang Zhan,Yucheng Zhang,Shuhong Zheng,Xin Li,Lingjie Liu,Wojciech Matusik,Zhengzhong Tu,Wenping Wang
subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
comment: Project page:this https URL. Jingdong Zhang and Jionghao Wang contributed equally
abstract:
Frontier language models are increasingly deployed as agents, and how well an agent performs depends not only
on its model but also on its harness: the prompts, tools, memory, and control loop through which the model acts.
When an agent is applied to a new problem, a natural question is whether it can use the feedback of the task to
improve the way it works, and not merely its answer. Most existing benchmarks keep the agent’s harness fixed and score
the solution it produces, or target large-scale model training. We introduce Flex-RSI, a benchmark for the recursive
self-improvement of agents on vision and robotics tasks under a fixed budget. In each round, an executor improves
the task solution, which is kept only if it scores higher on held-out validation data, and an improver then revises
the harness, including the executor and itself. Every run starts from the same general-purpose harness, and the
final solution is scored on hidden test data. Evaluating closed-source and open-weight models on tasks spanning
perception, reasoning, robot action, 3D reconstruction, visual creation, and infrastructure, we find that
self-improvement helps most when the agent builds its own solution, that feedback recording only success or failure
holds back open-weight models, and that open-weight models fall furthest behind where outputs must pass strict checks
of physical stability or exact correctness. Paired runs further show that editing the harness itself contributes to
the gains.
introduction:
Frontier large language models now routinely act as agents that write code, conduct experiments, and read the results
over multiple steps (Anthropic, 2026a; OpenAI, 2026b; Google DeepMind, 2026; Qwen Team, 2026b; DeepSeek-AI, 2026; GLM-5 Team, 2026).
An agent’s performance depends not only on the underlying model but also on its harness: the prompts, tools,
memory, and control loop through which the model acts. This raises a practical question for anyone who deploys an
agent on a new problem: given only the task, can the agent use the task’s feedback to improve the way it works under a fixed budget, and not merely its answer?

Most existing benchmarks run each model inside a fixed harness, often the vendor’s own, and score only the solution
or artifact it produces, mostly on machine-learning research tasks with a continuous
metric (Chan et al., 2025; Wijk et al., 2024); those that also let the agent revise its
harness (RSI-Exam Team, 2026) or that center on upstream model training at scale (OpenRSI Foundation, 2026) remain within
machine-learning research. We introduce Flex-RSI to measure how well a frontier agent improves both its solution and
its own harness on
general vision and robotics tasks, a setting in which agents are increasingly deployed, each attempt consumes real
compute, and the goal is a better solution within hours to days.

In Flex-RSI, the harness consists of two components that alternate over rounds (Figure 1a). The
executor improves the task solution: it modifies the solution, runs experiments, and evaluates them on the labeled
development data, and its candidate is kept only if it also scores higher on held-out validation data. The
improver then reviews the round and modifies the harness itself, including the executor’s prompts, tools, and
workflow as well as its own prompts, settings, and lessons. Every run starts from the same general-purpose harness
and, on each task, the same starter solution.

The tasks differ in what the agent must produce (a single answer or a solution it builds), how the evaluator scores
it (on a scale or only as success or failure), and how strictly the output is checked.
From experiments on 24 tasks spanning perception, reasoning, robot action, 3D reconstruction, visual creation, and
infrastructure (Figure 1b), with 18 closed-source and open-weight models, we find:

Tasks in which the agent builds the solution leave more room for self-improvement: tasks whose
solution is a single answer to each question leave little room to improve, while tasks in which the agent builds its own solution leave the most, and there models
pull apart (Figure 1c).

The granularity of feedback matters: feedback that scores each episode on a scale helps all models,
whereas feedback that records only success or failure leaves open-weight models barely improving on the solutions
they build.

Strict checks of physical stability and exact correctness pose the greatest challenge: outputs that
look plausible often fail checks of physical stability or exact correctness, and open-weight models fall furthest behind on them.

title: Ordered Policy Optimization
authors: Dongkyu Derek Cho,Pan Xu
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Robotics (cs.RO); Machine Learning (stat.ML)
comment: . Published in Proc. of the 40th Conference on Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
abstract: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) stabilizes policy updates by clipping the importance ratio between the new policy and the data-collecting policy. The standard rule uses one fixed clipping range for all samples. While this choice offers simplicity and effectiveness, it fails to distinguish statistically harmful extreme ratio values from large, yet tolerable changes. We study how to adapt the clipping radius to the reliability of the induced importance ratio distribution. Our case study demonstrates that reliable updates require controlling these extreme ratios, rather than merely verifying that individual ratios fall within a fixed interval. Motivated by this observation, we propose Ordered Policy Optimization (OPO). In each minibatch, OPO sorts the importance ratios, selects the extreme ratios that potentially have the largest effect on the update, and assigns them adaptive sample-wise radii instead of using the fixed clipping radius. These radii are derived from a prescribed tail profile, which specifies desired target values for the selected extreme ratios. The resulting objective remains first-order and requires only minibatch sorting and a modified policy loss. Experiments conducted on MuJoCo and Atari benchmarks demonstrate that this simple modification achieves strong performance relative to established baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/CrawlingKiming/ordered_ppo.
introduction:
Deep reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved strong empirical performance in domains such as games, robotic control, and large-scale model fine-tuning [22, 19, 15, 21, 20]. Among these approaches, policy-gradient methods optimize a parametrized policy
through gradient-based updates of the expected return [28, 22, 13, 12, 20, 31, 32, 29]. Their practical performance, however, depends critically on the stability of the policy update.

A fundamental challenge arises because policy updates typically evaluate a candidate policy using data collected under a previous policy [18, 20]. This necessitates an importance-weighted surrogate objective, whose behavior is governed by the likelihood ratio between the candidate and behavior policies. Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO) addresses this issue by maximizing the surrogate objective under an explicit constraint on policy discrepancy [18]. While theoretically robust, this constrained optimization can be computationally cumbersome for large-scale applications.

Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) replaces TRPO’s constrained optimization with a clipped first-order surrogate and has become a standard practical method [20, 9, 16, 30]. Its clipping rule acts pointwise on each sampled likelihood ratio using a fixed interval around one. Although effective, this rule does not directly control the tail behavior of the ratio distribution, which governs the reliability of the importance-weighted surrogate [27, 24, 33, 25].

To bridge this gap, we show that instability in updates based on the importance-weighted surrogate is driven by extreme likelihood ratios, rather than by the typical ratios found in the bulk of the distribution [25]. Our motivating analysis shows that a sampled ratio falling within a fixed clipping band does not

necessarily imply meaningful control of policy discrepancy. Moreover, the tail parameter of the ratio distribution governs the moment regime of the policy-update estimator. This insight suggests that the relevant object for stabilization is not a local pointwise clipping event, but the ordered tail of the empirical ratio distribution. Based on this observation, we propose Ordered Policy Optimization (OPO). OPO constructs teacher targets for the upper and lower empirical tails of the ratio distribution and translates these targets into adaptive sample-wise proximal radii. The resulting objective remains first-order and computationally simple, requiring only minibatch sorting and a modified proximal penalty. Thus, OPO preserves the computational efficiency of PPO while replacing fixed pointwise clipping with order-statistic-based tail control.

Contributions:
Our main contributions are summarized as follows.

We identify a statistical limitation of pointwise ratio clipping in proximal policy optimization. Through a motivating analysis, we show that the tail behavior of the likelihood ratio distribution governs the estimator regime of the importance-weighted policy surrogate.

Motivated by this insight, we propose an order-statistic-based proximal objective. This objective regulates the empirical upper and lower tails of the ratio distribution by inducing adaptive, sample-wise radii derived from prescribed tail targets, yielding a method that is straightforward to implement.

Empirically, we demonstrate that this simple modification yields strong performance on standard deep RL benchmarks, including MuJoCo and Atari.

Policy-gradient methods optimize stochastic policies through gradient updates. Trust-region methods stabilize these updates by constraining the discrepancy between successive policies
[22, 12, 18, 26, 27]. PPO replaces this constrained optimization with a clipped first-order surrogate, making it one of the dominant practical methods in deep RL
[20, 9, 16, 30]. Several subsequent works extend PPO by adapting the clipping range or by replacing the clipped objective with alternative proximal surrogates [6, 26, 27, 30]. These methods are designed to improve the stability of policy updates while preserving the computational advantages of first-order optimization [20]. Recent studies have also considered simple proximal objectives that regulate likelihood ratios more directly [6, 26, 27, 30]. Our method differs from this line of work in its underlying motivation. Specifically, it is motivated by the observation that the statistical regime of the importance-weighted surrogate is governed by the tail behavior of the ratio distribution. Accordingly, the proposed adaptation is induced by order statistics, rather than by a pointwise clipping rule alone.

The instability of importance-weighted estimators has long been recognized in the statistical literature [17, 24, 33, 25]. Extreme-value theory provides an asymptotic description of upper-tail behavior through threshold exceedances, which are approximated by a generalized Pareto law under suitable regularity conditions [17]. Pareto-smoothed importance sampling uses this perspective to diagnose and stabilize importance-weighted estimators, with the fitted tail parameter serving as a concise summary of estimator reliability. In that line of work, the role of extreme-value modeling is primarily diagnostic or post hoc [24, 33, 25, 7]. Our use of this perspective is different. We do not fit a generalized Pareto model within each policy update, nor do we use tail estimates solely for diagnosis. Instead, we prescribe a tail profile, use it to construct order-statistic targets, and thereby obtain a simple proximal objective for policy optimization.

1. We identify a statistical limitation of pointwise ratio clipping in proximal policy optimization. Through a motivating analysis, we show that the tail behavior of the likelihood ratio distribution governs the estimator regime of the importance-weighted policy surrogate.

2. Motivated by this insight, we propose an order-statistic-based proximal objective. This objective regulates the empirical upper and lower tails of the ratio distribution by inducing adaptive, sample-wise radii derived from prescribed tail targets, yielding a method that is straightforward to implement.

3. Empirically, we demonstrate that this simple modification yields strong performance on standard deep RL benchmarks, including MuJoCo and Atari.

title: HaNDF: Object-Conditioned Geometric Neural Hand Distance Fields
authors: Zuhao Liu,Melih Darcan,Zhengdi Yu,Riza Alp Guler,Tolga Birdal
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
abstract:
We propose, HaNDF, object-conditional neural distance fields as data-driven priors for modeling the plausible hand–object configurations, in the product manifold of hand articulations.
While recent unconditional generative priors showed success in modeling human pose, hands are versatile articulated bodies often found in interaction with other objects. This makes it crucial to develop a generative prior which can model the plausible hand poses conditioned on the object under interaction. To this end, our HaNDF proposes a geometry-aware, object-conditioned neural distance field, representing the plausible articulations in the zero-level set of a conditional field. We leverage tools from Riemannian geometry to (i) represent plausible hands in the zero level-set of an object-induced neural field, and (ii) project a given pose onto this field. Using HaNDF, we can also optimize for a plausible condition, determining the object under interaction.
Our extensive evaluations demonstrate that our HaNDF provides a flexible and powerful prior for hand–object interaction, suitable for applications such as pose refinement, reconstruction under occlusion, and physically plausible manipulation synthesis.
introduction:
Human hands are among the most versatile articulated systems, practicing rich and diverse interactions with objects. Modeling plausible hand–object configurations is therefore fundamental to applications in robotics, AR/VR, and 3D perception. Yet, recovering or generating such interactions from often partial observations remains challenging: the space of valid configurations is highly constrained, object-dependent, and non-Euclidean, where even small pose perturbations can lead to physically implausible grasps with interpenetration or loss of contact. A central requirement is thus a strong, queryable prior that encodes which hand poses are plausible given an object.

Existing approaches fall short of this goal. Generative models based on VAEs Rempe et al. (2021) or diffusion Shafir et al. (2023); Christen et al. (2024) learn distributions over poses or interactions, but operate in Euclidean latent spaces where distances lack geometric meaning, limiting their expressivity. Neural distance field Chibane et al. (2020) (NDF) variants such as PoseNDF Tiwari et al. (2022) or NRDF He et al. (2024) offer an alternative by modeling the manifold of plausible articulations directly and enabling projection via gradient descent. However, current NDF-based priors are human-body specific, unconditional, capture hand articulation independent of the object, and thus fail to encode interaction-specific constraints. Conversely, object-conditioned methods Kulkarni et al. (2024); Weng et al. (2023) typically treat articulation in Euclidean space or rely on task-specific pipelines, sacrificing geometric consistency. As a result, no existing approach provides a unified prior that is (i) geometry-aware, (ii) conditioned on object shape, and (iii) equipped with a meaningful distance for optimization.

HaNDF addresses this gap proposing a generative, object conditioned prior of hand poses. Our key insight is to model hand articulation on its intrinsic Riemannian manifold while treating the object as a conditioning signal that modulates the manifold of plausible configurations. Concretely, we learn a conditional distance field that predicts the geodesic distance to the nearest valid hand pose given object geometry, whose zero level set defines the object-specific interaction manifold. This formulation yields a continuous, geometry-aware energy landscape where Riemannian gradients provide principled projection, refinement, and sampling directly on the articulation manifold.
This perspective unifies multiple applications under a single framework without retraining: denoising, recovering physically consistent grasps from data, and generation of novel grasps. When integrated into reconstruction pipelines, HaNDF acts as a plug-and-play prior, improving robustness under occlusion without retraining task-specific models, as validated across three challenging benchmarks: HOI4D Liu et al. (2022), OakInk Yang et al. (2022), and DexYCB Chao et al. (2021).
In summary, our contributions are:

We introduce HaNDF, an object-conditioned Riemannian neural distance field for hand articulation, whose zero-level set defines a family of object-dependent plausibility manifolds.

We develop an object-specific distance-field training procedure with per-object latent fitting and nearest-pose supervision, together with a transformer architecture that jointly processes hand-joint and object tokens.

Based upon NRDF’s RDF-Grad, we enable object-conditioned projection, denoising, completion, and generation of MANO hand poses, and introduce an inversion procedure to retrieve and refine compatible object conditions.

1. We introduce HaNDF, an object-conditioned Riemannian neural distance field for hand articulation, whose zero-level set defines a family of object-dependent plausibility manifolds.

2. We develop an object-specific distance-field training procedure with per-object latent fitting and nearest-pose supervision, together with a transformer architecture that jointly processes hand-joint and object tokens.

3. Based upon NRDF’s RDF-Grad, we enable object-conditioned projection, denoising, completion, and generation of MANO hand poses, and introduce an inversion procedure to retrieve and refine compatible object conditions.

title: Open-HumanWAM: An Open Recipe for Scaling Human and Robot Experience for Embodied Foundation Models
authors: Juncheng Ma,Jiaxin Li,Jiankai Tu,Bo Liang,Guodong Lv,Yufan Deng,Junzhe Tang,Liangzhu Yang,Chen Bian,Shukai Gong,Yintianrun Zhang,Zicong Cao,Baohao Zhu,Jianxin Bi,Tengfei Yan,Yinyuan Zhang,Kewei Zhang,Xinglong Chen,Kaiqi Chen,Duomin Wang,Xiaotian Tang,Liang Tan,Li Li,Yuan Xu,Haosen Yang,Yuqi Wang,Jingfei Xia,Songyan Huang,Zhiyang Dou,Zhen Dong,Enze Xie,Tat-Seng Chua,Daquan Zhou
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)

abstract: Egocentric human video offers a scalable source of manipulation priors for robot learning, yet translating raw data scale into generalizable robot policies demands rigorous data curation and training recipes. We introduce Open-HumanWAM, the first fully open recipe for scaling egocentric pretraining to 50,000 hours, anchored by Open-HumanWAM-50K—a curated egocentric video corpus densely annotated with hand motion and natural language. Leveraging this corpus, we systematically investigate pure human pretraining via closed-loop simulation evaluations and uncover an empirical log-linear scaling law linking pretraining data hours to downstream robot success rates. Grounded in these findings, we develop HumanWAM-Vanilla, a world–action model pretrained exclusively on 50k hours of egocentric human video. Upon robot post-training, HumanWAM-Vanilla reaches 92.08% success on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean2Clean and 68.88% on Clean2Random, alongside a 14.17% mean success rate and a 19.00 mean progress score on RoboDojo. To push the capability frontier further, we explore joint human–robot pretraining with HumanWAM-Goal, a visual-goal-conditioned world–action model. Hybrid data scaling unlocks broad zero-shot generalization across both simulation and physical benchmarks, propelling post-trained RoboTwin 2.0 performance to new state-of-the-art levels: 92.70% on Clean2Clean and a substantial leap to 84.60% on Clean2Random. On physical robots, HumanWAM-Goal further exhibits emergent embodied in-context learning, dynamically adapting its manipulation behavior to unseen visual goals without parameter updates. To support reproducible scaling research in embodied AI, we open-source the Open-HumanWAM-50K corpus, data curation and pretraining pipelines, alongside the pretrained and post-trained HumanWAM checkpoints, inference code, and simulation evaluation suites.
introduction:
Learning from human manipulation offers a scalable path toward general-purpose robot intelligence [22, 73, 33]. Robot foundation models require diverse manipulation experience to acquire skills that transfer across tasks and environments, but collecting this experience through teleoperation is costly [23, 22]. Egocentric videos paired with hand-motion and language annotations offer a rich record of human interactions with objects across diverse scenes and tasks [20, 43]. However, developing effective egocentric pretraining recipes that consistently improve downstream robot performance as data scale remains under investigation.

Previous work has demonstrated the value of human experience for robot learning. EgoScale [73] shows that large-scale human motion pretraining improves dexterous robot manipulation, while Being-H0.8 [4] extends egocentric pretraining to joint visual and tactile world modeling. HumanScale [33] further shows that, after robot post-training, validation action loss on held-out real-robot trajectories decreases log-linearly with egocentric pretraining hours. Dyna-2 [14] extends egocentric pretraining to one million hours and reports a scaling law in zero-shot robot action prediction, with corresponding improvements in robot task performance after post-training. These studies establish the empirical value of egocentric scaling, motivating further analysis of data diversity and the robot supervision required for downstream adaptation.

We present Open-HumanWAM, a fully open recipe for scaling egocentric pretraining for robot learning. Within a unified world–action model framework, we explore pretraining exclusively on 100 to 50,000 hours of human egocentric data, using a common robot post-training protocol and closed-loop simulation for controlled and reproducible comparisons of downstream robot task success. With curated data and a unified action representation, we observe an empirical log-linear scaling law relating pretraining hours to out-of-distribution success rates across two different attention configurations. Beyond duration, data diversity is a key scaling dimension, as expanding task and scene coverage alongside duration produces steeper scaling curves than increasing duration at fixed coverage. Larger-scale egocentric pretraining also improves the sample efficiency of robot adaptation, yielding higher success rates at matched demonstration budgets.

Following this recipe, we develop HumanWAM-Vanilla, a vanilla world–action model pretrained exclusively on 50,000 hours of egocentric human data. After robot post-training, HumanWAM-Vanilla achieves 92.08% success on RoboTwin 2.0 [9] Clean2Clean and 68.88% on Clean2Random, together with a mean success rate of 14.17% and a mean progress score of 19.00 on RoboDojo [8]. The improvements extend to physical robots across multi-step, deformable-object, and long-horizon manipulation tasks. Under changes in tablecloth and lighting, mean success across four tasks increases from 2.5% without egocentric pretraining to 67.5% with HumanWAM-Vanilla, demonstrating stronger generalization.

To further push the model capability boundary, we extend our exploration to joint human-robot pretraining and propose HumanWAM-Goal, a world–action model with visual-goal conditioning. Human data provide broad manipulation experience, while robot data ground this experience in embodiment-specific perception and control [73, 25]. Visual goals specify desired object configurations and spatial relationships, providing task context for zero-shot execution.
With the specially designed unified action representation, HumanWAM-Goal architecture, and the hybrid training recipe, the co-trained model supports out-of-the-box execution without parameter updates during deployment.
We evaluate data scaling by expanding the robot corpus and the human data. The performance scaling trend persists in this hybrid data setting. On physical robots, adding 45.9k hours of human data to a fixed 14.6k-hour robot corpus increases mean zero-shot success across 20 tasks from 20.0% to 30.5%. On RoboTwin 2.0, HumanWAM-Goal achieves 13.94% mean zero-shot success rate. After post-training, it reaches 92.70% on Clean2Clean and 84.60% on Clean2Random, yielding a state-of-the-art average success rate of 88.65% on RoboTwin 2.0.

HumanWAM-Goal exhibits an emergent capacity for embodied in-context learning through visual goals. In real-robot experiments, the same policy adapts its execution to different desired outcomes specified by goal images without parameter updates. This capability is already present after joint pretraining and is retained when the model is post-trained for more complex, multi-step manipulation. Post-trained policies also follow goals depicted in egocentric human images, indicating that task-relevant spatial relationships can guide robot behavior across differences in embodiment and visual appearance.

To support reproducible scaling research in embodied AI, we open-source the Open-HumanWAM-50K corpus, data curation and pretraining pipelines, alongside the pretrained and post-trained HumanWAM checkpoints, inference code, and simulation evaluation suites. Open-HumanWAM-50K is a curated and aligned 50,000-hour egocentric pretraining corpus with hand-motion and language annotations, and our experiments demonstrate consistent gains in downstream robot generalization as pretraining on this corpus scales, with out-of-distribution success rates following an empirical log-linear scaling law.

The main contributions of this work are as follows:

A systematic study of egocentric scaling for robot generalization. We present Open-HumanWAM, a fully open recipe for scaling pure egocentric pretraining from 100 to 50k hours. We identify an empirical log-linear scaling law in downstream robot task success rates and systematically analyze the benefits of egocentric scaling for robot generalization and adaptation. Building on this recipe, we develop HumanWAM-Vanilla, which achieves success rates of 92.08% on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean2Clean and 68.88% on Clean2Random after robot post-training, alongside competitive performance on RoboDojo.

Emerging robot capabilities through hybrid human–robot data scaling. With HumanWAM-Goal, we show that scaling joint human–robot pretraining improves zero-shot task execution in simulation and on physical robots. The model also exhibits embodied in-context learning, adapting its behavior to visual goals without parameter updates. After robot post-training, HumanWAM-Goal achieves a state-of-the-art average success rate of 88.65% on RoboTwin 2.0, with 92.70% on Clean2Clean and 84.60% on Clean2Random.

A full-stack release for reproducible scaling research. We provide the complete resources for reproducing our scaling studies and HumanWAM models. The release includes Open-HumanWAM-50K, a curated and aligned 50k-hour egocentric corpus with hand-motion and language annotations, together with training code, model checkpoints and evaluation protocols.

1. 论文核心任务概括  
该论文提出了Open-HumanWAM，一个开放的预训练框架，旨在通过大规模的自我中心人类视频数据来提升机器人在操控任务中的表现。通过对50,000小时的自我中心视频进行预训练，论文展示了如何利用人类操作经验来提高机器人的适应性和任务成功率，并探讨了联合人类和机器人预训练的潜力。

2. 是否属于 World Model：是  
理由：论文中提到的“world–action model”框架核心在于学习如何通过人类的操作经验来预测机器人在不同任务中的表现，这符合World Model的定义，即学习世界如何随动作演化，并用于未来状态的预测和规划。

3. 是否属于 VLA：是  
理由：论文中提到的输入数据包括带有手部动作和自然语言注释的自我中心视频，这表明模型的输入同时包含视觉（视频）和语言（注释），而输出是机器人动作，因此符合VLA的定义。

4. 是否属于 Humanoid Loco-manipulation：是  
理由：论文的机器人平台涉及到物理机器人，并且任务同时包含了操控（manipulation）和运动（locomotion），需要协调全身动作，因此符合Humanoid Loco-manipulation的标准。

5. 最终标签总结  
该论文属于World Model、VLA和Humanoid Loco-manipulation。

6. 如果有歧义，请说明最容易混淆的点  
最容易混淆的点在于“world–action model”与传统的World Model之间的区别。虽然它们都涉及到状态预测和动作规划，但本论文强调了通过人类经验来进行预训练的独特性，这可能让人误以为它不完全符合World Model的定义。
